What the research showed is that the manner of practice decides the level; hours are only correlated with it. A demanding result became a comfortable permit: put the time in and you qualify. That is precisely the half he was arguing against. Ten years of experience, or one year ten times — Time served is not skill. Most roles stop generating new difficulty after the first year or two, and the years after that are repetition wearing a longer title. The honest question about anybody's growth is when they were last out of their depth. The threshold is different in every field — Deliberate practice is strongest where the rules hold still and the feedback comes back fast: instruments, chess, surgery. Where results arrive late and luck is loud, hours explain much less. One number cannot cross those boundaries. Change the method before you add the hours — The practical damage of the rule is that it sends people to spend more rather than to practise differently. When you are stuck, the variable with room left in it is the structure of the session, not its length. Where you are: you have put a long stretch into something and the results are flat. Ask first: when were you last
q: There is nothing special or magical about ten thousand hours.
The manner of practice decides the level. Hours are only correlated.

chapters.n: Good at hurdles, bad at choosing a road
chapters.w: Two completely different abilities
chapters.dek: Why people who succeeded at every stage go blank the moment the standards stop. What they never practised.
chapters.txt: Deresiewicz taught at Yale for ten years and sat on admissions. What he saw was young people extraordinarily good at clearing set hurdles — grades, competitions, internships, the CV — and unable to say what they wanted. They were superb at clearing hurdles and could not tell you where they were going. His typical scene: an outstanding student who has no idea why she chose the subject, only that she had to be best at it. He insists this isn't a personal failing. Someone optimised since childhood to meet every standard has never once practised deciding what matters. The two abilities don't substitute — 'Be the best at this' and 'decide what's worth doing' are different skills. The first is drilled constantly inside any evaluation system. The second can only be trained where there is no correct answer — so the smoother the run, the likelier the second is blank. Never having failed makes failure unimaginable — The price of an unbroken run is no experience of failing, so failure gets imagined as catastrophic. The result is avoiding anything you might not be good at, and a range that narrows year by year. The target is the system, not the students — The book reads easily as blaming young people for lacking independence. The author's subject is the filtering machinery that trains them this way — every step rational, and the sum a life with no direction. Where you are: you know exactly what counts as doing well, and can't answer what you want. Ask first: is this choice what
q: Superb at clearing hurdles, and unable to say where they were going.
Never allowed to fail, you imagine failure as unsurvivable.

chapters.n: Give yourself time with no scoreboard
chapters.w: Any standard becomes a thing to optimise
chapters.dek: How to find out what you actually want. The condition that has to be true first.
chapters.txt: Deresiewicz's prescription isn't a new major or a new job. It's a stretch of time with no evaluation attached — doing one thing that isn't scored, for long enough. The reasoning is direct: only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you actually want. Where a standard exists, people optimise it automatically, and the optimising drowns out the signal about whether you want to do this at all. The problem isn't that you can't think it through. It's that no environment lets the question surface. A score existing means you'll chase it — This isn't weak will, it's the default. Wherever there's a comparable metric, attention slides to it. So answering 'what do I want' requires temporarily leaving the places that have metrics. It only works if it's long enough — A few days tests novelty. The signal that counts is whether you still want to continue after the novelty has gone and it's got a bit boring. He's describing months, not a couple of weekends. Separate 'I want this' from 'this is the next hurdle' — This is the usable daily test. Facing an opportunity, ask whether what draws you is the content itself or the fact that it's the obvious next step on the current track. The second disguises itself very well as the first. Where you are: you're making a choice about direction. Ask first: is it the content that draws me, or is it simply the next hurdle? Have I done anything unscored lately? Where it goes wrong: reading it as a reason
q: Only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you want.
Wherever a comparable metric exists, attention slides to it.

chapters.w: Buy it when nobody wants it
chapters.dek: When is a thing cheapest? At the moment everybody agrees it is useless.
chapters.txt: Among the strategies Fan Li's teacher gave the state of Yue is one very simple rule: in drought, stock boats; in flood, stock carts; and so be ready for the shortage. In a drought nobody wants a boat and the price is lowest; after drought comes flood, and then a boat is dearest. He generalised it into a law of price: examine surplus and shortage and you know dear from cheap. What is dear to the extreme turns down; what is cheap to the extreme turns up. So sell the dear as if it were dung, and take the cheap as if it were pearls. Buy when the demand has gone — Price is set by present demand; value by future demand. The entire difficulty of this rule is that at the moment of buying, every visible piece of evidence says the thing is worthless. A decision with no evidence behind it is exactly what the method requires. The cycle is the premise. Not everything comes back — Drought and flood alternate, which is what makes stocking boats correct. If a decline is structural and won't return, buying cheap is catching a falling knife. Before using the rule you have to judge: is this a cycle or an ending? Money has to keep moving — There's a line of his that gets skipped: money should flow like water. What you stockpile is goods, not capital. Locking your funds in one place to wait for an appreciation is no different from burying them in the ground. Where you are: something is
q: In drought, stock boats. In flood, stock carts.
Sell the dear like dung. Take the cheap like pearls.

chapters.n: Long neck, beak like a bird
chapters.w: Read the ending off the person
chapters.dek: He left the moment Yue destroyed Wu, at the highest point. What he was reading when he decided.
chapters.txt: With Wu destroyed, Fan Li left at once and took a boat onto the lakes. He wrote to Wen Zhong, who stayed, and his reasoning was not about the situation but about the man: the king of Yue has a long neck and a beak like a bird's; you can share hardship with him, you cannot share ease. Wen Zhong stayed, and was later ordered to kill himself. Fan Li changed his name, went into trade in Qi, made a vast fortune, was offered the chancellorship, returned the seal, gave the fortune away, started again at Tao, and made and dispersed a fortune three times. Reading the person beats reading the situation — Situations change; a person's construction doesn't. Fan Li's judgement wasn't 'this is dangerous now' but 'here is what this man becomes when things go well' — a judgement that already held before Wu fell. It was just not yet needed. Sharing hardship and sharing ease are different capacities — The precision is in separating two relationships. People who carried something together can't necessarily divide something together. The first is held by a common enemy; the second demands restraint in dividing gains — far rarer, and only visible after the win. Letting go is harder than accumulating — He built a great fortune three times and gave it away three times. This wasn't a performance of generosity — returning the chancellor's seal in Qi, starting again at Tao, each time he abandoned a position already in hand. Many can accumulate. Almost nobody puts down what they already hold.
q: You can share hardship with him. You cannot share ease.
Three times he made a fortune, and three times gave it away.

chapters.n: Only the emperor can save them
chapters.w: If you cannot change it, change the sentence
chapters.dek: The Khitan have destroyed the dynasty and the plain expects a massacre. What can a man with no army do in that room?
chapters.txt: The Later Jin fell, the Khitan ruler Yelu Deguang entered Kaifeng, and the population faced plunder and slaughter. Feng Dao went to see him. Yelu Deguang asked: the common people of the empire, how can they be saved? Feng Dao answered: at this moment the Buddha could come again and not save them; only the emperor can save them. The Comprehensive Mirror records that the people of the plain escaped destruction because of that one sentence. It contains no argument at all. It re-describes a decision as something only he is large enough to make. When persuasion is impossible, change what the act is — Preaching mercy to a man who has just conquered you asks him to concede that he is in the wrong. Feng Dao argued nothing. He moved stopping the killing from you must back down to only you are able to. Same action, and one of them is a display of power. With no chips left, wording is the variable — He had no troops, no territory and nothing to trade. In an asymmetry that complete, the phrasing is the only thing still under his control. This is not a belief in clever talk. It is a reminder that even at zero leverage there remains one place where work can be done. What he preserved was people, not his name — Going to meet the conqueror at all was enough to earn him centuries of contempt, and it duly did. He chose an outcome that can be counted, the number of people not killed, and gave
q: The Buddha could come again and not save them. Only the emperor can.
The people of the plain were spared because of one sentence.

chapters.n: The old man of everlasting joy
chapters.w: A thousand years of argument
chapters.dek: He served four dynasties and ten emperors and named himself after contentment. The question is where his accusers and his defenders each stand.
chapters.txt: In his seventies he wrote An Account of the Old Man of Everlasting Joy, listing every office he had held, in a calm tone, saying that thinking over beginnings and ends he understood the way of heaven better. Ouyang Xiu called him a man without shame. Sima Guang called him the worst of treacherous ministers. Wang Anshi thought him a man at the level of a buddha, and Su Shi said he could bend himself to keep people safe. A thousand years, and both sides cite the same facts. The quarrel is about the object of loyalty — Ouyang Xiu's standard is loyalty to one house. Feng Dao's is loyalty to the people under the administration. The identical conduct is shameless serial betrayal under the first and steady adaptation under the second. The argument runs a thousand years because it was never about the facts. In a broken order, continuity is the scarce thing — Fifty-three years produced five dynasties and fourteen emperors, an average reign shorter than a decade. At that frequency, a man who preserved the administration, the tax registers and the un-sacked cities through every handover was supplying something rare. His critics wrote from inside a restored order. And he prevented nothing — The defence has a limit. He saved many people and altered not one succession, and left no institution behind. His method was minimising loss inside a settled frame, and the ceiling of that method is that it produces nothing new. On this point Ouyang Xiu was right. Where you are: somebody's choices leave you
q: Thinking over beginnings and ends, I understand the way of heaven better.
Ouyang Xiu called him shameless. Sima Guang called him the worst of traitors.

chapters.n: The first person not to fool is you
chapters.w: And you are the easiest one
chapters.dek: He put this ahead of every method in science. This page is about why the first line of defence points inward.
chapters.txt: At the 1974 Caltech commencement he gave the graduates one rule and called it the first principle: you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Twelve years later he sat on the Challenger commission, asked for a glass of ice water at a televised hearing, clamped a piece of the O-ring rubber, dropped it in for a few seconds and took it out. It did not spring back. NASA had hundreds of pages arguing the launch was sound. His appendix said reality must take precedence over public relations. The bias sits wherever your interest sits — Fooling yourself takes no dishonesty, only a stake. Wherever you would prefer a conclusion, your efficiency at finding supporting evidence rises sharply. So the check is not how honest you feel. It is whether the answer pays you. Write the disconfirming column first — The order changes the content. Write down what would show you are wrong before you write the support, and both columns come out more honest. Reverse it and you have already chosen a side by the time the second column starts. When the report and the world disagree, change the report — Challenger was not a shortage of engineering. It was an organisation that preferred a document. This holds anywhere there is a reporting line: if the reflex when numbers look bad is to adjust the wording, the problem has simply been forwarded. Where you are: assessing something you have a stake in. Ask first: does this conclusion pay me? If it does, how hard
q: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself.
And you are the easiest person to fool.

chapters.n: If you cannot teach it, you have not got it
chapters.w: Jargon is where the hole hides
chapters.dek: The internet sells this as a study hack in four steps. This page is about the harder claim sitting underneath it.
chapters.txt: David Goodstein once asked him to explain why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics. Feynman sized up his listener and said he would prepare a freshman lecture on it. He came back a few days later. I couldn't reduce it to the freshman level, he said, and that means we don't really understand it. The sentence everyone quotes about explaining things simply is not in his writing. What is documented is this, and the line found on his blackboard when he died: what I cannot create, I do not understand. Ban the jargon and the hole shows at once — A technical term is a compression, and compression only works if both sides can unpack it. Forbid the term and you have to unpack it yourself. Wherever you cannot, you were storing a label rather than an understanding. Deriving it once beats memorising it ten times — A remembered conclusion works on the question it came from. A derivation works on the whole class of questions, because on the way through you collide with why it could not have been otherwise. Those collisions are the structure of understanding. Teaching is the test, not the favour — The usual reading is that explaining helps the listener. His use runs the other way: he explained in order to find out whether he knew. Which means the more ignorant the audience, the better the instrument. Where you are: you think you understand something and are not certain. Ask first: without one term of art, can you take an outsider to the point of
q: I couldn't reduce it to the freshman level.
That means we don't really understand it.

chapters.w: Work out which one you are in
chapters.dek: The first sentence of the book is the whole conclusion. What the two categories save you from getting wrong.
chapters.txt: Carse opens with the entire thesis: there are at least two kinds of games, and a finite game is played for the purpose of winning, an infinite game for the purpose of continuing the play. A finite game has a start, a finish and a winner — a match, an election, a lawsuit. An infinite game has no end, its rules can change, and the only object is to keep it going — a culture, a marriage, a craft, a company that means to last. Confusing them produces two symmetrical mistakes. First ask whether there is a final whistle — Sorting comes before anything else. Does this have a defined end and a winner? A negotiation, a tender, a quarter are finite and deserve everything you have. A client relationship, a team, your own reputation are not scored that way at all. Finite tactics inside an infinite game spend the game — Beating people inside something unending consumes the players: suppliers crushed, staff drained, peers turned into enemies. Win every round and eventually nobody sits down with you, and in an infinite game no opponent means no game. Dragging out a finite game is the other way to lose — Treating something built to end as endless costs just as much: a lawsuit past its stopping point, a project that should close, a partnership renewed forever under the heading of giving it more time. Accepting the whistle is what frees your hands. Where you are: you are fighting something very hard, or you have been dragging something out for a
q: There are at least two kinds of games.
A finite game is played for the purpose of winning.

chapters.w: Rules are props, not walls
chapters.dek: The two kinds of player treat rules in opposite ways. What separates changing the rules from simply cheating.
chapters.txt: Carse sets the two players against each other. The rules of a finite game are fixed before play and may not change, because their whole job is to let the game produce a winner. The rules of an infinite game must change during play, and the only test of a change is whether more people can keep playing. Finite players treat rules as walls and strain inside them; infinite players treat them as props. Whoever must win is the one the rules will trap. Finite players train to be powerful; infinite players stay flexible. The right to change a rule comes from wanting play to continue — Changing rules and cheating look identical from outside. The difference is who benefits: change it so you win this round and it is cheating; change it so the play can continue and it is the infinite player's job. Ask whether the change widened the field or narrowed it. The sign the rules own you is that you only win by them — The longer you win inside one set of rules, the more your ability grows into the shape of those rules. Rankings, reviews and algorithms change, and years of accumulation reset. The defence is a standing question: if these rules were replaced tomorrow, what would I still have? Power is for what you have seen, flexibility for what you have not — Training to be strong prepares you for matches already played. Staying flexible admits that the match that matters has not happened yet. The two need different reserves: one is doing
q: The rules of an infinite game must change in the course of play.
Whoever must play, cannot play.

chapters.w: Where the sentence was collected matters as much as the sentence
chapters.dek: Written from a study it would be a maxim. The question worth asking is where the evidence for it was gathered.
chapters.txt: He was a psychiatrist in Vienna. In 1942 the whole family was deported; his parents, his brother and his pregnant wife all died in the camps. The central claim comes out of what he watched there: everything can be taken from a man but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances. The evidence is specific. We who lived in concentration camps can remember the men who walked through the huts comforting others, giving away their last piece of bread. There were few of them. Few is enough. It is an observation report, not a slogan — The same paragraph on a calendar is uplift. As a field note out of a camp it is data. He is reporting the result of a lower-bound experiment: with external conditions pressed to the floor of human experience, the capacity to choose an attitude was still there. In a minority, but there. Two battlefields, and only one of them was lost — The prisoners handing over bread could not change their situation. What they changed was who they were inside it. Those are separate fields: on the first they lost everything, and the second stayed entirely theirs. Telling the two apart is what gives a hopeless position somewhere to start. He made himself one of the subjects — In the camp he kept picturing himself after the war at a lectern, lecturing on the psychology of the camps, converting the suffering he was inside into material for work not yet done. Not self-deception:
q: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing.
To choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances.

chapters.w: Some targets disappear the moment you aim at them
chapters.dek: The people who make happiness the goal are the ones who miss it. The mechanism he gives, and the route around it.
chapters.txt: He puts it plainly. Success, like happiness, cannot be pursued; it must ensue. One must have a reason to be happy, and the reason does not live inside happiness. His instruction to his students is the same one: do not aim at success, because the more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it. In the clinic he kept meeting the reverse case — the harder someone forces sleep the longer they lie awake, and the closer they monitor their own happiness the more anxious they get. Some states are readings, not activities — Happiness, relaxation, confidence, being liked. What they have in common is that they are gauges on a process rather than the process. Chasing the gauge is breathing on the thermometer to warm the room. His clinical name for it is hyper-reflection: monitoring the state is what wrecks it. The route around it is the reason — If happiness needs a reason, then the reason is the thing to work on: something worth going into, one particular person you are answerable to. Get that in place and the state settles itself as a side effect. His whole therapy is built on the turn — treat the reason, not the symptom. The same holds for organisations — A team that manages morale, happiness and belonging as targets in their own right collects performed readings. Those are by-products of having done something that mattered, and a by-product cannot be manufactured directly. It only arrives through the actual product. Where you
q: Success, like happiness, cannot be pursued; it must ensue.
The unintended side-effect of one's personal dedication to a cause greater than oneself.

chapters.w: Even character has to be put on a schedule
chapters.dek: He drew up thirteen virtues, then did the thing nobody resolving to improve ever does. The design of the little book.
chapters.txt: In his twenties he listed thirteen virtues, temperance through humility. The list is not the interesting part; the execution design is. I judged it would be well not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once, but to fix it on one of them at a time. One virtue a week, the other twelve merely recorded and not demanded. A little book, a page per virtue, ruled into columns, examined every evening, a black spot for each fault. Thirteen weeks a course, four courses a year. He admits his scheme of Order gave him the most trouble. Working on thirteen is working on none — Attention is the only scarce resource in the system. Run everything at once and each item gets a thirteenth of it, nowhere near the strength required for anything to become a habit. Serial is not the slow way round. It is the only way anything accumulates. Record the faults, not the wins — What goes into the book is failure: a mark for every breach. That makes the evening check objective and cheap. You never have to appraise how well the day went, only answer whether it happened. Countable failures drive change harder than a vague sense of progress. The spots never came out and the system still ran — He kept at it for life and the Order column always had marks on it. A man buying an axe wanted the whole face bright, turned the grindstone a while, and decided he liked a speckled axe best. Franklin admits he is that
q: Not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once.
My scheme of Order gave me the most trouble.

chapters.w: He changed the sentence, not the opinion
chapters.dek: Somebody told him to his face that he was insufferable. What he changed was not what he thought but how he phrased it.
chapters.txt: The young Franklin loved to argue and won everywhere. A Quaker friend told him kindly that he was generally thought proud, overbearing and rather insolent, and gave him instances. He took it, and the remedy is unusually specific. I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction to the sentiment of others, and all positive assertion of my own. He banned the words: certainly, undoubtedly. In their place — I conceive, I apprehend, I imagine a thing to be so, or it so appears to me at present. He kept it fifty years. Changing the phrasing is doable; changing the character is not — Become humble is character engineering with no delivery date. Ban two words and substitute three phrases is a rule you can keep this afternoon. He did not wait to feel different — he started at the outermost operable layer. The sentences changed, the exchanges followed, and the character came last. An assertion forces a defence; a conjecture leaves a way in — It is certainly this turns the conversation into a win and a loss: the other person concedes or fights, and most fight. I conceive it to be this lets them add, correct, half-agree. They need not admit error in order to come closer to you, and lowering that cost is half of persuasion. Winning the argument and getting it done are different aims — What he wanted when young was refutation, and refuted people do not help you afterwards. Very few of those who go quiet have been persuaded; most have merely stopped
q: I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction.
I conceive, I apprehend, or I imagine a thing to be so.

chapters.w: Years of study, and not one word legible
chapters.dek: Years of hard study turn out to be the wrong thing. What he did the day after he found out.
chapters.txt: He was in his early twenties in Osaka, studying Dutch, which was then Japan's only window on the West, and he was very good at it. In 1859 he walked into the newly opened port of Yokohama and could not read a single sign on the street. They were all in English. He wrote later that it landed like a blow to the head: years of work, useless in this harbour. He did not go back to his Dutch. The next day he began hunting for English textbooks and started again from nothing. Useless is information, not a verdict — He did not write those years off, and he did not defend them by studying harder. He read the signs as a report on the wind: what has changed is the direction, not your capacity. Once the direction is clear, where the effort should go is obvious. Switch the same week, not next year — He began the day after he got home. Years of sunk cost make the instinct to give the old thing a little longer almost irresistible, and every day of waiting adds another chip to the track you are leaving. He simply started the new one at once. The old study was not wasted; refusing to switch is — He said afterwards that what he had built learning Dutch carried straight over: how to take a sentence apart, how to hold vocabulary, how to find someone to practise on. The content of a craft expires. The method you built while learning it does not. Where you
q: What is useless tells you the direction, not your capacity.
Every day of waiting adds another chip to the old track.

chapters.w: Learn what you will use tomorrow first
chapters.dek: What to study, and whether to keep studying. What he put ahead of the Confucian classics, and the reason he gave.
chapters.txt: An Encouragement of Learning opens by asking what learning even is. Not the memorising of difficult old texts, he answers, but practical learning: letter writing, bookkeeping, the abacus, reading a map, some physics and economics, the things you need every single day. He put those ahead of the Confucian classics, and his reason was blunt. A person has to be able to feed himself and finish what is in front of him before anything else is worth discussing. The pamphlets sold over three million copies, mostly to young people who did not know what to study. Sort by how often you will use it — His ordering rule has one term in it: frequency of use. Daily first, once a year later, someday last. He is not saying the later ones do not matter. He is saying a beginner has limited hours and should get fluent in the daily ones first. Feeding yourself is the first gate — Independence is the word he keeps returning to. Someone who does not live off other people can afford to have his own judgement. So what you learn early should serve that one thing: earn, deliver, ask nobody. Past that gate, nothing you study is frightening. Keep reading only if it lands in your hands — He is not against books. He is against reading something you cannot use and calling that study. Whether to continue is not settled by the level of the qualification but by whether the reading arrives as something you can now do. Where you are: you cannot tell
q: Learn what you need tomorrow first. Once a year can wait.
Learn what lets you stand, then what lets you travel.

chapters.n: Heaven creates no man above another
chapters.w: The gap is in study, not in birth
chapters.dek: You suspect you were born with less. Why the book opens on that sentence, and what its second half actually claims.
chapters.txt: The first line of An Encouragement of Learning: Heaven does not create one man above or below another man. Nobody arrives ranked. But he goes straight to the harder question. Then why is the real world so unequal? His answer is not consolation. He puts the cause somewhere a person can reach: the difference comes down to whether you studied. Not fate, not birth. In 1872 Japan this was incendiary, since the hereditary status system had only just been abolished and most people still believed in ranks. The gap was made after birth, which is why it can be closed. Move the cause somewhere you can reach — The worst thing about I was born with less is not that it might be false. It is that it parks the cause where nothing can be done. He moves it to whether you studied. That may not be the whole truth, but it moves, and a movable cause gives you work. He is better usually means he is earlier — Most of the difference he saw came from the order in which people met things, not from what they were born with. Someone looks steady because they practised something three years before you did. Translate stronger into earlier and most of the anxiety goes. Born with less is the cheapest explanation, so watch it — The moment that explanation is accepted, nothing further is required of you, because it was settled at birth. He objects to it not only because it is wrong but because it is so convenient. The more
q: Heaven does not create one man above or below another man.
The gap was made after birth, so it can be closed.

chapters.w: Pick a target nobody has to explain
chapters.dek: How do you take on an empire, and where? This is why the smallest item on the list was the right place to start.
chapters.txt: In 1930 Congress was arguing about how to run non-cooperation. Tariffs, land tax, self-rule: all of it large and complicated. Gandhi picked salt. British law monopolised its manufacture and taxed it, and every Indian ate it every day. On 12 March he left the ashram with 78 followers and walked 24 days and 240 miles to the sea at Dandi, where he bent down and lifted a lump of natural salt. With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire. Tens of thousands were arrested for making their own. Shrink the issue until it needs no explaining — Tariffs and self-rule take a speech to explain. Salt takes none, because every tongue already knows it. The ceiling on mobilisation is set not by how important an issue is but by the lowest effort needed to understand it. Choosing the issue is choosing how many can join. Pick the target that traps the other side — The salt tax raised very little, but arresting people for picking up salt looked appalling. Tens of thousands of ordinary arrests turned each act of enforcement into publicity for the movement. A good target makes repression costly and permission fatal. The 24 days of walking were part of the work — He could have taken a car to the coast and picked up salt the same afternoon. Walking made every village on the route a venue, gave the papers 24 days of running coverage, and let attention gather. Slowness here was not a cost, it was amplification. Where you are: you want to
q: With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire.
Nonviolence is the weapon of the strong.

chapters.w: However you win is what you get
chapters.dek: If the cause is right, can the method be rough? He closed the question in 1909 with a single image.
chapters.txt: In Hind Swaraj a reader asks Gandhi what is wrong with violence if it gets the British out. His answer is a comparison: the means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree, and the connection between means and end is as inviolable as the one between seed and tree. Sow a poisonous seed and no rose comes up. He follows it through. An India taken by force will be governed by people who are good at force, and that, he says, is English rule without the Englishman. How you won gets written into what you won — The method does not retire on the day it succeeds. It becomes the organising material of whatever comes next. Whatever capability won the fight is the capability the winners admire, and reward and promotion follow it from then on. Just this once has no once — Adopting a method is a one-way door. Once it has worked it is in the toolbox, and things in the toolbox come out by themselves at the next difficult moment. Only this time is, in practice, a long-stay visa issued to the method. The test of the end is applied to the means — Stated ends cannot be checked, because everybody claims to want justice. The means are the only observable part of a purpose. A movement that promises freedom and cannot tolerate dissent inside itself has already shown you what it will build. Where you are: a method that would get you there quickly is available, and it is not clean. Ask
q: The means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree.
As is the means, so is the end.

chapters.w: Four signals that predict a breakup
chapters.dek: He watches fifteen minutes of one argument. This piece is about what he is actually watching.
chapters.txt: Gottman recorded thousands of couples talking, coded expression, tone and heart rate frame by frame, then tracked who divorced years later. What predicted a breakup wasn't how fiercely they fought but whether four signals appeared, which he called the four horsemen: criticism (attacking the person, not the act), contempt (sarcasm, eye-rolling), defensiveness (returning the blame) and stonewalling (shutting the other out). The single strongest predictor of divorce is contempt — and the research found it affects the recipient's immune function. Criticism and complaint are different things — A complaint targets behaviour: you didn't do the washing up and I'm exhausted. Criticism targets character: you're just lazy. The first can be solved; the second can only be defended. Many people think they're raising an issue while every sentence defines the other person, and so the same problem runs ten years. Contempt is a slow poison, not venting — Eye-rolling, mockery, mimicking their tone — all of it says I am above you. It differs from anger: anger is about the event, contempt says the person is unworthy. It's the strongest single predictor in his data because it destroys the foundation, not one conversation. Defensiveness returns the ball, it doesn't clarify — 'I've been busy, and so have you' looks like explaining and is a counter-attack. Its function is to refuse any share of responsibility, and once both sides are defending, the conversation becomes mutual evidence and never reaches a solution. Where you are: the same thing gets fought about and every round escalates. Ask first: was that last sentence about the
q: The strongest single predictor of divorce is contempt.
Criticism targets the person. A complaint targets the act.

chapters.w: Whether you fight matters less than whether you stop
chapters.dek: Healthy relationships argue fiercely too. So where do they differ from the ones that break.
chapters.txt: One of Gottman's counterintuitive findings: happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight, they're the ones who repair while fighting. He called the move of reaching for the brake mid-escalation a repair attempt — a joke, an offered way out, a 'wait, we've gone off topic'. In stable relationships repair attempts succeed more often, and not because the technique is better: because the other person is willing to take it. That willingness depends on the balance built up beforehand. He put a number on it — in stable relationships positive interactions run about five to one against negative. Repair succeeds or fails on the ordinary days — The same joke defuses things in a relationship with a healthy balance and reads as not taking it seriously in one that's overdrawn. So what decides whether a conflict can be stopped is the unremarkable responses, presence and small concessions of the past weeks. Technique in the moment mostly fails. Taking the offered way out is harder than offering it — Offering it risks being refused; taking it means giving up winning this round. Most relationships stick on the second: they heard it, and 'why should I be the one to let it go' stops them. Insisting on winning wins the round and loses the relationship. Five to one is a balance, not a formula — The ratio gets misused as licence to say one cruel thing per five kind ones. Gottman means the everyday texture of the relationship should be mostly positive, not that praise offsets attacks. An attack costs far more
q: Happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight. They repair.
In stable relationships, positives run about five to one.

chapters.w: A quote is a service, not a verdict
chapters.dek: He turns the entire market into one manic-depressive business partner. What that story actually unlocks is smaller and stranger than it looks.
chapters.txt: Chapter eight asks you to imagine a partner in a private business. His name is Mr. Market and he turns up every single day with a price, ready to buy your share or sell you his. His moods are extreme: elated, he names an absurd figure; depressed, he sells everything cheap. The part that matters comes next. He does not mind being ignored, and he is back tomorrow with a new quotation. Which makes him useful in proportion to how unstable he is, provided you use his prices rather than catch his mood. A quote is an option, not a grade — Most people read the tape as a live score on their own judgement, so a fall means they were wrong. The parable separates the two. A price is one man's mood today, and you have three responses: buy from him, sell to him, or ignore him. The third is where the initiative lives. Volatility is the service you are not charged for — An emotional partner is not the risk; he is the only source of your return. Without his depressions nothing is ever cheap, and without his manias nothing is ever dear. Complaining about swings is complaining that your one supplier keeps turning up for work. Do not let him do your valuation — The discipline sits in the fine print. Using his prices requires a valuation of your own, or you cannot tell a bargain from a trap and contrarianism decays into reflex. Whether he is servant or master depends on whether you brought your own
q: One of your partners, named Mr. Market, is very obliging indeed.
He is back again tomorrow with a new quotation.

chapters.w: The room you leave for being wrong
chapters.dek: He said the whole secret of sound investment fits in three words. The question is what those three words are actually buying.
chapters.txt: The last chapter of the book is the answer, and its title is the phrase. Distill the secret of sound investment into three words, he writes, and the motto is margin of safety. Pay fifty cents for a dollar of value, and the gap is not an expected profit. It is room for bad luck and for your own arithmetic being wrong. His definition of investing is colder still: thorough analysis, safety of principal, an adequate return, and anything short of that is speculation. Note the order. What you are buying is surviving your own error — The margin does not make a correct judgement pay more. It makes a wrong one affordable. Its price is set by self-doubt: the valuation could be thirty per cent out, the industry could turn, something unmodelled could arrive. Size the discount to how much you distrust your own estimate. A good asset with no margin is still dangerous — Graham is explicit that the counter-example is not a bad company. It is a good company bought at the wrong price. Quality and safety are two independent variables, and the largest losses tend to start with the sentence that something this good does not need a discount. The margin comes from the price, not from your confidence — Conviction cannot serve as a buffer. The more certain a judgement feels, the easier it is to conclude the discount is unnecessary, which is exactly when it should be widest. So the rule has to be mechanical: below this discount, no action, however sure you are.
q: Distill the secret of sound investment into three words: margin of safety.
An investment operation promises safety of principal and an adequate return.

chapters.w: Opportunity arrives from people you rarely see
chapters.dek: Who to ask when you're looking for work. Your instinct gives the wrong answer; here's what the data gave.
chapters.txt: In 1973 Granovetter surveyed 282 people about how they found their jobs. Among those who got there through a personal contact, 56% said they saw that person only occasionally, and 28% said rarely — the people who mattered were the ones they barely knew. That runs against instinct: your closest friends want to help you most. But the reason isn't willingness, it's information. Your circles overlap almost completely with your closest friends'; someone you rarely see is standing in a different network. What matters isn't willingness, it's whether the news is new — Close friends are more willing to help and hold almost the same information you do — same people, same news. A weak tie is not more generous. He is standing somewhere else, holding the part you can't reach from where you are. So maintain breadth, not depth — This changes where the effort goes: rather than pouring all of it into a few people, keep more weak ties in the 'still knows who you are' state. The cost is tiny — an occasional message, a hello with no request attached — and that's enough to keep the line usable. When you move, weak ties are what breaks first — Change city or leave an industry and what disappears isn't the close friends — those survive — it's the wide band of people you saw occasionally. That's exactly the layer that supplies new opportunities, so the drought after a move isn't imagined. It's structural. Where you are: you're looking for something — a job, a partner, customers —
q: Of people who found work through a contact, 56% saw them only occasionally.
Your closest friends want to help most. The useful news sits further out.

chapters.n: No strong tie is a bridge
chapters.w: The people closest to you know what you know
chapters.dek: It sounds like a turn of phrase. It's a structural result, and here is what it rests on.
chapters.txt: Granovetter states it flatly: no strong tie is a bridge. The reason isn't sentiment, it's geometry. If you're close to A and close to B, then A and B probably know each other — close people introduce each other, and the circle closes. Once it's closed, the three of you know largely the same things, and none of you is a route to anywhere outside. Only rarely-used ties can be bridges, because only they have non-overlapping networks at each end. Closure is what strong ties inevitably produce — This isn't a question of social strategy, it's geometry: closeness means frequent contact, and frequent contact makes your friends meet each other. Closure itself is good — it's where support and trust come from — but it also means information circulates rather than arrives. To test whether a tie is a bridge, look at the overlap — The test is simple: if this person knows most of the people you know, he isn't a bridge; if you share very few mutual contacts, he probably is. A bridge's value has nothing to do with how close you are and everything to do with the overlap at each end. A group's health shows in how many bridges it has — Applied to a team: an organisation made entirely of strong ties is warm inside and slowest to react to anything outside. What needs protecting is the few people who don't quite fit in and spend time elsewhere. They are the bridges, and bridges are what cohesion squeezes out first. Where you are: you want
q: No strong tie is a bridge.
Close to A and close to B? A and B probably know each other.

chapters.w: Become your own successor
chapters.dek: Intel was built on memory chips and nearly died of them. What was said in one office in 1985.
chapters.txt: By 1985 Japanese makers had driven memory prices through the floor, Intel had lost money for several quarters, and the argument over whether to hold the business had run for a year. Grove asked Moore: if we got kicked out and the board brought in a new chief executive, what do you think he would do? Moore answered without hesitating: he would get us out of memories. Grove looked at him and said, why shouldn't you and I walk out the door, come back, and do it ourselves? Intel amputated and went all in on microprocessors. A successor's view is the same machine with the feelings removed — A new chief executive sees exactly the data you see. One thing differs: no sunk cost, no credit from the old days, no this is what we were founded on. The test borrows his eyes, and the answer usually turns out to have been there already, held under by feeling. Walk out and walk back in. Both steps count — The precision of the image is that it has two halves. Walking out sheds the old identity; walking back in executes under the new one. The first alone is avoidance, seeing clearly and not moving. The second alone is butchery, cutting without having changed your mind. Doing it yourself is how you keep the people who do it — The half of his sentence that gets dropped is by ourselves. Wait for a board to bring somebody in to do the identical thing and the company bleeds two more years first. Do
q: If we got kicked out, what would a new chief executive do?
Why shouldn't you and I walk out the door and do it ourselves?

chapters.n: Inflection points and the people who warn you
chapters.w: The channel bad news travels down
chapters.dek: When the tenfold change arrives the top floor is almost always last to hear. His prescription for that structural lag.
chapters.txt: Grove calls a change that rewrites the foundations of an industry a strategic inflection point: one factor moves by a factor of ten and the old map is void. Its cruellest property is that it comes with no alarm bell, and by the time the data is clear the best window has shut. His remedy is a kind of person, the helpful Cassandras: the middle managers and front-line staff who feel it first. He asks management not to be cleverer but to let bad news travel faster than good, and to stay close to the frightened messenger. The turn is late in the data and on time in the feel — Early in a tenfold change the statements still look healthy, because existing customers carry you a year or two on inertia. The first signals are qualitative: the questions customers ask, where the hiring market moves, how deals are now lost. By the time those reach a report they are an obituary. How the Cassandras are treated decides whether the alarm exists — Somebody always felt it earlier. The question is what happened to them when they said so. If the last person to bring bad news was quietly frozen out, the warning system shut down that day. Not nobody saw it: everybody who saw it learned to be silent. Put money behind the unease at the edge, not just an ear — Hearing the Cassandra is only step one. His practice was to fund the unease: real budget for hedging experiments, so a judgement at the edge gets a
q: A strategic inflection point rarely comes with an alarm bell.
Let bad news travel faster than good news.

chapters.w: Look at the accounts before the values
chapters.dek: Why does saying it again never land. He inverted the order: check the storehouse first, discuss propriety second.
chapters.txt: Shepherding the People is the first chapter of the Guanzi, and it opens not on morality but on storage. Whoever holds land and shepherds people attends to the four seasons and guards the granaries. A state with wealth draws people from far away; land brought under cultivation keeps them where they are. Only then comes the famous line: when the granaries are full the people know propriety; when food and clothing suffice they know honour and shame. The order was counter-intuitive then. Teaching first was the mainstream. He put it second — not because instruction is wrong, but because below a certain floor it does not work. Conditions are the premise of behaviour, not an excuse — The same person under different resource conditions makes entirely different choices. So when behaviour disappoints, examine the conditions before the attitude — leave the conditions alone and replacing the person produces the same result. The order cannot be reversed — Talking about values and then about pay, versus getting the pay right and then talking about values, produces very different outcomes. The first sounds like vision substituting for wages; only the second is actually setting a standard. His sequence is storehouse first, and propriety follows. The four bonds are a result, and a guardrail — He names propriety, right, integrity and shame as the four bonds of the state, and says that when they fail the state perishes. But he places them after the granaries: they are upper structure needing material support, not a precondition you can demand from nothing. Where you are:
q: Full granaries, and the people know propriety.
Propriety, right, integrity, shame: the four bonds of a state.

chapters.n: Government succeeds by following what people want
chapters.w: Dig the channel where the wanting goes
chapters.dek: A policy that will not go through is rarely an execution problem. The single measure he used to test one.
chapters.txt: Government flourishes by following the hearts of the people, and fails by going against them — he reduces policy success to one test. Then he makes it very concrete: people hate toil, so give them ease; people hate poverty and low standing, so make them prosperous and honoured; people hate danger, so keep them secure; people hate being cut off, so let them raise families. All four begin by naming what people do not want, and design from there. He does not try to reform desire. He digs it a channel. List what they do not want first — Designing a measure, people habitually start from the benefit it brings. His sequence starts from what the other side finds hateful, then makes sure the measure does not touch it. Avoiding the aversion decides acceptance more than offering the benefit does. Against the grain, enforcement has no ceiling — A rule that violates a widespread preference is never opposed openly; it is quietly worked around. The workarounds get more sophisticated, supervision costs rise to chase them, and the chase never closes. That is not an execution problem. It is a design problem. Following is not indulging — Following the hearts of the people means setting the path along the direction of the wanting, not removing the constraint. He was simultaneously a severe legislator, with tight household registers, military organisation and market regulation. The direction is followed; the route is governed. Where you are: a rule you consider entirely reasonable is meeting resistance everywhere it lands. Ask first: what does this rule
q: Government flourishes by following the people, and fails by opposing them.
A rule against the grain is not opposed. It is bypassed.

chapters.w: Fight with prices
chapters.dek: How do you actually make a rival yield without a single soldier. One economic campaign, run end to end, long ago.
chapters.txt: Duke Huan of Qi wanted Chu subdued. Guan Zhong's method was not an army: he had Qi buy live deer from Chu in quantity at prices driven far above what farming returned. The people of Chu put down their tools and went into the hills after deer. Money piled up in Chu and the fields went to weeds. Qi had spent those years stockpiling grain. At the right moment Qi closed the border and stopped buying. Chu held money and deer and could buy no grain: four in ten of the people of Chu came over to Qi. Not one battle; the production structure changed instead. Change their incentives, not their intentions — Persuading an organisation to change its behaviour is extremely hard; changing the prices it faces is easy. He never asked anyone in Chu to abandon farming. He only made deer more profitable, and every household in Chu completed the rest themselves. The more they earn, the worse their position — Chu's books at the time looked superb: exports booming, reserves piling up, household income rising. The danger was inside the prosperity — it rested on demand that one rival decided unilaterally. To judge a business, ask whether its buyer could vanish overnight. The stockpiling is where it was won — Bidding the price of deer up is only the first half. What decided the outcome was the grain Qi quietly accumulated in those same years. Every economic manoeuvre needs a matching preparation on your own side, or it is just money given away. Where you are: head-on
q: Four in ten of the people of Chu came over.
Where profit lies, no mountain is too high to climb.

chapters.w: Decide which one this is before you speak
chapters.dek: The most important decision in a conversation gets made before it starts. This asks which of the two decisions this one is.
chapters.txt: The first chapter puts two words above everything else: opening and closing are the way of heaven and earth. To open is to let out; to close is to draw back. The principle underneath is plain — the mouth is the door of the heart, and when the door opens what is inside goes out, when it shuts the intent stays in. So before an exchange you settle one thing: how much of me does this person see, and how much stays. Neither is better. Only the wrong one for the occasion is. Settle open or closed before you settle words — Most people prepare content — what am I going to say. His order puts a layer in front of that. Is this one an opening or a closing? Get that wrong and the more elegantly you speak the more damage you do. You open so that he opens — Opening is not only expression, it is extraction. Show part of your own footing and he has a reason to show his. So it goes in order: open something small and survivable, watch whether he follows, and only then decide how much further to go. Closing is chosen silence, not absence — Closing is an active withdrawal. You may close so that he has to come and take it, or close in order to end the thing. Without that distinction, closing decays into awkwardness, and awkwardness reads as something to prod. Where you are: an important conversation, and you are working on what to say in it. Ask first:
q: Opening and closing are the way of heaven and earth.
The mouth is the door of the heart.

chapters.w: To make him talk, stop talking
chapters.dek: How do you get a person who does not want to talk to talk? The answer is four reversals, and one precondition under them.
chapters.txt: The Reacting chapter runs a set of paired instructions: to hear him speak, be silent; to have him open out, draw in; to stand high, stand low; to take, first give. Behind the pairs is a harder demand. Knowing begins with yourself, and you know yourself before you know others — because every judgement you make about another person has to pass through your own instrument, and an instrument nobody has calibrated adds error to everything it measures. Silence is the strongest question — People find a silence uncomfortable and move to fill it. So ask, and then add nothing: no softening, no restating, no second question. It routinely returns more than three further questions would have. That is what the first reversal means. Give first, or there is nothing to take — To take, first give is a sequence rather than a posture. Information, concessions and goodwill all obey it: until something has been put down, the other side has no reason to start an exchange. What you put down should be real and bounded. Calibrate your own instrument first — Know yourself and then you know others is the precondition for everything else here. Your reading of a person is mixed with your own taste, the mood you are in, and what you already think about people like him. Uncalibrated, more information only loads a crooked scale. Where you are: you need the real position out of someone who is not saying much. Ask first: what am I putting down first, and can I hold my tongue after
q: To hear him speak, be silent. To take, first give.
Knowing begins with yourself; know yourself, then you know others.

chapters.w: Measure at the peaks, not in the middle
chapters.dek: What a person says day to day and what he actually wants are rarely the same. This asks when the reading comes out true.
chapters.txt: The Weighing chapter is almost coldly specific about timing. Go to him at the height of joy and press on what he wants, and having wanted it he cannot hide it; go to him at the height of fear and press on what he dreads, and having dreaded it he cannot hide it. The Sounding chapter supplies the matching technique: rub gently along the line of what he wants, test and probe, and the inside answers. Not an interrogation. A light touch, and then watching. What people say at rest is edited — In a level state a person says what he believes he ought to say. To reach the real preference you have to watch when there is no attention left over for editing: very pleased, very frightened, very tired. Not manipulation. Choosing the observation window. Touch lightly, then watch the reaction — Sounding means to rub, not to press. Put out a small hypothesis that can be denied at no cost, then watch the direction and the speed of what comes back. The reaction is the answer; the content of the reply matters much less. Use it to understand, not to work someone — The method plainly invites manipulation, and he says himself that the sage works in the dark. The larger value is in reversing it: knowing when other people are unguarded tells you when you are, and big decisions do not belong at either peak. Where you are: trying to work out what the other side actually cares about. Ask first: the information I am holding
q: Approach him at the height of joy and his wants show.
Rub gently at what he wants, and the inside answers.

chapters.w: Move the cause off the people
chapters.dek: The whole book is an answer to one question asked to his face. Why the answer moved from people to place.
chapters.txt: In 1972 Diamond was walking on a beach in New Guinea when a local politician named Yali asked him: why is it that you white people developed so much cargo and brought it to New Guinea, but we black people had little cargo of our own? Diamond knew Yali's people were in no way less clever than Europeans. The fashionable answers were race and culture. His was environment: which plants and animals could be domesticated, the shape of the continents, the history of germs. Different starting conditions, compounded for millennia, come out as cargo. Rule out they are just not capable first — It is the laziest attribution available and it terminates the inquiry. Diamond disproves it before he earns the right to look for real variables: inside their own environment New Guineans show no deficit at all. Take the people out and what is left is the part you can change. The gap is compound interest on the starting conditions — Eurasia had fifty-six species of large-seeded wild grass and thirteen domesticable large mammals; the Americas had one and Australia none. That head start ran through food surplus, population, specialisation, technology and immunity for thousands of years. Environment does not cancel present responsibility — He explains where a long-run gap came from, not that individuals and this generation have nothing left to do. Turning environment into fate is the same early clock-out as blaming race. The use of it is to name the structural handicap, then work the parts of the structure that move. Where you are: a group
q: Why is it that you white people developed so much cargo?
History followed different courses for different peoples because of differences among peoples' environments.

chapters.w: What a starting line looks like
chapters.dek: Eurasia lies sideways; the Americas and Africa stand upright. Why a fact from school geography is worth a chapter.
chapters.txt: Diamond's prettiest argument needs only a map. Eurasia's main axis runs east to west, while the main axis of the Americas and of Africa runs north to south. East-west means one latitude — comparable daylight, rains, temperature — so a crop domesticated once travels thousands of miles sideways: wheat went from the Fertile Crescent to Ireland and to India. North-south means crossing latitudes, and maize moving north out of Mexico had to be re-adapted to a different day length, which cost it centuries. Nobody tried harder. The shape of the map was paying a dividend. Neighbours that are alike pay a dividend on spreading — The real content of an east-west axis is that adjacent units are built the same way, so one solution copies cheaply. Before expanding, ask it directly: is the next market at the same latitude — habits, channels, regulation — or across one? What blocks the spread is usually the middle stretch — Maize was held up by the isthmus and the deserts of Central America. Source and destination matched well enough; the ground in between did not. In any chain diffusion the bottleneck sits in the transfer zone, which resembles neither end. The dividend comes from structure, so go and choose the structure — You cannot change an axis, but you can choose which one you stand on. The same effort inside a structure where a solution replicates sideways, against one where every step must be re-adapted, is an order of magnitude apart after ten years. Where you are: you are choosing the direction of
q: Eurasia's main axis runs east-west; the Americas' and Africa's run north-south.
Places at the same latitude share day length and seasonal variation.

chapters.w: Morale broken into checkable items
chapters.dek: Facing an opponent stronger on every axis, how do you make a team believe? He said nothing encouraging at all.
chapters.txt: Before Guandu, Yuan Shao had more men and more grain, and Cao Cao's side was broadly pessimistic. Guo Jia did not give a speech. He made a list. Shao has ten defeats, you have ten victories, and then set them out one at a time. Shao is thick with ceremony, you follow what is natural. Shao is outwardly generous and inwardly suspicious, employing men while doubting them; you use a man without doubt and fit him to the work. Shao plans much and decides little. Ten items later, the judgement was no longer a feeling. Break the whole judgement into items checkable one by one — We can take them is a single impression nobody can argue with. Supporters and objectors each produce examples and neither moves. Split it into ten and each item can be granted or refuted on its own; anyone who disagrees has to say which one fails. Name where they are strong, or nobody believes the rest — The ten items do not dodge Yuan Shao's advantages: more troops, more territory, greater standing, all true. Because none of that is avoided, the differences that remain carry weight. A comparison listing only your own strengths reads as a pep talk. Each difference has to land on something you can do — Not one of the ten is we want it more. Judgement means using a man without doubting him; strategy means acting once the plan is set. Each names an organisational behaviour that can be kept or wrecked. One vague item spoils the whole table. Where you
q: Shao has ten defeats and you have ten victories.
He employs men and doubts them; you use a man without doubt.

chapters.w: Speed is what is left after subtraction
chapters.dek: Everyone said a thousand-mile raid was too risky. He said the risk was not the distance but what you were carrying.
chapters.txt: In 207 Cao Cao wanted to march north against the Wuhuan, and his generals objected: with the army beyond the frontier, Liu Biao might send Liu Bei against the capital. Guo Jia judged that Liu Biao would only talk and would never trust Liu Bei with troops, and pressed for the campaign. At Yi county he raised something more urgent still. Speed is the essence of war; a thousand-mile raid with heavy baggage cannot seize the advantage. Leave it behind and march light day and night. Cao Cao did, went out by Lulong Pass, and broke the Wuhuan at White Wolf Mountain. Speed is not running faster, it is carrying less — The pace of a long march is set by its slowest part, and the slowest part is always the baggage. The only way to be quick is to decide what not to bring. That is subtraction, and preparation is almost always addition. Accept the price of travelling light before you go — Leaving the baggage means no supply and no line of retreat if it goes badly. Marching light is not free; it trades margin for error against speed. So the decision rests on one prior judgement: does this have to be fast, or can it be slow? Answer the fear everybody already has — He did not skirt the worry about the capital; he ruled on it first, and only then proposed the raid. Meeting the largest objection head on is what makes the rest of a plan movable at all. Where you are: something has to
q: Speed is the essence of war.
Leave the baggage, march light, and come at them unlooked for.

chapters.w: Do not press, and they turn on each other
chapters.dek: The remnants fled onto somebody else's ground. Do you chase? The plan he left behind runs against the instinct.
chapters.txt: Beaten, Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi fled to Gongsun Kang in Liaodong. The generals urged pursuit and the taking of Liaodong in one stroke. Cao Cao said there was no need: Kang would send him their heads. He withdrew. Shortly afterwards Kang killed both brothers and sent the heads on. Asked why, Cao Cao said, he has always feared Shang; press him and they combine, ease off and they plot against each other. The judgement had been left to him by Guo Jia before he died. Outside pressure welds enemies together — Two parties watching each other will drop the watching the moment a larger threat appears outside. So when a crack already runs through the other side, the last thing to hand them is a common enemy. Withdrawing puts the conflict back where it was — Leading the army home was not giving up. It handed the principal conflict back to the other side's interior. The move looks like doing nothing and is in fact very specific: removing the reason they have to stay united. The judgement rests on the relationship, not on strength — He has always feared Shang. The whole basis of the plan is an old wariness that existed long before you arrived. Without that ledger between them, withdrawing is simply letting a tiger back into the hills. Where you are: the opponent has broken up and you are weighing whether to finish the pursuit. Ask first: is there already a conflict inside them, and does my pressure make it larger or smaller? Where it goes
q: Press him and they combine; ease off and they plot against each other.
Do not pursue. Kang will behead them and send them to you.

chapters.w: Be visible whenever anyone looks
chapters.dek: The usual way to survive outranking your emperor is to shrink. He did the opposite, and could explain the arithmetic.
chapters.txt: He had put down the An Lushan rebellion and retaken the capital twice, and the eunuchs at court denounced him for years. His answer was not seclusion. His mansion in the Qinren ward took up a quarter of the ward, three thousand household members lived in it, and the gates were left open to anyone who wanted to walk in. A son asked him to shut them. Five hundred of my horses eat state fodder, he said; if I build a wall and someone accuses me, who is left to say what I was doing? Visible beats quiet — Keeping a low profile only reduces how often you are noticed. It leaves every unobserved hour available to whoever wants to describe it. An open house removes the guessing itself: if anyone can see what you are doing, an accusation has nothing left to fill in. Slander lands on what cannot be checked — His reasoning was exact. Once a wall stands between you and everyone else, whether a charge sticks depends on other people's mouths rather than on the facts. So make sure any charge can be held against the record on the spot. It costs, and it never stops costing — Open gates mean giving up privacy and comfort, for decades. The moment you start closing them, every year of openness before that becomes the contrast that convicts you. This is not a clever move; it is a condition you have to keep paying for. Where you are: your position or your resources have started people talking. Ask first:
q: His merit covered the empire and his ruler did not suspect him.
The man who hides is the one who has to be checked.

chapters.w: Trading a battle for who you are
chapters.dek: Hundreds of thousands of troops on the border, ten thousand men on his side. This is about why he took his helmet off.
chapters.txt: In 766 Pugu Huai'en told the Uighurs and the Tibetans that Guo Ziyi was dead, and brought a joint army of several hundred thousand up to Jingyang. Guo Ziyi had a little over ten thousand men. He judged that the Uighurs had fought alongside him for years, respected him, and had been lied to. So he brought no troops: he took off his helmet, unbuckled his armour, threw down his lance and rode forward with a few dozen horsemen. Their chiefs looked at each other and said, it is him, and dismounted to bow. First work out why they came — An army at your gate that was tricked into coming is a different problem from one that came prepared. The first thing he established was that their reason for marching was the report that he was dead. Overturn the false premise and the march has no cause. Taking the armour off was the only available proof — To prove that he was alive and that he was the man, talking was useless, an envoy was useless, and arriving with soldiers would have confirmed the hostility instead. Walking over stripped puts your life up as the evidence. Trust cannot be declared, only staked. The move spends a deposit you cannot make quickly — The conditions are severe: years of fighting beside these men, faces they knew, respect they actually held. Without that accumulation the same gesture is suicide. Nerve at the decisive moment is a withdrawal against decades of credit. Where you are: something is bearing down on you and
q: He took off his helmet, unbuckled his armour, and rode forward.
Huai'en lied to us. He told us the Duke was dead.

chapters.n: Don't build a system that needs good people
chapters.w: Make the right move the cheap one
chapters.dek: A system that only runs when people are conscientious hasn't started working yet. How to design rules that don't need it.
chapters.txt: Han Feizi puts it coldly: I do not count on people being good to me; I make it so they cannot do wrong. He offers an arithmetic. Wait for arrow shafts that straighten themselves and in a hundred generations you get no arrows; wait for wood that rounds itself and in a thousand you get no wheels. Yet everyone has arrows and wheels, because someone invented the jig that straightens them. His conclusion: government cannot wait for sages. It builds tools. Conscientiousness is scarce and can't be the foundation — Depending on people to be conscientious stakes the system's stability on its least controllable variable. His alternative is the jig — the tool that straightens timber. Rules don't exist to improve people. They exist so that ordinary people produce acceptable results. Make the right road the least effortful one — The practical version of 'make it so they cannot do wrong' is to build the non-compliant road so it costs more than the compliant one. If going round the process is faster than going through it, no amount of exhortation matters. People are choosing the cheaper path. Don't design for the rare case — The commonest misuse is constraining everyone to stop one or two. Han Feizi is describing universal tools, not patches aimed at individuals. The cost of a rule is borne by everybody and the benefit accrues against a few. That ledger rarely balances. Where you are: the same class of problem keeps recurring and you've raised it many times. Ask first: is the right road currently more
q: I do not count on people being good. I make wrong impossible.
Wait for arrows that straighten themselves and you get no arrows.

chapters.w: Reward and punishment can't be lent out
chapters.dek: What power actually consists of. It turns out to be two things, and neither can be handed to anyone.
chapters.txt: Han Feizi states it like a definition: the ruler controls his ministers by two handles, and the two handles are punishment and favour. Killing is punishment; reward is favour. His example is the state of Qi, where the minister Tian Chang obtained ranks and stipends from the ruler to distribute to the officials, and lent grain by a large measure while collecting by a small one, putting the people in his debt. The ruler ended up hollow. His verdict: Tian Chang wasn't too strong. The ruler gave away the handle of favour. Power's substance is reward and consequence — Titles, grades and reporting lines are the form. What actually decides who listens to whom is who can grant good outcomes and who can bring bad ones. Everything else can be delegated; hand over these two and the seat is empty. The name remains and nobody is looking at you. Lending them out is easy; taking them back is not — Once one person exercises reward and punishment for long enough, the organisation re-forms around them. Taking it back is no longer a question of authority — you face a network of dependence, and everyone who benefited will instinctively defend them. Deliver both yourself — Letting someone else announce the good news and carrying the bad yourself sounds considerate. It gives away the favour and keeps the punishment. Han Feizi advises the opposite: both must come from you, or people only remember whoever handed them the good thing. Where you are: you're nominally responsible for something and can't move it. Ask
q: The ruler controls by two handles: punishment and favour.
A tiger masters a dog by claws. Lend them out and it reverses.

chapters.n: Match the deed to the word
chapters.w: What was said, what was done
chapters.dek: The hard part of review isn't setting standards. It's what you do when the standard and the facts disagree.
chapters.txt: Han Feizi's method is matching form to name: the official states what he will accomplish (the name), and you check it against what was actually produced (the form). His extreme example: Marquis Zhao of Han fell asleep drunk, and the keeper of the hat, seeing him cold, covered him with a robe. On waking the marquis punished both the keeper of the robes and the keeper of the hat — one for neglect, one for overstepping. Overstepping is the worse harm, because it dissolves the boundary. The principle being established: your own words are the measure. The standard comes out of his mouth — Let the name define itself and the task define itself. Not a target imposed from above but a commitment stated by the person carrying it. At review there is then no arguing about whether the standard was reasonable — he set it. The only question left is whether it was met. Overshooting counts too — Form exceeding name is also pursued. Doing more looks good, and it means the judgement at commitment time was wrong, and it usually consumed someone else's resources. A system that punishes only shortfalls trains everyone to commit as low as possible. Reconcile against the page agreed beforehand — If the ruler is chosen at review time, the whole thing becomes retroactive approval. Matching requires the name first and the form after, with no change in between. Change it once and the system reverts to personal favour. Where you are: it's review time and the two of you disagree on whether it
q: Let the name define itself, and the task define itself.
Deed fits the task and task fits the words: reward. Otherwise: punish.

chapters.n: With the river at their backs
chapters.w: Take the retreat away first
chapters.dek: Drawing up with a river behind you is the classic blunder, and he won anyway. Two preconditions get left out of the telling.
chapters.txt: At Jingxing, Han Xin had tens of thousands of raw recruits against two hundred thousand Zhao. He sent two thousand light horse with red banners to hide behind the Zhao camp, then drew his main body up with the river at its back. The Zhao laughed at a man with no retreat. His troops feigned a rout, the Zhao poured out after them, and the two thousand rode in and changed every flag to red. Asked afterwards, he said: throw them onto dead ground and they will live. Then the part that matters: these were men levied off the market, and on live ground they would have run. Dead ground is for a particular kind of troops — He gave the precondition himself: these were men driven in off the market, not a seasoned force that could be manoeuvred. Cutting the retreat is a remedy for that kind of army, not a general method. Used on trained troops it simply wastes them. The visible half is never the whole thing — What everyone remembers is the line drawn up against the river. What decided it was two thousand horse and a camp full of swapped flags. The theatrical part, the part with an audience, is usually cover; the move that settles the outcome happens quietly elsewhere. If you cut the retreat, cut it properly — With the river at your back means the way out is actually gone, not apparently gone. If the ranks know there are boats on the river, the device stops working at once. A half-burned bridge
q: Throw them onto dead ground and they will live.
These are men levied off the market; give them ground and they run.

chapters.w: The middle is the dangerous place
chapters.dek: He held the chance to split the empire three ways and the chance to walk away whole. Taking neither is what killed him.
