chapters.txt: With Qi pacified and a large army under him, Kuai Tong urged Han Xin to set up on his own, saying the balance of the empire hung on him alone: he whose valour overawes his lord stands in danger, and he whose merit covers the world goes unrewarded. Han Xin wavered, said the king of Han had treated him generously and he could not bring himself to betray him, and after a second appeal still did not decide. His command was taken, he was moved from king of Qi to king of Chu, demoted to marquis of Huaiyin, held in the capital, and finally killed for revolt. Refusing both roads is choosing the worst one — Setting up alone and standing down each have a price, and each price can be worked out. Whoever stops in the middle believes he has lost nothing and is in fact carrying both risks: still holding force that frightens people, with no plan for using it to protect himself. Holding power you do not intend to use is the danger — People assess your threat by your capability, not your intention. His refusal to betray was sincere, but sincerity is invisible from outside; what is visible is the army. Valour that overawes the lord names exactly this: the danger comes from the strength existing at all. Hearing a sentence and using it are different things — When the hares are dead the hounds are cooked. He had heard that from Kuai Tong long before the end and quoted it only on the way to
q: He whose valour overawes his lord stands in danger.
The hares dead, the hounds are cooked; the birds gone, the bow stored.

chapters.n: Your relationships at 50 predict your body at 80
chapters.w: More accurate than cholesterol
chapters.dek: What actually decides how healthy you are late in life. What eighty years of tracking put in first place.
chapters.txt: In 1938 Harvard began following 268 sophomores, later adding 456 boys from Boston's poorest neighbourhoods. Every two years they asked how life was going; every five they ran medical exams. It is still running. Robert Waldinger, the fourth director, says the sturdiest finding in all of it is this: how satisfied you are with your close relationships at fifty predicts your health at eighty better than your cholesterol does. Not income. Not fame. Not class. It runs through the body — This one gets read as a greeting card, but it lands on hard measures: people in chronically strained relationships report more chronic pain in later life and show earlier memory decline. The researchers keep repeating that this isn't about mood. The body settles the bill. A relationship that survives isn't the same as one that protects — There's an unwelcome line in the data: a long, high-conflict, mutually draining marriage does more damage to health than separating. What protects you is the quality inside it, not whether it's still standing. 'Staying for the kids' does not balance on this ledger. The window to change it is later than most people assume — Most people decide after midlife that the circle is set. In this study the clearest improvements came from people who started in their fifties and sixties — reconnecting with estranged family, turning acquaintances into regular company. Fifty is not too late for eighty. Where you are: you're trading health for career, or filing relationships under 'later'. Ask first: in the last month, how many times did I
q: Your body at eighty is decided by your relationships at fifty.
A marriage held together for the children bills both bodies.

chapters.n: Relationships need training, like a body
chapters.w: Untrained, they decline
chapters.dek: Everyone knows a body declines without training. So do relationships. What social fitness actually asks you to do.
chapters.txt: Waldinger attached a phrase to the study's conclusion: social fitness. Relationships behave like muscle — you don't finish them, and untrained they decline. Very few people in the study fell out with anyone. They moved once, changed jobs once, got busy for a few years, and by the time they looked up the numbers were still in the phone and the people were gone. The action he gives is small: pick one person and get in touch this week, not to arrange anything, just to say how things are. It isn't whether you have them, it's whether it moved recently — Most people judge that they 'have friends' from their contact list and their memory. What does the work is the live part — the people you have actually exchanged something with in the last six months. Counted that way, the number is usually far smaller than assumed. Small moves beat plans — 'We should get together more' almost never happens, because it names no day and no person. What works is the smallest step: one message to one person about nothing in particular. The bar is low enough to survive a busy month, and going quiet is what relationships can't survive. Which gap to fill depends on which one is empty — The study separates relationships by what they do: someone to fall back on, someone to enjoy things with, someone to say the true thing to, someone whose judgement you want. They don't substitute. Find the empty slot first, then decide who. Where you are: you don't think
q: Nobody sets out to lose a friend. They get busy and it goes quiet.
'We should get together' fails because it names no day and no person.

chapters.w: The count doesn't matter, the catch does
chapters.dek: The shortest way to measure your relationships. Why this question is so hard to fool.
chapters.txt: The study has long used one very short question to measure relationships: if you were sick or frightened at two in the morning, who could you call. It beats 'how many friends do you have' because it asks three things at once — whether the person exists, whether you believe they'd pick up, and whether you could bring yourself to dial. Miss any one and the answer is blank. Plenty of socially busy people have no name here; plenty of quiet ones name two or three immediately. Three tests in one question, so it can't be gamed — Someone to call tests supply. Believing they'd answer tests quality. Being able to dial tests you. Other people supply the first two; only you can clear the third — and a lot of people stall there, carrying it alone rather than making the call. No name doesn't mean no one — This answer is found by trying, not by thinking. A relationship you've never asked anything of is one whose strength you don't know. And asking the first time is usually easier than imagined — most people feel trusted rather than imposed upon. Turn it around: whose name are you — The question works in reverse. Does anyone think of you at two in the morning? Being someone's fallback runs both ways, and being permanently filed as 'lovely, but I wouldn't trouble them' is a shallow relationship. Letting people impose on you is its own kind of reliability. Where you are: you want to know how solid your relationships actually are, and
q: If something happened at 2am, who could you call.
No name may not mean no one. It may mean you never asked.

chapters.w: Nobody can hold the whole picture
chapters.dek: A paper of a dozen pages, later voted one of the century's most important in economics. What assumption it destroyed.
chapters.txt: The 1945 paper attacks an assumption everybody was making: collect the data centrally and the centre can compute the best allocation. His refutation takes the ground out from under it. The knowledge we must make use of never exists in concentrated or integrated form, only as dispersed, incomplete and often contradictory bits held by separate individuals. The kind that matters most is knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place, which cannot be reported upward without going stale. Prices solve that: when tin is short, users need no reason, only the new number. Local knowledge goes false on the way up — What the front line holds is immediate, specific and attached to a situation. Each level of aggregation strips out the time and the detail, so what arrives at the top is a stale average. An organisation that waits for reports steers today with yesterday's blur. Move the decision to where the knowledge already is — His conclusion follows: since that knowledge cannot travel, send the authority to it and let whoever stands in the situation decide inside a mandate. The centre's job is not to decide for them but to supply signals — price, cost, priority — that carry the wider picture. Inside the organisation you also need something priced — The beauty of a price is compression: it explains nothing and transmits weight. Most internal coordination fails because what gets passed around is reasons and stories with no shared measure of importance. Put a number on a scarce resource and the scramble turns into arithmetic. Where
q: The knowledge we must make use of never exists in concentrated or integrated form.
The price system is a mechanism for communicating information.

chapters.w: The curious task of economics
chapters.dek: He defined his own discipline's task as pouring cold water, not forecasting. Why the cleverest people need that water most.
chapters.txt: The title of his last book is the diagnosis: the fatal conceit, the idea that man can shape the world around him according to his wishes. His definition of the discipline became the famous line. The curious task of economics is to demonstrate how little men really know about what they imagine they can design. Markets, language, law and morals all work, and none of them was designed; they grew through countless trials. The designer's fatal position is that he has to pretend to hold knowledge scattered across millions of heads. A grown order has load-bearing walls you cannot see — Each clause in a set of old rules may be holding up a problem you never meet. They were filtered by elimination rather than argued into place. The rebuilder's risk is not a shortage of ideas; it is being unable to tell which wall is carrying weight. The cleverer you are, the further you push design — Conceit scales with intelligence: the better you are at running a system through in your head, the easier it is to forget the variables the real one contains. His cold water is aimed at clever people. Design is legitimate over the patch where you genuinely hold the relevant knowledge. The alternative is to make trial and error run — Accepting that knowledge cannot be centralised is not an argument for doing nothing. It swaps designing the best solution for designing an environment that sorts solutions: parallel attempts allowed, failure made cheap, winners left free to spread. You design the track, not the
q: The curious task of economics is to demonstrate how little men really know.
How little they know about what they imagine they can design.

chapters.w: The shift that starts when work ends
chapters.dek: Housework and care have never appeared on a timesheet. Who ends up paying when nobody counts them.
chapters.txt: In 1989 Hochschild gave the thing a name: the second shift. Women with jobs came home to another one — cooking, cleaning, children, ageing parents, all unpaid and absent from every statistic. Adding paid and unpaid hours from the time-use surveys of the period, she found women worked about 15 hours a week more than men, which over a year is an extra month of 24-hour days. The power of the concept isn't the accusation. It made invisible labour countable. Work that misses the timesheet is paid for by whoever does it — Any work that isn't measured gets treated as something done in passing. It doesn't disappear for going unrecorded; it becomes one person's invisible load, and that person often has no language to complain in, because on paper nothing happened. List it before you divide it — Most negotiations about chores fail not because nobody will share but because the two people are looking at different lists. Write every task down with the hours it takes each week and the argument moves from 'you don't appreciate me' to a table you can work on. Care time can't be compressed, only moved or dropped — You can stay up late and write a document faster. You cannot feed a child faster or sit with a sick parent faster. Care work is close to rigid in duration, so 'efficiency' barely applies. It can only be taken over by someone else, or not done — and then someone else pays. Where you are: the work at home lands on you, and
q: About 15 hours more a week. A year of that is an extra month.
The first shift is at work, the second at home. Only one pays.

chapters.w: That smile isn't hers
chapters.dek: Some jobs ask you not only to do the work but to feel the right thing. What that requirement costs.
chapters.txt: In 1983, after fieldwork with flight attendants, waiters and debt collectors, Hochschild named emotional labour: work that requires you to display a prescribed feeling — warmth for the attendant, hardness for the collector. Her central observation was alienation. That smile is not 'her' smile, and over time the worker becomes estranged not only from the expression but from what she actually feels, unable to tell which happiness is her own. She placed it beside physical labour: required feeling is workload, only nobody clocks it. Surface acting and deep acting cost differently — Surface acting is putting the face on while knowing you're putting it on. Deep acting is persuading yourself you really feel it. The first exhausts through tension; the second exhausts because afterwards you can't find yourself again. Both have a bill. They arrive at different times. Only once you count it as work can you schedule recovery — As long as feelings are treated as your own private business, no rest can ever be arranged for them. Admit that it's workload and you start scheduling recovery the way you would after physical work, instead of expecting the feeling to bounce back on its own. The cost rises with the distance from what you feel — The further the required feeling sits from the real one, the more expensive it is. Being asked for warmth while you're grieving costs far more than being asked for calm while you're calm. The most damaging roles aren't the busiest — they're the ones that most often require the opposite of what you
q: That smile is not 'her' smile.
In time you're estranged not just from the face but from what you feel.

chapters.n: A craft that ended in one night
chapters.w: 1 July 1978
chapters.dek: What it looks like when an entire trade disappears at once. What happened to the compositors the morning after.
chapters.txt: On 1 July 1978 the New York Times set its last edition in hot metal. The same day, photocomposition took over. A documentary filmed that night: the machines still roaring, the compositors locking up the final page, then the power off. The trade took years to learn, and the Linotype keyboard has nothing in common with a typewriter. What came out of those years was a body of skill that worked in exactly one place. The next morning there was no position for it in the building. Not a slow decline, a single switch — Inside an industry, replacement is rarely gradual. Once the equipment is installed and the workflow cuts over, the old roles stop as a block rather than thinning year by year. People counting on a few years of cushion usually do not get one. The more specific the skill, the harder it travels — The Linotype layout means something only on a Linotype. Years of muscle memory in those keys are worth nothing anywhere else. The closer a skill sits to one particular machine, the more precisely it retires on the day that machine does. Check what your skill is attached to — Within the same job, knowing how a page reads and how a headline should break is not attached to the Linotype. Finger speed on that keyboard is welded to it. The question is how far a given skill sits from one specific piece of equipment. Where you are: a new way of working is spreading in your trade, and most of what you
q: Inside an industry, replacement is rarely gradual.
A skill welded to one machine retires when the machine does.

chapters.n: The most valuable part went first
chapters.w: The thing they were fastest at
chapters.dek: Why the most skilled are often replaced first. The conditions under which mastery turns into a liability.
chapters.txt: The compositors everyone respected were the fast ones. Lines set per minute was the trade's public scoreboard. Photocomposition arrived and the whole board was void, because the machine set faster than any of them and never tired. What followed was counterintuitive. The most skilled took the hardest hit, since their entire worth was staked on the one thing being replaced. The ones who had never been fastest, but who understood something besides speed, were the ones who could move. The scoreboard was set by the trade, not by you — The thing you compete to be first at was usually chosen for you long before you arrived. When that board is voided, the people near the top lose most, because they have put every chip on a position that can be lifted away whole. Mastery blocks the view of other directions — Getting very fast at one thing pays clearly, so people keep putting the hours there. When it stops counting, nothing else has been started. This is not unwillingness to learn. Every single year, continuing to sharpen the main thing was the best available move. Keep one thing that is not on the board — Skills off the scoreboard pay slowly and attract no attention at the time. Because they attract no attention, they are also not in the first wave of what gets matched. They cannot replace the main skill. They decide whether you are standing when it is voided. Where you are: you rank high on your trade's public scoreboard, and tools are closing in on the
q: The most skilled took the hardest hit.
Every year, sharpening the main thing was the best available move.

chapters.w: Not the fastest hands
chapters.dek: Why some people came through the same shock. What the ones who stayed were actually holding, rather than luck.
chapters.txt: Photocomposition, and computer setting after it, did not leave newspapers without people. It changed which people. The job moved from setting metal fast and clean to knowing why this page is laid out this way. Someone who understood type sizes, which line must not break, what an editor's one-sentence change pulls along with it, could do the work on any tool. Someone whose whole skill lived in hand speed had very little to show once the new equipment arrived. Say why, and changing tools costs you nothing — In any job, how it is done belongs to the tool and why it is done that way belongs to judgement. The first expires with the equipment; the second travels with the person. Most people train only the first, because it shows results the same day. Get the tacit part into words first — The most valuable thing in an old hand is often the part they cannot state: they see instantly that something is wrong and cannot say why. Tools match the half that can be stated. The unstated half needs stating even more urgently, or it cannot be handed on at all. The ones who crossed had started half a step early — Learning on the day the new equipment is installed is a different starting line from having played with it for a year. Half a step is not much. Touching the new thing while the old work still pays is far cheaper than after it stops. Where you are: the tools in your trade are turning over and
q: How it is done is the tool. Why is judgement.
Tools match the half of a craft that can be stated.

chapters.w: Put the rule where the cheating is possible
chapters.dek: Adulterating medicine is easy and almost never detected. What is worth studying is where he chose to hang the rule about it.
chapters.txt: In 1878 he wrote two characters for his pharmacy, Hu Qing Yu Tang: No Cheating. Underneath ran a note. No trade can afford the word cheat, and medicine, which holds lives, least of all; he would not take a fat profit with an inferior drug, and he asked the managers to hold this as their own. The board was not hung at the front for customers. It faces inward, where only the staff and the managers pass it every day. A second board, One True Price, faced the shop floor. Put the rule on the side where cheating is possible — A customer cannot tell good herbs from bad, so no external check exists. Hanging the board inward concedes that the only available constraint is internal, and that an internal constraint needs a physical reminder people walk past daily. A rule posted where outsiders read it is mostly advertising. Where nothing can be verified, honesty is an asset choice — In a trade the buyer cannot audit, adulteration pays immediately and invisibly. Giving up that informational advantage converts a certain current profit into something long-dated and unseeable. His bank failed and he was ruined; the pharmacy is still trading. Two boards, two audiences — One True Price faces out; No Cheating faces in. He treated them as separate jobs. Outward you owe a clear promise; inward you owe an enforceable discipline. A promise without the discipline eventually breaks, and a discipline nobody announces builds no expectation at all. Where you are: there is a step the customer could never audit,
q: No trade can afford the word cheat; medicine, which holds lives, least of all.
I will not take a fat profit with an inferior drug.

chapters.w: What it costs to bet everything once
chapters.dek: The richest merchant in the empire lost everything inside two years. The interesting question is which step was the mistake.
chapters.txt: From 1882 he used his bank and his silk business to hoard raw silk, meaning to control supply and force the foreign houses to his price. The first year worked; they had to pay. Then Europe turned. Silk prices fell, the Italian crop came in large, and the foreign buyers simply bought elsewhere. His money was locked in silk for a season, while the deposits funding it could be withdrawn in a day. With Zuo Zongtang dead he had no protection at court, a rumour started, and the branches were run on at once. Cornering a good whose supply you do not own — A corner only works if you control the supply and the buyer has nowhere else to go. Raw silk failed both tests, because China was not the only source and Italy was having a good year. Before squeezing anyone, establish whether they have a second seller. Long bets on short money — Silk needed a year or more to come back. Deposits could leave in an afternoon. An asset that outlasts its funding looks completely normal in calm weather and fails on the first tremor. What finished him was not the wrong view; it was the mismatch. A borrowed advantage expires with the lender — Cheap funding, government deposits and official convenience all rested on one patron. That kind of advantage looks like capability while it lasts and reveals itself as a lease when it ends. Sorting your moat means separating what you grew from what you rent. Where you are: you are convinced something will
q: A corner needs the supply, not only the money.
Across five thousand years of trade, the first man is Fan Li.

chapters.w: Entering before the market exists
chapters.dek: He has his own name for how the company chooses. How to stay alive inside a market that does not exist yet.
chapters.txt: He describes the choice in one phrase: we go after zero-billion-dollar markets. Not billion-dollar markets. Markets whose present size is zero, where nobody is competing because nobody is yet buying. CUDA is the case. From 2006 the graphics chip was rebuilt for scientific computing and handed free to researchers everywhere, and the spending looked terrible on the statements for close to a decade, until deep learning arrived and everyone discovered the AI world was standing on his foundations. His explanation: if the market already exists, you are playing a game somebody else wrote the rules for. A zero market buys the seat where the rules get written — Enter a mature market and the product, the channels and the standards belong to somebody else; you are scoring on their board. Enter at zero and the toolchain, the developer habits and the interfaces are yours to write. What you buy is not a head start. It is the referee's chair. Getting through it takes two lines of blood supply — A zero market pays nothing for ten years, so what keeps the company alive? Two tracks. Gaming cards as the mature business feeding cash, CUDA as the zero track burning it. Without the first the second is suicide; without the second the first is merely a good business. Which zero to pick is read off physics, not off research — A zero market has no users to survey, because the demand is not there to ask about. His basis was harder: the growth curve of demand for computation, the physical advantage
q: We go after zero-billion-dollar markets.
There are no competitors there, because there are no customers yet.

chapters.w: The second story in the Taipei address
chapters.dek: One of the three stories he told the graduates is about giving up. Why he says retreat is hardest for the ablest.
chapters.txt: At the 2023 Taipei commencement he told the story of leaving mobile chips. Nvidia had entered mobile processors early, then saw giants ringing the category and the margin being squeezed out, and knew that dropping it meant dropping the biggest growth story it had. They dropped it, and moved the chips toward robotics and AI. Then he named the psychology out loud: retreat does not come easily to brilliant, successful people like you; but strategic retreat, sacrifice, deciding what to give up, is core to success. Hence the second half of the famous line: run, don't walk. The abler you are, the dearer admitting defeat costs — A clever person's record holds no failures, and that is precisely the burden. Retreat is not a business adjustment for him, it is a threat to identity: the story I never give up is what stops him doing the right thing. Watch for star teams defending ground that should be given up. Retreat on the structure, not on this quarter's fighting — Mobile chips were still growing when they left. What they read was not the quarter but the structure: giants subsidising the modem, a visible ceiling on margin, their own comparative advantage sitting elsewhere. Retreat timed off the fighting always comes too late to bring the troops out whole. A retreat has to become a redeployment the same day — The period that took them out of mobile put the engineers onto the robotics platform. The value of a retreat is not the loss it stops but the freed strength having somewhere
q: Retreat does not come easily to brilliant, successful people.
Strategic retreat, sacrifice, deciding what to give up, is core to success.

chapters.n: There was never a thing there
chapters.w: Subtraction is harder than addition
chapters.dek: Two verses. Everyone admired one; the other went to an illiterate kitchen worker. What separates them.
chapters.txt: The fifth patriarch asked his students for a verse to decide his successor. Shenxiu, the head monk and everyone's expected heir, wrote on the corridor wall at night: the body is a bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror's stand; polish it constantly, let no dust settle. It is an entirely correct account of practice — wipe daily, keep the dust off. Huineng, illiterate and pounding rice out the back, had his written beside it: there was never a tree, nor any stand; there was never a thing there, so where would dust settle? He doesn't dispute the polishing. He asks where the mirror came from. Shenxiu's verse isn't wrong. It's heavy — 'Polish it constantly' is executable, checkable and almost impossible to get wrong. The trouble is it can never be finished: as long as you assume a mirror that gets dirty, wiping has no end. A great deal of effort is stuck in that correct, infinite loop. Ask who installed the premise — Huineng's move pushes the question back a layer: don't optimise the solution, audit the setup. 'There was never a thing there' means the object you keep wiping may be one you erected yourself. Remove the premise and the whole discipline goes with its anxiety. Subtraction is hard because it has no progress bar — Adding a method gives you something to do immediately. Removing a premise gives you nothing to do at all. The second pays far better and shows no progress along the way, so most people keep wiping. Where you are: something you're
q: There was never a thing there, so where would dust settle?
Not the wind moving, not the flag moving. Your mind is moving.

chapters.n: The practice is here, not elsewhere
chapters.w: There is no better place to start
chapters.dek: People wait for a quiet enough setting to begin. Why Huineng said that setting doesn't exist.
chapters.txt: Asked whether a layperson could practise at home, Huineng was flat about it: the teaching is in the world, and awakening is not apart from the world; to seek it outside the world is to hunt for a rabbit's horns — the thing simply isn't there. He pulled the whole practice back into daily life: if the mind is level, what need of precepts; if conduct is straight, what need of meditation. He lived it too — after receiving the transmission he spent fifteen years among a band of hunters, taking the days as they came. There is no better place to begin — Waiting for a quieter environment, an emptier calendar, a riper moment is itself a form of avoidance. To seek it outside the world is to hunt a rabbit's horns — the fully-prepared place doesn't exist, because the conditions never all arrive. The ordinary thing in front of you is the training ground — Huineng breaks practice down into specific actions inside specific relationships: how you treat your parents, how you treat those above and below, what you do when treated unfairly. None of it needs separate time. It already occupies all of your time; it just wasn't counted as practice. Complete form isn't the same as the thing done right — 'What need of precepts, what need of meditation' doesn't abolish either. It warns that form serves substance. When someone's forms are immaculate, that is often exactly when the substance has gone wrong — the form became the substitute. Where you are: you're waiting for a
q: The teaching is in the world. Awakening is not apart from it.
To seek it outside the world is to hunt for a rabbit's horns.

chapters.w: Read the ground, not the book
chapters.dek: The emperor offered to teach him the classics of war and he declined. The question is whether that was arrogance or judgement.
chapters.txt: Emperor Wu wanted to teach him Sun Tzu and Wu Qi. Huo Qubing answered that what matters is how the plan for this campaign is drawn, and there is no need to study the old military texts. The line has been read as a boy's arrogance for two thousand years. His campaigns say otherwise. At seventeen he took eight hundred riders hundreds of li beyond the main army; at nineteen he ran two long flanking marches through the Hexi corridor; at twenty-one he reached Mount Langjuxu. Han doctrine was infantry and cavalry together, advancing along a grain road. His war was all cavalry, long range, and had no rear. A manual encodes the last generation's constraints — Sun Tzu and Wu Qi were written when the mass of an army was infantry and chariots and the grain road set the marching radius. Huo Qubing had decades of imperial horse-breeding behind him. The tools had changed, so the best answer had changed, and the book holds the old one. Refusing the template is not refusing to think — The weight of his answer falls on the word plan. He did not fight on instinct; he drew a fresh scheme for every campaign. What he threw out was the general template, not the work. People collapse the two, and only the second is actually arrogance. The method came with the man attached — No rear, high intensity, raids run back to back: this asks for a body and a tolerance of risk almost nobody has, and it forbids caution. Which is why
q: What matters is the plan for this campaign, not the old texts.
A manual is the best answer to a problem you no longer have.

chapters.w: A supply line is also a leash
chapters.dek: The hard limit on any long march is grain. This one is about how he took the limit away altogether.
chapters.txt: The Records compress his method into one line: he took his food from the enemy, and so marched extraordinarily far without his grain ever running out. Han expeditions were governed by the grain road, and the marching radius was set by the distance from the rear. He swapped the constraint out: no baggage train, resupply from the Xiongnu camps he broke on the way. That is what made a raid of two thousand li possible. The same chapter records the other half of him. Sent out with dozens of carts of palace food, he came home throwing away fine grain and meat while his own soldiers went hungry. A supply line is a lifeline and a tether — A grain road gives you a radius, and a radius gives the other side a number he can compute. Giving it up costs you safety and buys something else: he can no longer predict you. He deploys against your supply capacity, and you appear where his arithmetic says you cannot be. Living off the land means winning every time — The hidden premise is that every encounter must be won, won quickly, and won with enough taken. Lose once, or win slowly, and the column starves within days. So it is not the easy option. It moves the risk out of logistics and into fighting strength. The same chapter records what he was bad at — Raised at court, high-born, careless of his men: he did not know what the ranks were going through, and threw good food away rather than share
q: He took his food from the enemy and never ran short.
A supply line gives you a radius. A radius can be computed.

chapters.n: The hidden dragon does not act
chapters.w: Newly in place, do not move yet
chapters.dek: Just arrived, just promoted, just moved. This one asks why the first line of the first hexagram says do not act.
chapters.txt: The six lines of Qian read from the bottom up as one dragon moving from hidden to flying to overreaching. The bottom line has four words: the hidden dragon does not act. The dragon is under water. Not for lack of power, since a dragon is a dragon. The position is still lowest, and force used from there is all your own, with all of the risk on you. One step up is the dragon appearing in the field. A step above that, the noble man is busy all day and wary at night. Capacity and the right moment are two different times. Being able and being due are two different times — The first line and the fifth are both the dragon. What differs is not power but position. Rushing to prove yourself in a new place spends your own force and carries all the risk; from the second or third line the same act is far easier. Not acting is accumulating, not waiting — The hidden dragon is not lying down. The third line is explicit: busy all day, wary into the evening. The time under water goes on reading the ground and gathering what you will need. What is waited for is a change of position, not a change of mood. Every line has its own move, and skipping costs — The six lines give six different pieces of advice because the positions differ. Acting from the first line as though you stood at the fifth is using force that is not yours to use. Knowing which
q: The hidden dragon does not act.
Being able and being due are two different times.

chapters.w: The line above the peak
chapters.dek: What the risk is when everything has gone your way for a long time, and why the top line is not the best one.
chapters.txt: Counting up Qian, the fifth line is the dragon flying in the heavens, which looks like the summit. There is one line above it. The top line reads: the overreaching dragon repents. The Commentary on the Words glosses that word: to know advancing and not retreating, to know preserving and not perishing, to know gaining and not losing. Three knowings against three not-knowings. A whole ascent spent learning advance, preservation and gain, and never once practising the other half. At the highest point the missing half is what brings you down. There is a line above the summit, and it repents — Most people take the fifth line for the end; the hexagram is not finished. Keep pushing in the same direction after the dragon is flying and you arrive at the top line. The problem with a peak is not the height, it is adding after you have reached it. What is missing is not the skill of advancing — To know advancing and not retreating. A run of good fortune trains half a person. Advance, preserve and gain become fluent; retreat, perish and lose are never rehearsed. What the summit calls for is precisely the unrehearsed half, which is why people fall. Repentance is not ruin, it is a warning — The line says repents, not disaster. The overreaching dragon does not necessarily die of the fall, but will certainly regret not having stopped at the fifth. It is written for someone still in the air: the position one step above yours is that one. Where you are:
q: The overreaching dragon repents.
To know advancing and not retreating, gaining and not losing.

chapters.w: Run it to the limit and it turns
chapters.dek: What to prepare when everything is going well, and what to hope for when it is jammed. Why the two sit side by side.
chapters.txt: Among the sixty-four, the eleventh is Tai, free passage, and the twelfth is Pi, blockage. They are placed next to each other, and the top line of Tai already reads: the wall falls back into the moat. The last position of the smooth run is itself the beginning of the turn. It works the other way too, since the top of Pi reads standstill first, then joy. The Great Commentary states the rule. At the limit it changes; changed, it passes through; passing through, it lasts. Not a fated cycle: every state carries its own end inside it. The turn is written into the top line of Peace — The wall falling back into the moat is not in Pi; it is in Tai. The reversal does not begin when the bad days start, it begins at the last position of the good ones. The moment most worth preparing is the one that looks least like it needs preparing. At the limit it changes, so being jammed is the condition — People try to change things while they still just about work, and cannot, because the limit has not been reached. Fully jammed, change becomes possible, because the old way has run out and nobody is defending it any more. Adjacent means neither one lasts — Tai does not stay Tai and Pi does not stay Pi. The same sentence is a warning to whoever is up and a comfort to whoever is down. What matters is reading which hexagram you are in rather than treating the present as permanent.
q: The wall falls back into the moat.
At the limit it changes; changed it passes through, and so lasts.

chapters.n: The way of thinking is a multiplier
chapters.w: And it can be negative
chapters.dek: He reduced a life to a single multiplication. Why only one of the three factors carries a sign.
chapters.txt: The formula: the result of life and work equals way of thinking times enthusiasm times ability. He explains the notation. Ability and enthusiasm run from zero to a hundred; the way of thinking runs from minus a hundred to plus a hundred, the only factor with a sign. So ordinary ability with enormous enthusiasm can outproduce an able but arrogant and idle talent, while a man whose thinking is negative does more damage the abler and the keener he is. He called his own gifts ordinary, and offered this as the arithmetic available to everybody. The factor with a sign needs examining on its own — Assessment forms are usually all positive scales: ability out of ten, drive out of ten. The formula points at a structural gap. One dimension is not how much but plus or minus: who takes the credit, what he does with rules, how he treats the weak when things go well. An ordinary person's odds sit in the two positive factors — Ability improves slowly and has a ceiling. Enthusiasm and the way of thinking can change today. Kyocera began with neither technology nor money behind it, and those two are what he bet on: effort and direction at full marks, and let multiplication overturn the natural gifts. Multiplication means any single factor can veto — In an additive system a weakness is covered by a strength. Not in a product: any factor near zero pulls the total near zero, and any factor turned negative turns the total negative. So the formula is also a
q: Result of life and work equals thinking times enthusiasm times ability.
The way of thinking runs from minus a hundred to plus a hundred.

chapters.w: Six months of asking before he started
chapters.dek: Before entering telecoms he interrogated himself for half a year. What that self-examination was actually guarding against.
chapters.txt: Japanese telecoms opened in 1984 and Inamori wanted to take on the giant NTT with the strength of Kyocera. He did not move. Every night before sleep he put two questions to himself: is my motive pure, is there any self-interest in it? Is this really about lowering the country's phone bills, or about being told that Inamori is remarkable? He asked for six months, and only once he was sure of a motive wholly good, with no private interest left in it did he found DDI. Twenty-six years later he took the bankrupt Japan Airlines through the same gate. The motive check guards against deforming later — A venture with private interest mixed into it shows no problem at the start, because self-interest and the common good often travel the same road. The fork comes in the hard moments. What was done for glory gets dropped when the glory goes; what was done for vanity bends. Six months, because self-interest wears a disguise — Ask once whether you have a private motive and the answer is always no; self-interest's first skill is finding a public-spirited account of itself. He asked for half a year to see what was still standing after each wave of feeling had gone out. A pure motive is a mobilisation order, not a talisman — A leader with nothing to gain borrows strength nobody else can: staff worked for a salaryless man of seventy-eight because what is he in it for had no answer, and the airline was profitable within the year. But he never
q: Is my motive pure? Is there any self-interest in it?
A motive wholly good, with no private interest left in it.

chapters.w: The sense of owing is the lever
chapters.dek: Of the six principles he puts this one first. Why the side that gives first is the side holding the initiative.
chapters.txt: Cialdini states the rule plainly: we should try to repay, in kind, what another person has provided us. How deep does it go? In 1985 Ethiopia, in the middle of poverty, civil war and famine, sent five thousand dollars to earthquake victims in Mexico, because Mexico had sent aid when Ethiopia was invaded in 1935. The debt had held for fifty years. The other face of the rule is that it can be switched on. A flower, a can of Coke, a free sample, and the return regularly outruns the gift. Being in debt does not require your consent — The strongest feature of reciprocity is that the favour can arrive uninvited and the obligation still forms. You did not ask for the small gift, and having taken it you find refusing the request hard. The initiative sits with whoever gives first. The return is usually out of proportion — The rule asks for repayment and says nothing about matching value, and people overpay to be rid of the feeling quickly. In Regan's experiment an unasked-for Coke produced raffle ticket purchases worth several times its price. The small favour is the cheapest lever here. The defence is to reclassify, not to refuse — Cialdini's counter is not to turn gifts down, which costs too much socially. It is to relabel: if the favour is a sales device then it is not a favour, and the rule stops applying. Favours are owed to favours, and tactics are owed nothing. Where you are: you have taken something small from someone and are
q: We should try to repay, in kind, what another person has provided us.
There is no duty more indispensable than that of returning a kindness.

chapters.w: When unsure, we watch each other
chapters.dek: Everyone hates canned laughter and everyone laughs more with it. This is about the conditions that make the principle strongest.
chapters.txt: Cialdini's definition: we determine what is correct by finding out what other people think is correct. Networks keep the laugh track although audiences say they dislike it, because experiment after experiment shows it works. But the principle is not constant, and he names two amplifiers. The first is uncertainty — when we are unsure of ourselves and the situation is ambiguous, we are readiest to accept the actions of others as correct. The second is similarity: people read mainly from people like themselves. In an unclear situation, people read each other — When the facts are plain, people look at facts. When they are not, people look at each other. The danger is that everyone is doing it at once, so a group with no information quotes itself into an apparent consensus. Newer and murkier makes the loop stronger. Similarity picks the reference group — People do not follow everyone, they follow people like themselves. So a case study persuades in proportion to how closely its subject resembles the listener, not to how impressive it is. A giant's success story is weaker than a peer's. In a crowd, responsibility is divided by the crowd — The bystander effect runs on two layers: everyone reads everyone else's stillness as evidence that nothing is wrong, and everyone assumes somebody else will act. Cialdini's advice to a person in trouble is therefore very specific. Single one person out of the crowd. Where you are: you cannot make the call, and you notice you are checking what everyone else does. Ask first: did these
q: We determine what is correct by finding out what other people think is correct.
When uncertainty reigns, we accept the actions of others as correct.

chapters.w: The textbook moves that put you out
chapters.dek: Every generation of disk-drive leaders was killed by the next. Why the autopsy keeps reading: cause of death, good management.
chapters.txt: Christensen spent years on disk drives because the industry turned over fast enough to watch: leader after leader wiped out by the following generation. His finding was blunt. Good management was the most powerful reason they failed to stay atop their industries. These firms listened to their best customers, invested aggressively in what those customers asked for, and put capital behind the highest returns. Sustaining technologies improve the mainstream measure and incumbents almost always win them. Disruptive ones start out worse on that measure, thinner on margin, wanted by nobody important, and are therefore declined by a rational process until they grow up from the edge. Listening to your customers hides the change of track — Your best customers want more of what they already have, because they are locked into the same value network you are. The first users of a disruptive product are people you have never served, so polling your existing customers is polling the wrong panel entirely. The financial model vetoes disruption automatically — Disruptive products carry lower margins, smaller markets and uncertain demand, so on any return-on-investment sheet they finish last. The more rigorous the allocation process, the faster it kills them. That is not short-sightedness; it is a process correctly running the wrong comparison. Overshoot is the signal light — Christensen names an observable warning. Once mainstream performance runs past what most customers can use, the basis of competition migrates, from performance toward convenience, price and size. Disruption enters exactly there, as good enough but cheap and simple. The day people call your product
q: Good management was the most powerful reason they failed to stay atop their industries.
Precisely because these firms listened to their customers, they lost their positions of leadership.

chapters.n: Small markets cannot save big companies
chapters.w: A mismatch of growth needs
chapters.dek: Big firms do not fail to see the new market; they decline it. Why the refusal is arithmetic, and the remedy he proposes.
chapters.txt: Christensen's second principle is cruel in its plainness: small markets don't solve the growth needs of large companies. A four-billion-dollar firm holding twenty per cent growth has to find eight hundred million in new revenue a year, and a market worth forty million today rounds to nothing. To a forty-million company the same market is a doubling. By the time it is large enough to be worth entering, the first movers hold positions nobody can shift. His remedy for the incumbent is one line: give the job to an organisation small enough to get excited about small orders. The same opportunity is two things under two denominators — An opportunity's pull is not its absolute size but its ratio to the body weighing it. On a large organisation's scales the small one always loses, which is not about eyesight but about the denominator. Asking the main process to incubate it is asking an elephant to sit on an egg. Waiting until it is clear means waiting until the walls are up — Enter when the market is big sounds prudent, but the rules, channels and customer relationships of a new market are written by whoever is already there. Latecomers do not arrive at open ground, they arrive at somebody's home field. Markets that do not exist cannot be analysed, only joined. Independent means independent down to budget and scorecard — The keyword in the remedy is independence: its own cost structure, its own definition of profitable, independent enough that it never competes for a line on the parent's budget sheet.
q: Small markets don't solve the growth needs of large companies.
Markets that don't exist can't be analyzed.

chapters.n: Focus is what you say no to
chapters.w: The things you cut are the good ones
chapters.dek: Everyone says they are focused. What makes his definition worth reading is that it points the opposite way from the instinct.
chapters.txt: Apple in 1997 had dozens of overlapping product lines and was close to insolvent. He drew a two-by-two on a whiteboard — consumer and pro, desktop and portable — one machine per square, everything else cancelled, including the Newton, which had years of work in it. At WWDC that year he said the part people leave out: people think focus means saying yes to the thing you have got to focus on; it means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. And then the harder sentence — that he was as proud of the things they had not done as of the things they had. The test comes from good ideas, not bad ones — A bad idea does not require focus to refuse; it dies on its own. What dilutes a company is the hundred directions that are genuinely decent — each with a champion, a deck and a reason. The whole difficulty of focus is that every cut lands on something that was right. The number of squares is the discipline — The grid works because it is a physical constraint. There are four squares; for something new to enter, something has to leave. Without a container that hard, focus always loses to one more will not hurt — addition needs no argument, only subtraction does. Give credit for what was not done — Organisations reward shipping, so everyone starts things and nobody stops them. As proud of what we have not done is a medal for subtraction — markets not entered, features not
q: Focus means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are.
As proud of what we have not done as of what we did.

chapters.w: Collect first, connect later
chapters.dek: A dropout sat in on a class with no use whatsoever. The famous line about it is usually run in the wrong direction.
chapters.txt: The first of the three Stanford stories is about dropping out: with no required courses left to take, he sat in on the calligraphy class that fascinated him — serifs, the space between letter pairs — with no prospect of any of it being useful. Ten years later, designing the Mac, all of it came back, and the Mac became the first computer with beautiful type. His summary: you cannot connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that they will somehow connect later — because looking forward there is no evidence at all. Connecting is hindsight, not a forecast — The common misuse runs the line forwards: that you can work out in advance which dots will join up. He is saying the reverse. In the moment he walked into that classroom there was no argument for it. The causality only exists afterwards; beforehand it was a bad use of a term. Pick dots by obsession, not by usefulness — If forward reasoning cannot justify the choice, the choice needs a different signal, and his was curiosity to the point of absorption. That is not romance, it is odds: you go deeper into what grips you, and only a dot that goes deep is worth connecting to anything. Shallow dots join to nothing. Trusting they connect is what lets you commit now — The function of trust here is not comfort, it is solving a problem in the present: without it nobody puts real time into work with an unclear
q: You cannot connect the dots looking forward, only looking backwards.
You have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future.

chapters.w: You can feel the return the same day
chapters.dek: Filing exercise under the gym leaves the cheapest medicine unused. What it's actually changing.
chapters.txt: A high school in Naperville, outside Chicago, ran an experiment: move PE to first period, and stop measuring who runs fastest — students only had to hold their own high heart-rate zone. That cohort went on to score far above their peers in international maths and science assessments. Ratey uses it to show the link isn't mystical: exercise prompts the brain to release proteins that support neuron growth and connection, which he calls fertiliser for the brain. Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain. Change the motive from your shape to today's state — Aim at your body and the return arrives months later, carried entirely by willpower. Aim at attention and mood and you can feel the return within hours. The second is real, and easier to sustain, because the feedback is fast. Intensity matters more than duration — Naperville had each student hold their own high heart-rate zone rather than race each other. That's good news for ordinary people: you don't need long sessions, you need the heart rate to actually have gone up. Fifteen real minutes beats an hour of strolling. Put the hard thing after the exercise — If the window after exercise is when new connections form most readily, then schedule accordingly: the hardest learning or thinking goes after. Moving PE to first period was exactly this logic. Where you are: your head won't turn over and you're forcing it. Ask first: when did I last actually raise my heart rate? Is twenty minutes of moving a better trade than another hour
q: Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain.
The growth factors physical activity releases are fertiliser for the brain.

chapters.n: When anxious, move before you think
chapters.w: Start with the physiology
chapters.dek: The more you think, the worse it gets, and knowing that doesn't stop it. Why this is the moment to go outside.
chapters.txt: Ratey points out how physical anxiety is: the body has already gone on standby and the hormones are circulating, and talking yourself down at the cognitive level barely reaches it. Exercise works because it acts on that system directly — burning off the standby hormones and giving the brain the signal that you already ran and the danger has passed. That explains a common experience: after a walk the thing is less frightening, and nothing about it has changed. So his advice is blunt: when the feeling is jammed, handle the physiology first, the thinking second. Bring the arousal down before you reason — Reasoning at high arousal is extremely inefficient, with yourself or with anyone else. The order should be: get the body down — walk, breathe, leave the room — then return to the content. It's also why reasoning mid-argument doesn't work. Rumination has to be interrupted, not resolved — The twentieth pass over the same thought produces no new information, only a deeper groove. You don't get out of that loop by continuing to think. It needs an external action to break it, and exercise is the most reliable — it occupies attention and burns the hormones at once. Don't let it replace the problem — Exercise lowers the intensity of anxiety. It doesn't resolve what caused it. What you buy is a state in which you can think properly, not an escape. The thing is still there when you get back — you can just see it more clearly. Where you are: something has gone round
q: Anxiety is heavily physical. Talking yourself down barely reaches it.
Exercise gives the brain the signal that the danger has passed.

chapters.n: You can't run the afternoon on the morning's programme
chapters.w: Not wrong. Expired
chapters.dek: Something feels wrong around forty. Is it a fault? Jung said it's the hour.
chapters.txt: Jung compared a life to a day. In the morning the task points outward — a career, a family, a place in the world — and the standards come from outside and genuinely work. His observation was that many people stall in midlife not because their capacity declined but because they are still running the afternoon on the morning's programme. His line is severe: what was great in the morning will be little at evening. Not that the programme was wrong. It expired. Stalling is usually the hour, not a malfunction — Someone in their late thirties doing well and suddenly unable to summon anything looks first for a defect: tiredness, wrong industry. Jung offers another reading — the morning's task is largely done, the afternoon's hasn't been picked up, and the gap between them is the feeling. The morning's fix fails twice as hard in the afternoon — Stuck in the morning, the answer is push harder and ask for more. Use that again in the afternoon and it only packs the empty place fuller. Plenty of people add in midlife — bigger house, higher title — and find the feeling entirely unchanged. The afternoon's task points inward, not outward — Jung says the direction reverses: from acquiring to sorting, from proving outward to picking back up the parts of yourself that never got used. The judge changes too — the morning is scored by others, the afternoon only by you. Where you are: you're in your thirties or forties, doing reasonably well, and increasingly unable to summon anything,
q: What was great in the morning will be little at evening.
Adding more in the afternoon only packs the empty place fuller.

chapters.n: What you push down comes back
chapters.w: It jumps out of other people
chapters.dek: The kind of person you can't stand — why they can enrage you instantly. Jung said part of you is in there.
chapters.txt: Jung called the part of yourself you deny and push down the shadow. To become an acceptable person, everyone suppresses something: ambition, laziness, temper, wanting to be seen. Those things don't disappear. They move somewhere you can't see, and then jump out of other people. So the kind of person you least tolerate usually carries the very thing you won't own. The harder it was pushed down, the faster you're enraged. Disproportionate dislike is a signal — Not liking someone is ordinary. But if the reaction is out of proportion — the mention of them irritates you, you have to comment even when it doesn't concern you — it is probably not only about them. Ordinary dislike doesn't consume this much. Suppressed things don't vanish, they reroute — Jung's framing is conservation-like: what isn't acknowledged finds another exit. It can become fault-finding in others, a sudden loss of control, or a physical complaint. Acknowledging it is the least-effort option available. Owning it isn't acting on it — Admitting you'd also like to slack off, be praised, have the ambition, is not the same as slacking or grabbing. Jung means putting it back into consciousness where it can be managed — what's hidden can't be, what's on the table can. Where you are: there's a type of person you can't think about without anger, and you know your reaction is too big. Ask first: which exact quality am I reacting to? Write it down, then ask whether I have it and never let it out. Where it goes wrong: using it
q: When the dislike is out of proportion, it isn't only about them.
What you push down doesn't vanish. It changes exit.

chapters.n: Wear the mask long enough and it grows in
chapters.w: Necessary, but it has to come off
chapters.dek: What happens after years inside a role. Jung says the mask isn't the problem — here's where the problem is.
chapters.txt: Jung used the word mask for what a person puts on outside: the post, the identity, the version of you others expect. The mask is necessary; without it you can't deal with the world. The danger lies elsewhere — wear it long enough and you take it for yourself. Then every judgement starts from the role, and when the role is removed — retirement, redundancy, children leaving — whoever is left finds they don't know who to be. A mask isn't dishonesty. It's a necessary interface — The voice you use at work, the way you are with clients — masks, and they should exist. Jung isn't asking anyone to take theirs off. He's asking that you can tell them apart: which part the role requires and which part is yours. Telling them apart is what keeps it removable. The moment the role is taken is the moment you find out — Retirement, redundancy, children leaving are the same event: the mask removed from outside. How badly you panic then measures how much of what you built grew only on the role. The more complete the panic, the less the separating was ever done. Keep one area the role can't reach — In practice: hold on to something unrelated to your identity — an interest, a set of people who don't know your job title. Its usefulness isn't in how important it is but in not moving when the role does. It's what you're standing on when the role goes. Where you are: you've been in one role for years
q: The mask is necessary. The trouble is taking it for yourself.
What's left when the identity goes can't be seen in advance.

chapters.n: After losing to it, he changed the rules
chapters.w: Let people bring machines to the board
chapters.dek: When a machine wins at your craft, what's left of it. Why Kasparov invited the computer onto his own board.
chapters.txt: He beat Deep Blue in Philadelphia in 1996. In the New York rematch of May 1997 it beat him 3.5–2.5, the first time a world champion lost a formal match to a machine. A year later he staged an event in León under new rules: each side brought a computer to the board and could consult it at any time. He called it Advanced Chess. The reasoning was plain — calculation was already lost, so stop competing on who calculates faster. First identify what's no longer worth competing on — The day machines won on depth of calculation, the 'who sees furthest' track closed. Training on a closed track has no exit however hard you train. The first step isn't redoubling effort; it's striking the lost item off your own list of what you're worth. Change the rules, not the effort — He didn't train harder and he didn't switch fields. He changed what the contest permits. When a tool matches an ability, the valuable position moves to how the tool gets used — and somebody has to define that position before it exists. Inviting the tool in holds better than keeping it out — A contest that bans tools survives only on enforcement, and collapses the moment enforcement slips. A contest that permits them is measuring something else — something that doesn't expire as tools improve, because it improves alongside them. Where you are: a core skill in your field has been matched by a tool, and you're still training on the old track. Ask first: which item in
q: Calculation was already lost, so stop competing on calculation.
The first step isn't more effort. It's striking out what's lost.

chapters.n: The winner wasn't the best human or the best machine
chapters.w: It was the pair with the best process
chapters.dek: What human plus tool is actually good at. Why two amateurs won a tournament where everyone could use a computer.
chapters.txt: A freestyle online tournament in 2005 admitted grandmasters and supercomputers, with humans and machines free to team up. The winners were two American amateurs, Steven Cramton and Zackary Stephen, running three ordinary PCs. Their method was to ask all three and apply their own judgement only where the three disagreed. Kasparov later compressed it: a weak human plus a machine plus a good process beats a strong human plus a machine plus a poor one. The value moves from answering well to asking well — Where all three machines return the same answer, adding a person adds nothing. The human value concentrates entirely in the few moves where they disagree — finding the disagreement and judging which side to believe. That is a different job from playing chess. Process makes up for ability; ability can't make up for process — The amateurs won on a stable checking routine. The grandmasters lost by treating the machine as a reference and calling it themselves at the end. The first doesn't depend on how you feel that day; the second does. That is how weaker players beat stronger ones. Don't keep only one tool — With one machine there is no disagreement to look at — you either believe all of it or none of it. Three aren't valuable because the compute adds up. They're valuable because the places they disagree mark exactly where the problem is genuinely hard. Where you are: you already use the tools, and what you get out looks like what everyone else gets out of the same ones.
q: Where all three agree, adding a person adds nothing.
The human value sits in the few moves where they disagree.

chapters.n: He spent years arguing the match didn't count
chapters.w: Conceding is cheaper than appealing
chapters.dek: What the first year after being replaced usually looks like. What he did, and what he said twenty years later.
chapters.txt: After the loss he told the press that IBM had used human intervention mid-match, and demanded a rematch. IBM refused, and dismantled Deep Blue — leaving him without even an opponent to play again. He told that version for years. By the time he wrote Deep Thinking in 2017 he had withdrawn it himself: Deep Blue won, and that is all. The 1997 explanations were what he couldn't accept at the time. Appealing and moving on can't run in parallel — The effort to prove that match didn't count and the effort to work out what to train next come out of the same person in the same stretch of time. The first buys no new skill even when it wins. The other side isn't waiting for your post-mortem — IBM dismantled the machine, which shows the pattern: whatever replaced you doesn't need your agreement and won't hold a rematch open for you. Hoping to end this by getting the other side to concede is usually a wait with no end. Conceding isn't surrendering — The same year he accepted the loss he was staging a tournament under new rules. Accepting a result and giving up the craft are two different things — accepting it first is what freed his hands to change the track. Nobody swallowing their pride changes anything. Where you are: a tool or a new method has beaten you, and most of your energy is going into explaining that it's unfair or that it isn't actually good. Ask first: how many times this month have I
q: Whatever replaced you does not need your agreement.
Proving it didn't count and deciding what to train next cost the same hours.

chapters.w: Not famous, but deep enough
chapters.dek: Creators assume fame has to come first. This asks whether that assumption is necessary at all, and what replaces it.
chapters.txt: In 2008 Kelly worked out an arithmetic problem for independent creators: a creator needs to acquire only 1,000 True Fans to make a living. One thousand customers at a hundred dollars is a hundred thousand, which is enough for one person. His definition of a true fan is hard: someone who will buy anything you produce, who will drive 200 miles to see you sing, who buys the hardback and the paperback and the audio version of the same book. The value of the sum is not the number. It is that fame has been taken off the list of requirements. A thousand can be counted one at a time; a million cannot — This is the solid part of the sum. A thousand people, three a day, takes a year, and that is a schedule you can execute. A million is not something effort assembles, it is a lottery ticket. The two ask for completely different working days. A hundred dollars a year is a question about what you make — Run the number backwards and it turns into a design brief: what do you have to produce in a year that someone who genuinely likes you will spend a hundred dollars on? It pushes you off make more content and onto make one thing worth buying, which is different work. Kelly says this can become a second full-time job — He never sold it as the easy road. Maintaining a thousand direct relationships, answering mail, shipping orders, running events, is slow and absorbing work, and done properly it
q: A creator needs to acquire only 1,000 True Fans to make a living.
A True Fan is defined as a fan that will buy anything you produce.

chapters.w: The money has to reach you directly
chapters.dek: The sum carries a second condition almost everyone skips. This is what happens to the arithmetic once you skip it.
chapters.txt: Kelly set two conditions and most people remember only the first. The second is this: you must have a direct relationship with your fans; they must pay you directly. Put a platform in the middle and everything changes. It takes a cut, it holds the list, it decides who gets to see you. His 2008 reference points were blogs and MySpace. The present is tighter: a service like Spotify will hand you chart positions and never hand you an address. This is not a footnote to the essay. It is the switch that decides whether the sum works. Whoever holds the list holds your living — There is one test. If this platform throttles or bans you tomorrow, can you still reach those thousand people? If you cannot, you never had a thousand fans. You were renting somebody else's traffic and calling it an audience. The cut takes more than money, it takes the feedback — With a platform in between you cannot see who bought, why they bought, or when they stopped. What you lose is not only the percentage, it is the information that would let you improve. The expensive part of a direct relationship is the feedback, not the cash. Fix the exit before you chase the growth — Order matters here. Settle how do I take these people with me before you spend a year growing on somebody else's surface. Done the other way round, the day your follower count looks best tends to be the day your leverage is lowest. Where you are: you have
q: You must have a direct relationship with your fans; they must pay you directly.
The platform gives you chart positions. It never gives you an address.

chapters.w: Two different things
chapters.dek: The doctor says it is manageable and your life has caved in. Why Kleinman insists these are two separate things.
chapters.txt: Kleinman is a Harvard medical anthropologist and a practising psychiatrist, and his career turns on splitting one word into two. Disease is what the clinician creates: the numbers on the chart, the lesion in the organ. Illness is the lived experience of symptoms and suffering: the pain, the fear, the things you can no longer do, the person you have become at home. Modern medicine spends almost all of its effort on the first, and what people are actually undergoing is the second. The two sides are not discussing the same object, which is why they so often fail to meet. Normal results is not the same sentence as you are fine — A chart can declare a lesion gone. It cannot declare gone what the months did to a life. Plenty of people feel worse once treatment ends, because medicine has completed its task and the other half has nobody assigned to it. It was never on the form. What the patient says about it is evidence — Kleinman treats the account a person gives of their own sickness as a serious source: what they call it, what they think caused it, which part frightens them most. None of that is a medical fact, and all of it decides whether they take the drug and come back. Split the words and the work becomes visible — While the two are fused there is only one available move, which is to treat. Split them and there are two tracks: one belongs to the clinician, the other to you and the
q: Illness is the lived experience of symptoms and suffering.
Disease is what the clinician creates out of that experience.

chapters.w: The last one asks what you are afraid of
chapters.dek: What to ask, and what to be asked, in a consultation. Why Kleinman's list has these eight questions on it.
chapters.txt: In 1978 Kleinman and two colleagues published a short set of questions for clinicians, since known as the explanatory model interview. What do you call this problem. What do you think caused it. Why did it start when it did. What does it do to you, and how. How severe is it, and how long will it last. What treatment should you have. What trouble has it caused you. And last: what do you fear most about it. Seven of them ask how the person understands the thing. The eighth asks what frightens them, which is usually what is actually in the way. They ask about the person, not the pathology — Not one of the eight asks about symptoms, because the clinician can find those without help. They ask after the explanation the person is carrying around: cause, timing, consequence. That explanation can be wrong and it still governs every decision they make afterwards. The fear and the clinical priority rarely match — What the clinician is watching and what the patient is dreading are usually different objects. The clinician has the numbers. The patient may be afraid of never lifting a grandchild, of becoming a burden, of losing the job. Unasked, every reassurance lands beside the point. The list works on yourself and on your family — It is not reserved for clinicians. Run it before you take someone to an appointment and you know what to ask on their behalf. Run it on yourself and the fear and the judgement come apart. The written answers are usually
q: What do you fear most about this illness?
Seven questions ask for understanding. The eighth asks for the fear.

chapters.n: When Curing Fails, Care Does Not
chapters.w: Ten years looking after his wife taught him this
chapters.dek: Some illnesses cannot be cured. What is left to do. The answer Kleinman reached after ten years of caring for his wife.
chapters.txt: Joan Kleinman was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's in her fifties. For the next ten years her husband looked after her, until she died. He was the field's leading authority on caregiving and says he was not remotely ready: he had taught it his whole life and only learned what it costs when it was his own. He wrote the decade down, and the book rests on one distinction. Cure has a point at which it fails. Care does not. Medicine arrives at a place where it can do nothing, and being there is still available on the last day. Cure and care are two different goals — Cure asks whether this can be made to go away, and the answer is sometimes no. Once it is no, anyone working to that goal has nothing left to do. Care asks whether today can be made a little easier, which has an answer every single day, and the answer stays in your hands. Most of care is presence, not technique — What he returns to is not nursing skill. It is being there: recognising which version of the person turned up today, absorbing whatever comes up without warning, staying a while longer in the hours they are still themselves. No training required, only time, which is the scarcest thing. The carer is being used up, and that is a separate line — The least forgiving pages in the book are about his own collapse: exhaustion, guilt, resentment surfacing where he did not want it. He insists this is structural rather than moral.
q: Treatment can be handed over. Being there cannot.
When medicine hands it back, what you can do is not zero.

chapters.n: The con artist does not build trust
chapters.w: He uses the need you already have
chapters.dek: The first question after being taken in is how could I be so stupid. That question is itself the wrong one.
chapters.txt: Konnikova worked through a large number of cons and arrived somewhere counter-intuitive: the con artist does not manufacture trust, he finds a need you already have and uses it. The opening stage, what the trade calls the put-up, answers three questions about the mark. Who is this person, what do they want, and how does that want get me what I want. So the hinge is not intelligence, it is whatever you happened to be short of at the time. Which is why the educated and the worldly are on the list too. Ask which want it answered — When an offer moves you, hold off on whether it is true and ask why it lands now. The answer usually points at whatever you were most short of. This order matters, because checking gets steered by wanting and you go looking for what supports it. Being taken in is about circumstance, not intelligence — Filing it under I was stupid does two kinds of damage. It is inaccurate, and it makes the story too shaming to tell, so the same con keeps working on the next person. Filing it under what was I short of produces something you can actually change. Rules beat vigilance — Vigilance fails in the presence of wanting, because wanting is the thing eroding it. What works is a rule set in advance: above this amount, sleep on it; a second person has to look at it; there has to be an independent source. Made cool, applied hot. Where you are: somebody has made you an
q: The con artist does not build trust. He uses the need you already have.
Who is this person, what do they want, and how do I use it.

chapters.n: A transition is the dangerous window
chapters.w: When the old method stops fitting
chapters.dek: One person's judgement is roughly constant across a life, yet the losses cluster in a few stretches. This is about which ones.
chapters.txt: Her answer is the transition. Cons land most easily in periods of upheaval, when something new is happening and the old way of reading the world no longer covers it. A move to an unfamiliar city, a divorce, a death, redundancy, retirement, a sum of money arriving. What these share is not fragility, it is the absence of a usable template, which is why any explanation that hangs together sounds unusually credible. The practical value is direct: it turns not being conned from a personality into a calendar. The risk is a missing template, not low spirits — The real problem in a transition is that old experience does not map onto the new situation. You have never rented in this city, never handled an estate, never held this much money. What is missing is a reference, and a reference is exactly what the con supplies. Put the dangerous months in the diary — This is the operational part. For the first months after a move, a new job, a death or a large payment, add a procedure in advance: anything above a set amount goes past somebody who is not inside the situation with you.
