The same window rebuilds, so do not only defend — In the same stretch that old templates stop working, new habits and relationships form most easily. So a transition should not be spent entirely on defence. Split it: put procedure around judgement, and do more, not less, of the meeting people. Where you are: you have just been through a large change, a new
q: Cons land hardest when something new is happening in your life.
The danger is not that you are weak. You have no template.

chapters.w: One of them needs a comparison and the other does not
chapters.dek: Self-esteem is the word this generation grew up inside. The question is why it goes missing exactly when it is needed.
chapters.txt: Self-esteem runs on an algorithm: I am better than others. It draws its power from comparison, so it is at full strength when things go well and is first to leave when you fail. The moment you need it most is the moment it is not there. What she puts in its place does not compare: self-compassion asks not am I good enough, but what do I need now that this hurts. Across studies it does better on most measures — lower depression and anxiety, more motivation to correct mistakes — without the fragility of having to keep winning. Comparison is the fuel, so it fails in the trough — As long as better than others sits inside the definition, supply depends on continuing to win. One failure and the supply is cut, which is precisely the moment support was required. Self-compassion does not depend on rank, so it is still present in the trough. It does not lower the bar, it raises the will to fix things — The standing objection is that being kind to yourself makes you slack. The data point the other way: moving attention off am I a failure and onto what do I do about this makes people readier to admit errors and quicker to start repairing. Shame makes people hide. The usable test is whether you would say it to a friend — This is the most operable thing in her work. Take the sentence you are saying to yourself and say it, word for word, to a friend in the identical position.
q: The question is not am I good enough. It is what do I need.
Self-esteem needs you to be better, so it leaves when you fail.

chapters.n: Three parts, all present at once
chapters.w: Take one away and it turns into something else
chapters.dek: Self-compassion gets summarised as be nicer to yourself. It is three components, and they have to hold at the same time.
chapters.txt: She breaks it into three: self-kindness, common humanity and mindfulness. The point is that all three have to be present at once, because removing one turns it into a different thing. Kindness without common humanity is self-pity: why is it always me. Common humanity granted while you go on berating yourself is gritted teeth. Watching the pain clearly and refusing to be kind is detachment. So these are not three suggestions, they are three parts; a machine missing one is not running slightly worse, it is not that machine. Common humanity is the part that gets skipped — The most damaging thing inside pain is rarely the pain. It is the sense that it is only me. Acknowledging that many people have been through this is not consolation, it removes the premise. Skip it and the kindness left over degrades into self-pity. Mindfulness is neither amplifying nor denying — Both directions are out: sinking in and replaying it, and insisting it is fine. What is asked for is seeing how big the thing actually is, with nothing added and nothing taken off. Without that step the other two have nowhere to land. Remove one and it changes name, so check them one at a time — The model earns its keep as a diagnostic rather than as encouragement. When it hurts, go down the three, and usually only one is missing; supplying that one is enough. Most people are missing common humanity, a smaller number are missing mindfulness. Where you are: you know you should go easier on yourself, and
q: Self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness — all three at the same time.
Kindness without common humanity is self-pity.

chapters.w: The shape of the blind spot
chapters.dek: One sentence draws the border of self-knowledge. This is why the first admission is easy and the second nearly impossible.
chapters.txt: La Rochefoucauld was a defeated nobleman of the Fronde who spent his later years turning what he had seen at court and in the field into a few hundred maxims. Number 89: everyone complains of his memory, no one complains of his judgment. Admitting a poor memory costs nothing, since it is a hardware fault. Admitting poor judgement concedes that the ground under every past decision was unsound, and nobody can carry that. Number 31 travels with it: if we had no faults, we would not enjoy noticing them in others. People only admit faults that leave the base intact — Memory, stamina, a weak second language: these cost nothing to concede, because none of them disturbs the belief that you are a person who sees clearly. The real blind spots sit in the class nobody will own. A volunteered fault can usually be crossed off the list. Failures of judgement get rewritten by memory — After a bad call, memory quietly adds a layer of narrative: the information was thin, someone misled us, the luck was strange. A few rewrites later, no misjudgement has ever occurred. The only defence is writing the call and the reasons down at the time. Finding fault in others is a painkiller — Number 31 names the payoff in eager correction. Attention on somebody else's defects gives temporary relief from noticing your own. So the moment your urge to criticise runs hottest deserves suspicion: it tracks your position, not their error rate. Where you are: you are reviewing what happened, and the conclusion has
q: Everyone complains of his memory, no one complains of his judgment.
If we had no faults, we would not enjoy noticing them in others.

chapters.w: The disguise tells you the exchange rate
chapters.dek: He wrote hypocrisy up as an act of homage. Inside the sneer there is a working method for reading a place.
chapters.txt: Number 218: hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue. Vice has to dress as virtue in order to circulate, and that fact alone proves virtue is the hard currency there, since nobody disguises themselves as something worthless. The whole book runs this operation. Our virtues, he writes, are most frequently but vices disguised. Neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily. He is not arguing that people are wholly bad. He is taking the wrapping off so the structure of the exchange underneath becomes visible. What people fake tells you what the place pays for — Whatever people imitate is the currency of that environment. Where everyone performs long hours for the boss, hours are money. Where everyone competes to sound profound in meetings, talk outranks delivery. The direction of the pretence reads truer than the values on the wall. The existence of the disguise is worth more than exposing it — If vice has to dress as virtue to pass, then the norm requiring the dress has real value, because it constrains the surface of behaviour. A place where nobody bothers to pretend has stopped treating virtue as currency, and that is the deeper rot. Run the same operation on yourself — The hardest thing about the book is that it exempts nobody, the author included. Taking apart one of your own moral positions to see the interest underneath is not self-abasement. It lets you predict where you will wobble when the interest moves. Where you are: you have noticed that someone's good deed has an
q: Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.
Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised.

chapters.w: Theory comes after the result
chapters.dek: Theorists on both the left and the right attacked Singapore. This is about the single question he used to dismiss all of them.
chapters.txt: He told interviewers the same thing for forty years: he was not an ideologue, he was not enamoured of any theory, and reality and common sense were what guided him. One test decided everything. Does it work? Let's try it and if it does work, fine, let's continue it. If it doesn't work, toss it out, try another one. So the policy mix fits no spectrum: state-built housing next to unrestricted trade, harsh criminal law next to a sovereign fund. Inviting in multinationals was read across the developing world as selling out. He did not argue. He waited for the numbers. The theory is the map, the result is the ground — A theory earns its keep before you set out, by choosing a starting point. Once real feedback exists it outranks the theory: when map and ground disagree, the map is wrong. Most arguments are absurd because the ground is already visible and both sides are still comparing maps. Working has to be defined in advance — The pragmatism has a premise people skip: what counts as working was fixed beforehand — employment, housing, savings rates, hard numbers nobody can dress up. Without that, pragmatism decays into finding a story for whatever happened. Working costs you a decade of being wrong in public — Bringing in multinationals made him a traitor to the developing world's intellectuals in the 1960s; dependency theory said that road ended in vassalage. He carried the name for ten years until the results arrived. Anyone unwilling to pay that tax stays on the theoretically correct
q: Let's try it and if it does work, fine, let's continue it.
If it doesn't work, toss it out, try another one.

chapters.n: I would get up from my sickbed
chapters.w: Welding yourself to the outcome
chapters.dek: A sentence spoken on the edge of handing over, and it frightened people. This is about what such a binding buys and what it poisons.
chapters.txt: At the 1988 National Day Rally he was sixty-five and about to hand over. He told the country the line everyone has quoted since: even from my sick bed, even if you are going to lower me into the grave and I feel something is going wrong, I will get up. It was not rhetoric running away with him. It described his relation to the place exactly: he had built it piece by piece, from the day of the weeping press conference that followed expulsion from Malaysia. He then stayed in cabinet for more than twenty years. The binding buys a promise nobody else can make — The line is credible because it cannot be withdrawn. He welded the rest of his life to the outcome and left no exit marked leave if it goes badly. A hired executive cannot structurally offer this: their rational stopping point is the edge of the promise. The same sentence is the successor's ceiling — A predecessor who announces he will rise from his sickbed means every decision the next person makes is being examined by those eyes. That is the poison: the course is protected, and the room the next generation needs in order to be wrong and grow is gone. Bind yourself to the result, not to the seat — What he bound himself to was something going wrong — the country's outcome, not his own office. That distinction decides what the binding is. A predecessor watching results is insurance; a predecessor missing the chair is a shackle. The test is how
q: I feel something is going wrong, I will get up.
Bind yourself to the result, not to the seat.

chapters.w: The base camp or the capital
chapters.dek: In the middle of the An Lushan rebellion the emperor wanted his capitals back. This is about why Li Bi called that the worst move.
chapters.txt: In 757 Emperor Suzong asked how to end the rebellion. Li Bi's plan: let Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi pin the rebels down, running them back and forth between Guanzhong and Hebei until they were exhausted, then drive straight at Fanyang, An Lushan's home and base, where the families and the baggage were. Suzong wanted the two capitals first. He got them, the rebel core withdrew to Hebei, and the war ran six more years. Your Majesty wanted the capitals quickly, so the rebels grew strong again and we grew weak again. The conspicuous target is rarely the decisive one — The two capitals were the symbol, the legitimacy, the place everyone was watching. Fanyang was the supply, the families, the way home. Taking the first lets you announce a victory; taking the second ends the war. The return curves are not the same shape. Leave the base and they have somewhere to rebuild — Driving an opponent off and removing him are different outcomes. While the base stands, whatever you pushed back goes home, refills, reorganises and returns. So the quality of a victory is measured by whether the other side can still recover. Announcing early has a price, and it is payable — Suzong was not stupid. A newly enthroned emperor needed something he could proclaim, and that need was real. The price was six years. Every decision made in order to have something to report should be costed that way first. Where you are: there is a conspicuous target and a decisive one, and resources for only
q: Strike Fanyang, destroy the nest, and the root is gone for good.
You wanted the capitals quickly, so they grew strong and we grew weak.

chapters.n: He would not take the office
chapters.w: What refusing a post buys you
chapters.dek: He entered the centre of government four times and went back to the mountains four times. This is about what refusing rank bought him.
chapters.txt: Li Bi served four emperors — Xuanzong, Suzong, Daizong, Dezong. Each time he was fetched at the worst hour; each time he left once the thing was done. Suzong tried to give him office and he answered, I take no grain and have no household; what office could I hold? The emperor slept on a facing couch and rode beside him, and he still called himself a guest and wore a Taoist's robes. He remonstrated constantly — against killing Prince Jianning, against suspecting loyal commanders, against deposing the heir. Some of it was taken. He finally accepted the chancellorship in his sixties. With no seat, your words are not discounted — Once you hold a post, everything you say is heard as serving that post. Speaking as a guest, Li Bi gave the listener no motive to subtract. That is the structural reason he could keep saying the least welcome things for forty years. The ability to leave is the strongest chip — He could go back to the mountain at any moment, and he actually did. Advice from someone who can walk out weighs differently from advice from someone whose living depends on staying. What gets called backbone is usually an exit being available. The price is that you never hold the execution — No office means someone else carries out your plan. Fanyang refused is the ceiling of that arrangement: he could propose and could not decide. Taking the chancellorship at last is the admission that advice alone stops working at some point. Where you are: you have
q: I take no grain and have no household. What office could I hold?
He declined firmly, and asked to follow as a guest.

chapters.n: Ninety per cent of the time, thinking about failure
chapters.w: Think about losing before winning
chapters.dek: The richest man in Hong Kong describes his own split of attention, and it is not what you'd expect.
chapters.txt: In interviews Li Ka-shing has been blunt about it: ninety per cent of my time I spend considering failure. His image is a mechanical watch — one gear slightly faulty and the whole watch stops, and a company is the same. From his plastic-flowers days the habit was set: before a project starts, work through the ways it can fail. When success comes it needs very little thinking about. Beside it runs his rule on cash: a company can go bankrupt while profitable. Through decades of expansion his gearing stayed low. Rehearsing failure is insurance on the decision — Ninety per cent on failure isn't pessimism, it's a division of labour: failure modes are finite, listable and preventable. Having gone through each and set a gate, you can spend the remaining tenth committing hard. Optimism without that step stakes the company on luck. Find the gear that stops the whole watch — The watch image is precise about 'one gear'. What sinks a company is often not the main business but some unremarkable connector — a guarantee given, a maturity mismatch, one key person. So rank risks by whether they stop the watch, not by how big the business is. Cash flow is the floor under every failure case — Every rehearsed way of dying converges on the same place: is there enough in the account to get through. So his answer isn't don't take risks. It's make sure no single failure can cut the cash. Low debt isn't caution. It buys more chances to be wrong. Where you are:
q: Ninety per cent of my time, I spend considering failure.
One gear with the slightest fault and the watch stops.

chapters.w: The two characters on his office wall
chapters.dek: A businessman famous for expansion looks up at a scroll telling him to stop. Stopping and not daring aren't the same.
chapters.txt: Li Ka-shing's office carries a scroll with two characters usually read as 'know where to stop', from a classical line: know where to stop and then you can be settled. Alongside it is the principle he repeats: never forget stability while growing, never forget growth while stable. In practice that meant selling down in overheated property, and walking away when a bid passed his line — moves others read as missing the market. He hung that scroll during Cheung Kong's most aggressive expansion. The faster you accelerate, the more you need a brake pad in permanent view. Write the stop before you sit down at the table — In practice this means writing the exit condition before every entry: above this price we don't chase, past this amount we don't add, at this date we don't renew. Written while unemotional, it needs no heroism to execute. Recalculating 'is it worth it' in the room is calculating your pride. What stops is the exposure, not the ambition — This gets misread as contentment with a little. His record says the opposite — decades from plastics to property to ports to telecoms, the ambition never paused. What was capped was the exposure of any single bet. Aggressive on direction, limited per bet: the second is what keeps the first alive. Hang the brake pad where you see it daily — Framing those two characters on the office wall is mechanism design. This is the string that goes first when things are going well, so the reminder has to be physically present —
q: Know where to stop, and then you can be settled.
Never forget stability while growing; never forget growth while stable.

chapters.w: One source is not listening
chapters.dek: The emperor asked what makes a ruler clear-sighted. The answer he got describes an information structure, not a virtue.
chapters.txt: Taizong asked Wei Zheng what separates a clear-sighted ruler from a benighted one. Listening to all sides makes you clear; trusting one source leaves you in the dark. Then the examples: Yao and Shun opened the four gates, so no one could screen them off; the Second Emperor of Qin trusted Zhao Gao alone and did not know the realm had risen until it was over; Yang of Sui trusted Yu Shiji, and provinces were in revolt while the news never reached him. The conclusion is practical: when a ruler hears widely, the great ministers cannot block, and what is below reaches the top. Screening you off requires no lying — Zhao Gao and Yu Shiji need not have lied in every sentence; they only had to control which reports went up. When all information passes one person, that person decides the world you see without inventing anything. The root is the number of channels, not anyone's loyalty. The channels have to be strangers to each other — The value of hearing all sides comes from independence between the sources. Three accounts drawn from the same meeting and the same document are one thing heard three times. Real breadth requires people with no shared boss and no shared interest. Measure how fast bad news arrives — Yang of Sui's problem was not an absence of bad news; it was that bad news could not get to him. The most direct gauge of an organisation's information health is one number: from the moment a clear problem occurs to the moment you
q: Listening to all sides makes you clear; one source, dark.
Hear widely and the great ministers cannot block what comes up.

chapters.w: What holds you up can turn you over
chapters.dek: The line has been recited for over a thousand years. Under Taizong it was a piece of daily working discipline.
chapters.txt: Taizong told his attendants that the way of a ruler must begin with keeping the people whole; injuring the people to serve yourself is like cutting flesh off your thigh to fill your stomach — the belly fills and the body dies. To the crown prince he repeated one figure again and again: the ruler is the boat, the common people are the water; water carries the boat and water can capsize it. The image comes from Xunzi; in these years it was used as a check to run before every call on the people's labour. It was there to be applied, not admired. The thing holding you up is the thing that overturns you — What makes the figure sharp is the identity: it is not one force supporting you and a different force opposing you. The force carrying you is the one that can turn you over. So stability does not come from suppressing it; it comes from never taking it to the tipping point. Cutting the thigh happens gradually — The belly fills and the body dies describes a slow process: each extraction from below relieves the immediate difficulty at once, while the cost is spread across a future nobody is looking at. That is why it is almost always the best move this period, and exactly why it is dangerous. Keep one person whose job is to disagree — Wei Zheng remonstrated on more than two hundred matters and repeatedly left the emperor nowhere to go, and stayed. With bronze as a mirror you straighten your
q: Water carries the boat, and water can capsize it.
The belly fills and the body dies.

chapters.n: The argument at the start of Zhenguan
chapters.w: He took the slower road
chapters.dek: You inherit a wreck. Harsh law, or lenient rule? He picked the option everyone told him there was no time for.
chapters.txt: Early in the Zhenguan years the country was exhausted. Taizong asked what to do. Wei Zheng argued for government by benevolence and right. Feng Deyi rebutted him forcefully: after the Three Dynasties human character grew thin, which is why Qin used law and Han mixed in force — they wanted to transform people and could not. He called Wei Zheng a bookish man whose advice would wreck the state. Taizong went with Wei Zheng. Some years later: traders camped in the open, there were no more bandits, the jails stood empty, and doors were left unbarred. Taizong told his court: this is what Wei Zheng urged on me. The realistic-sounding option is usually the faster one — Feng Deyi's evidence was all historical experience and sounded far more solid than Wei Zheng's case. But his real advantage was not being right; it was showing results sooner. Harsh law works within the year, transformation takes several. The side called realistic usually has the short cycle. To beat a prejudice, take its premise to the end — Wei Zheng's counter was hard: if human character really declines one generation after another, by now everyone would be a ghoul, and there would be nothing left to transform. He did not out-read his opponent in history. He showed the premise produces an absurdity. Choosing slow means carrying the years in the middle — The result showed up several years later, and through those years there was nothing to display while Feng Deyi's route could be proposed again at any moment. The difficulty of a
q: Traders camped in the open, and the jails stood empty.
The side called realistic is often only the faster one.

chapters.n: The three men he was not the equal of
chapters.w: Saying out loud who is better than you
chapters.dek: At the victory banquet he asked why he had won, then answered himself. The answer is not modesty. It is an exercise of power.
chapters.txt: At a banquet in the southern palace at Luoyang he asked his officers why the empire had come to him and not to Xiang Yu. Someone said he was generous where Xiang Yu was grudging. He said they knew only half of it. In the tent, planning what settles a victory a thousand miles away, I am not the equal of Zhang Liang. For the state, the people, the supply lines, not the equal of Xiao He. For an army of a million, not the equal of Han Xin. These three are exceptional men, and I could use them. Xiang Yu had one Fan Zeng and could not. Naming who is better puts a price on a seat — Saying in public that a man beats you at one thing does two jobs at once. It fixes the value of his seat, and it makes plain who did the fixing. Handing out valuations is not handing over power; the man who prices the others is standing above them. He defined his own skill as the using — His account of himself was not that he was good at everything. It was that he could use these men. That one move takes a leader off the track where he competes with his own staff, and on that track the ceiling is whoever is the weakest person he can bear to keep. One Fan Zeng, and he could not use him — Xiang Yu's problem was never a shortage of talent. It was talent he would not let decide anything. Recognising ability
q: In the tent, settling a victory a thousand miles off, Zhang Liang beats me.
These three are exceptional men. I could use them. That is all.

chapters.n: Three clauses, and the rest repealed
chapters.w: A rule nobody can recite is not a rule
chapters.dek: He reached the capital first and held the entire legal code of an empire. He replaced it with three sentences.
chapters.txt: First into the passes, he took Xianyang, called together the elders and the powerful men of every county, and said they had suffered under the harsh laws of Qin long enough. Then the announcement: a covenant of three clauses only, that a killer dies, and that wounding a man or robbing him answers for itself. Every other Qin law was repealed. He sent his own men out with the Qin officials to explain it in the villages. They brought oxen and wine to feed the army; he refused, saying the granaries were full and he did not wish to put anyone to expense. Three, because three can be remembered — A rule works in proportion to the share of people who can recall it. Qin law was complete and unmemorable, so to an ordinary man it was a minefield he crossed daily. Three clauses can be recited, and recitation is the precondition of both obedience and trust. Subtract first, add later — Taking over a mess, the instinct is to write more rules. He did the opposite, cut down to three, and established the minimum order that had to hold. Everything else waited. Trust is the thing you build first; complexity is what you earn the right to add. Refusing the oxen is the second half of the same move — Announcing a rule is speech. Turning down the food is the act. The granaries are full, I do not wish to put you to expense — declining at the one moment he could have taken anything he liked did
q: The elders have suffered long enough under the harsh laws of Qin.
Three clauses only: a killer dies, wounding and robbery answer for themselves.

chapters.w: A foot under the table, and a new answer
chapters.dek: Half the sentence is out of your mouth before you see it is wrong. What he did next looks bad, and was right every time.
chapters.txt: Han Xin, having taken Qi, sent a letter asking to be made acting king of it. Liu Bang, penned in at the time and waiting daily to be relieved, read it and swore at the messenger. Zhang Liang and Chen Ping trod on his foot under the table. He understood, kept swearing without a pause, and turned the whole sentence around: a real man who settles the feudal lords becomes a real king, so what is this acting? Zhang Liang was sent with the seal to install Han Xin properly. Turning round beats being right the first time — His first reaction was wrong, and already spoken. What he had was not accuracy but the ability to change track the instant a signal arrived, and to fold the first half of the sentence into the new direction. People differ in judgement. They differ far more in turning speed. Keep a channel open for the foot — None of this works unless somebody nearby dares to tread on your foot while you are shouting, and unless you know what the pressure means. That channel is not a gift of character. It is built by years of letting yourself be interrupted and not punishing it. Face is the cheapest chip on the table — Reversing looks bad, and reversing from a curse to a coronation looks worse. He never hesitated at these moments, because he treated his own dignity as a cost he could pay at any time. Xiang Yu priced it high, at Hong Gate and again at the river. Where
q: A man who settles the lords becomes a real king. Why acting?
Zhang Liang and Chen Ping trod on his foot, then spoke into his ear.

chapters.w: Being right was never the hard part
chapters.dek: A speculator famous for speed put the credit somewhere unexpected. The chapter explains why sitting is harder than being right.
chapters.txt: His own summary is not what anyone expects from him. It never was his thinking that made the big money, he says; it was his sitting. He had watched the alternative all his life: men who saw the move coming and made nothing from it, shaken out by every pullback or cashing a small gain early. Men who can both be right and sit tight are uncommon, he concludes, and that is the whole difficulty. The hard part is not the analysis. It is that every day of sitting is a day of refusing to act. The money lives in the back half of the hold — A large move does not pay out evenly. The early stretch is the choppiest and the most testing; the compounding happens later. Getting off partway takes the uncomfortable section and hands over the valuable one, which is how people are right about direction and collect almost nothing. Not moving is an action that needs defending — Sitting is not the easy option; it is continuous resistance. The news, the swings and every friend's better idea all argue for a change. So it needs fortification: write the original thesis and the conditions that would falsify it, and permit movement only when one of those trips. Sitting only protects a judgement that is right — The sentence says right and sitting tight, and the two conditions are joined by an and. Using it to keep a broken position alive is the expensive misreading. Patience and stubbornness look identical from outside; the only test is whether
q: It never was my thinking that made the big money for me.
It always was my sitting. Got that? My sitting tight!

chapters.n: Hope and fear, the wrong way round
chapters.w: The instinct points in the wrong direction
chapters.dek: Four fortunes and several bankruptcies, distilled into one rule about two emotions pointing the wrong way.
chapters.txt: He traced his losses to a single inversion. When the position goes against a man he hopes, waiting for it to come back, and the loss grows. When it goes his way he becomes afraid of losing the profit, so he takes it early. His rule swaps them outright. Instead of hoping he must fear; instead of fearing he must hope. Fear the small loss becoming a large one and cut. Hope the small gain becomes a large one and hold. And he adds why it never stops working: speculation is as old as the hills, because people are not new. The instinct runs exactly backwards — Hoping over a loss and fearing over a gain is not a character flaw; it is the factory setting for humans facing gains and losses. Losses make people gamble and gains make people lock in. So the inversion cannot be run on reminders. It has to be run by mechanism. Cut fast, because a loss accrues interest — Hope applied to a loss compounds. Every extra day adds sunk cost, makes the admission harder, and raises the stake required to get back to level. That is where the fear belongs: not fear of this loss, but of the version that starts dictating every later decision. The rule does not excuse you from the work — Cutting losses and running winners assumes you can say what counts as going against you. Without a thesis set in advance, the inversion degrades into buying strength and selling weakness. His own ruin came in the stretches when
q: Instead of hoping he must fear; instead of fearing he must hope.
He must fear that his loss may develop into a much bigger loss.

chapters.w: Noticing is only the first step
chapters.dek: Invest in what you know is his most quoted line and his most misused. The half that gets dropped is the work.
chapters.txt: He ran Magellan for thirteen years at twenty-nine per cent a year, and his signature find came from a supermarket. His wife liked a pair of tights called L'eggs, so he looked into the maker, Hanes, and the stock became one of his best. Investing without research, he warns in the same book, is like playing stud poker and never looking at the cards. The find is a lead, not a decision. And the amateur's real edge, he argues, is seeing the change in your own work and life six months to a year before Wall Street. What you see on the floor is a leading indicator — An analyst reads the quarterly. You see what feeds it: which brand keeps going out of stock, which store has a queue, which supplier everyone in your trade is quietly switching to. Those run about two quarters ahead, provided you log them as leads instead of retelling them as anecdotes. Between liking a product and buying a company sits a questionnaire — A good product answers the demand side only. His checklist is on the supply side: how much of the revenue comes from this, how heavy the debt is, how many years of growth remain, whether the success can be repeated. Most I use it so I understand it losses skip that page. Knowing it well has its own blind spot — Investing inside your own industry gives a real information advantage and a real emotional debt. You will overrate the importance of your own link in the chain and underrate
q: Investing without research is like playing stud poker and never looking at the cards.
Never invest in any idea you can't illustrate with a crayon.

chapters.w: Holding is harder than choosing
chapters.dek: His fund compounded at twenty-nine per cent for thirteen years, and most of the people in it did worse. The gap has an anatomy.
chapters.txt: Magellan rose more than twenty-fold in his thirteen years, and Fidelity's own figures showed the average holder captured far less, with many losing money. They bought after the run and redeemed on every fall. The key organ for investing, he says, is the stomach, not the brain. His measure of normal is bracing: his big holdings could fall thirty per cent in an ordinary year, and if you cannot sit through a decline of fifty per cent, he writes, you should not own stocks at all. Drawdowns are the toll, not the accident — The path of a good asset includes regular sharp falls. That is the terrain, not a malfunction. Treat every drop as an incident and you will get out at each of them and watch the thing leave without you. The question before boarding is what will hold you through the fall. Dodging the dip costs more than the dip — Stepping out to avoid a fall requires being right twice, on the exit and on the re-entry. Miss either and you permanently forfeit a stretch of the return, and long-run returns are concentrated in a handful of days. Sitting it out sounds prudent and is the most expensive habit available. Stomach capacity is designed, not inherited — How much you can hold through is set by position size and by a written plan. A stake big enough to cost you sleep will break any conviction on a bad night. Decide in advance what happens at each level, so panic executes a document instead of a feeling.
q: The key organ for investing is the stomach, not the brain.
More money is lost preparing for corrections than in the corrections themselves.

chapters.w: How men live, not how they ought to live
chapters.dek: He has been abused for five hundred years over one sentence. This asks what that sentence actually claims.
chapters.txt: Chapter 15 opens by separating him from everyone before him. Many have imagined republics and principalities that were never seen or known to exist; but how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live that a man who neglects what is done for what ought to be done learns his own ruin rather than his preservation. That is not a recommendation to do harm. It is a statement of subject matter. He intends to write about how politics runs, not about how it should run. Design on ought, and it leaks on day one — Any arrangement resting on people being expected to behave has been built on an untested assumption. The realist order is the reverse: watch what people do when nothing is constraining them, and design for that. Concede first, handle second. Describing is not endorsing — He has been misread for five centuries because people took the description for the proposal. The distinction still costs money. Explaining why a mechanism works and recommending it are separate acts, and refusing to study the ugly ones leaves you unable to name what hit you. Necessary harm still has to be costed — He does not abolish morality, he turns it into an account that has to be settled. What does the thing you may have to do cost, can you carry that, is there a substitute? We don't do that sort of thing is cheap to say and useless on the day. Where you are: writing a rule, and quietly assuming people will co-operate with
q: How one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live.
A man who professes goodness in everything will come to ruin.

chapters.w: Deterrence has an edge, and he names it
chapters.dek: Loved or feared is the question everybody knows. The answer has a second half, and the second half matters more.
chapters.txt: Best to be both, he says, but the two are hard to hold together, and if one of them has to be given up, it is far safer to be feared than loved. The reason is structural: love runs on the other person's willingness, fear on means you hold yourself. Then comes the clause that rarely travels with the quotation. The prince must avoid being hated, and the way to avoid it is specific — keep off their property and their women, because men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of a patrimony. Love is theirs to withdraw, fear is yours to hold — Compliance built on goodwill ends the moment the other person changes his mind, and you cannot stop him changing it. This is not an argument for coldness. It is an argument against resting your stability on a variable you do not control. Hatred is the line you cannot cross — Fear and hatred are one step apart, and the step is whether you touched what the person treats as his own foundation. Penalties inside the rules produce fear. Reaching for dignity, property or family jumps straight to hatred, and hatred will pay any price to hit back. Deterrence has to be predictable — Fear that works is built on consistent follow-through, not on unpredictability. Someone nobody can read produces dread and paralysis rather than order, because when consequences cannot be forecast the safest move available to everybody is to do nothing. Where you are: setting a precedent on something, and swinging between
q: It is far safer to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both.
Inspire fear in a way that avoids hatred, even without love.

chapters.n: Fortune and the half left to you
chapters.w: Half is luck; the other half has a deadline
chapters.dek: How much is fate and how much is mine? He gives a ratio, and then says exactly when the half that is yours can be spent.
chapters.txt: Chapter 25 puts a number on it: fortune is the arbiter of one half of our actions, but she leaves the other half, or nearly so, to be governed by us. Then the image everyone remembers. Fortune is a violent river that carries everything before it when it floods; yet in quiet weather men can raise dykes and embankments, so that when the water rises again it runs off in a channel. His conclusion is not resignation. It is that the half you govern has to be finished before the flood. The window for preparing is the calm — Dykes cannot be built during the flood. Inside a crisis the room for choice is tiny, and nearly every move that helps had to be completed while nothing was happening. What an organisation survives is decided by what it spent when spending looked unnecessary. The cautious man loses when the times turn — His counter-intuitive point: a method succeeds because it happens to suit the moment. When the moment changes and the method does not, it fails. People almost never change their nature, so the caution that made a man is what finishes him when boldness is wanted. Concede the half that is not yours — Charge the whole result to yourself and you will be arrogant in good years and shattered in bad ones. Granting half to fortune concentrates attention on the half that moves, including the uncomfortable version of the question, asked after a win rather than after a loss. Where you are: everything is going well, and you
q: Fortune is the arbiter of half our actions; she leaves us the rest.
In quiet weather men can raise their dykes and embankments.

chapters.n: Turning the trial into a platform
chapters.w: Setting your own terms inside their venue
chapters.dek: Facing a possible death sentence, his lawyers urged a plea. This is why he read a statement from the dock instead.
chapters.txt: The Rivonia charges carried the death penalty. Mandela made a decision that was terrible law: he would not give evidence and would not be cross-examined, but would read a statement from the dock, trading the chance of acquittal for hours nobody could interrupt. The closing passage became the most famous courtroom speech of the century. It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die. He got life, not death. The world outside had heard those hours. Work out which arena decides it — Inside the rules of the court he could not win, because the evidence was there. But the trial was also running in a second arena, the watching world. He gave up the one he could not win and put everything into the one he could. Before judging the odds, work out who is judging. Giving up the defence bought wholeness — Under cross-examination his case would have arrived in fragments shaped by the prosecution's questions. Refusing bought one unbroken account. Breaking you into pieces is the main way an opponent controls what you can say, and dropping the exchange is sometimes how you keep the structure. Prepared to die was calculated — The line was not rhetoric. The prosecution was asking for death, so saying it in court was a public surrender of the posture of trying to survive. That visible cost is what made the statement unanswerable. Credibility is bought with exposure. Where you are: you have
q: It is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.
I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination.

chapters.w: Requisition the enemy's symbol
chapters.dek: Black spectators had spent years cheering the opposition. This is what he accomplished on the day he put the shirt on.
chapters.txt: The Springboks were a white team and an emblem of apartheid, and black South Africans had long supported whoever they played. At the 1995 World Cup final Mandela walked onto the pitch in the green and gold jersey, wearing the captain's number 6. A crowd of sixty thousand, mostly white, was briefly stunned, then chanted his name. South Africa won and he handed the trophy to the white captain. Five years later he gave the method away: sport has the power to change the world, the power to inspire, the power to unite people in a way that little else does. Destroying a symbol makes enemies, taking it over makes belonging — A new order normally abolishes the old symbols, renames the team, redesigns the badge. That confirms to the other side that they are losers being settled with. He reversed it: keep what they treasure exactly as it is and wear it himself. The emblem unchanged, the meaning replaced. Reconciliation has to be spoken in their language — A hundred speeches about forgiveness would have done less for that community than wearing the jersey once. Speeches were his language and rugby was theirs. A message sent in the receiver's own language needs no translation, and goodwill that needs translating arrives discounted. The resistance he had to hold off was his own side — The hardest opposition did not come from white South Africans. Most of his own party wanted the Springboks abolished, and he pushed this through over them. The first obstacle to reconciliation is never the enemy's hostility,
q: Sport has the power to change the world.
It has the power to unite people in a way that little else does.

chapters.w: Untie one knot at a time
chapters.dek: Everything is urgent and all of it is yours. The question is not effort but which knot to pull first.
chapters.txt: Written at Yan'an in 1937, the essay turns a tangle into a diagram. At any stage many contradictions exist at once, but only one of them is principal, and its existence and development determine the rest. Find it and the other problems change shape on their own. Miss it and effort gets spread evenly across ten urgent things, which looks like working on everything and lands on nothing. Every later application repeats the same opening question: what is the principal contradiction of this stage? The principal one is not the loudest one — The principal contradiction is not the most urgent item and not the hardest. It is the one whose solution changes the shape of the others. Until you have found it, more action ties the knot tighter. Finding it is half; cutting the rest is the other half — Better to sever one finger than to wound ten. Naming the priority is the easy half. The other half is genuinely putting the rest down, which means not doing them this stage, not doing them later. Spreading effort is usually reluctance, not blindness. When the stage turns, the knot moves — The principal contradiction is not fixed. Solve this one and the next stage surfaces a different one. The common death is holding on to yesterday's priority until the situation has changed the question and you are still answering the old one. Where you are: several things are all sounding at once and none of them feels droppable. Ask first: which single one, solved, would loosen most of the
q: Among the many contradictions, one is principal and determines the rest.
Grasp the principal contradiction and every problem is readily solved.

chapters.w: Knowing arrives through doing
chapters.dek: You understood the idea and nothing changed. This one asks where knowledge comes from, and answers: from carrying something out.
chapters.txt: Written at Yan'an the same year as On Contradiction. Two failures were common in the ranks: one man memorised manuals and treated conclusions drawn on somebody else's battlefield as his own knowledge; another charged on instinct alone. The essay refuses both. Real knowledge comes out of doing, then has to be checked against what happened, then done again. If you want to know the taste of a pear, you must change the pear by eating it yourself. Memorising without that loop is what he called book worship. Knowledge comes out of doing — Following an argument is not the same as being able to run it. A judgement that has never been struck back at by events is a sentence nobody has paid for yet. What survives hardens after you have taken something out into the world. Doing once is not the loop — One pass is not enough. Do without looking back and all you keep is fatigue. Look without going again and all you keep is an impression. Knowledge is a circle: act, review, act again, and the review has to be able to change the next act. A book hands you the result, not the circuit — What somebody wrote down is the product of a loop they finished. You get the conclusion; the trials, corrections and second attempts are not on the page. So reading can shorten your route and cannot walk it for you. Where you are: a shelf of method and not one live situation of your own. Ask first: which already-finished thing has
q: If you want to know the taste of a pear, eat it.
Practice is the criterion of truth.

chapters.w: Trading time for strength
chapters.dek: The weaker side that fights at the stronger side's tempo loses. This one is about changing the shape of the war itself.
chapters.txt: After Xuzhou and Nanjing in 1938, two errors were loud: that China was finished, and that victory would be quick. The lecture puts fought and unfought battles on one diagram, strategic defensive, strategic stalemate, strategic counter-offensive. It is not a forecast of dates; it is a rule about what may not be done. Do not trade your main force for the news value of one city. Do not seek a decisive battle before the fist has formed. Survive first, then talk about winning — The weaker side's first objective is not to destroy the other but to remain impossible to destroy. While the main force exists, time exists. Gamble it away and time goes to zero the same afternoon. Stalemate is not a pause, it is a change of rules — The middle stretch looks most like no progress. It is the war moving off the quick decision the stronger side is good at and onto the attrition you can survive. Whoever cannot bear the stalemate will reach for a decisive battle early. The counter-offensive waits for the fist — Going over to the attack is not a change of mood. It is scattered strength gathered into something that can be moved as one. Attacking before that is a donation; staying in stalemate after it wastes time on a stage that has already ended. Where you are: you are the weaker side and they want it settled this week. Ask first: is this engagement buying time or spending it? Where it goes wrong: trading the main force for visible small
q: Both the defeatists and those who promise a quick win are wrong.
Weapons matter in war, but the decisive factor is people.

chapters.w: Fight the war your weapons allow
chapters.dek: Someone else's victory does not transfer. This one asks what a method has to look like given your ground, your people and your weapons.
chapters.txt: In 1936 the Red Army was still in the northwest, and two imported methods were in fashion: Soviet field manuals, and the memory of the Northern Expedition. He put both down and asked a prior question. What is the character of war on this particular ground? Against a stronger and larger opponent, the method cannot be the stronger side's method. The essay turns opposition to book worship into a battlefield rule and writes concentrate a superior force and destroy the enemy one by one as an operating order. Against book worship — Opposing book worship is not opposing study. It is refusing to skip the look at your own ground. How the Soviets fought and how the Northern Expedition fought are other people's answers; imported as doctrine, the first engagement is lost on terrain. Concentrate a superior force — Concentrate and destroy them one at a time: three against one, finish, then move to the next. Spread out, it looks as though fighting is happening everywhere and nothing is punched through. On Contradiction says what to put down; this says how to place what is left. Your battlefield is not theirs — Where you are weaker and smaller, the method built for parity does not apply. Fighting with the weapons you have is not consolation; it is nailing the method to your actual strength instead of to the strength you are reading about. Where you are: you are holding a method that won for somebody else, on ground unlike yours. Ask first: how many of the conditions that method depends
q: No investigation, no right to speak.
Concentrate a superior force and destroy the enemy one by one.

chapters.w: Put it on the table
chapters.dek: The call was right and everyone still went their own way. This one is about getting a group to actually move on one judgement.
chapters.txt: March 1949. The organisation was about to change from fighting to administering, and what he wrote down was twelve rules of craft rather than a line of argument: how to run a meeting, how to question the people below you, how to push ten things along at once without noise, how to turn I think into I have counted. The earlier essays settle the judgement; this one starts after it. One person seeing clearly and a group moving accordingly are two different problems. Put the problem on the table — A disagreement that is not aired does not go away; it moves into the corridor afterwards and ferments. Tabling it is not about arguing. It lets whoever objects finish the reason out loud, because a reason left unfinished comes back in some other form. Learn to play the piano — All ten fingers move, but they do not come down together. Push only one thing and the rest rot; press ten evenly and what comes out is noise. The craft is in sequence: which is the melody this stretch, what accompanies it, who takes over next. Have the numbers in your head — Any quality shows up as a definite quantity. Feedback is good is an impression, not a situation. Retention is thirty-eight per cent this month against forty-one last month is a situation. Without quantity, the discussion is won by whoever is loudest. Where you are: the direction is settled and the group is still each running its own reading of it. Ask first: has the disagreement been finished
q: Put problems on the table; a meeting that hides them settles nothing.
Ten fingers all move, but pressed down together they make no tune.

chapters.n: What stands in the way becomes the way
chapters.w: The line, and the mechanism under it
chapters.dek: The most quoted line in the book, and the only one many English readers ever meet. Here is what surrounds it.
chapters.txt: He wrote it as emperor, in a reign with almost no quiet year in it: plague, war on the Danube frontier, a trusted general in revolt. The note reads: the impediment to action advances action; what stands in the way becomes the way. The mechanism is in the lines around it. The mind turns whatever blocks it to its own purpose, the way a fire takes what is thrown on it and makes flame out of it. The obstacle is not removed. It is burned. What is blocked is the route, not the destination — Almost always the thing in the way has closed one particular path you had imagined. Separate the path from the goal and most obstacles change from this cannot be done into take another road. People who cannot separate them read a route failure as a goal failure. The fire image is about capacity — A small fire is smothered by a large log; a big one turns the log into more of itself. So the same setback lands differently on different people, and the difference is not in the setback but in how much was already burning. What you absorb depends on what you stocked. The conversion has to name an action — Turn adversity into fuel is a slogan until it produces a next step. His use is concrete. This thing has blocked one route, so ask what it exposed, what it freed up, and whose real attitude it just showed. All three questions have specific answers. Where you are: something you planned has
q: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
A fire makes flame and brightness out of everything thrown into it.

chapters.w: Pull the scale back
chapters.dek: A year from now most of this will be gone from memory. The exercise is how to borrow that later view now.
chapters.txt: He runs the same drill over and over: pull the eye back until the thing in front of him is small. Asia and Europe are corners of the universe, he writes, and the whole ocean a drop. He reminds himself that the men with the loudest names are long gone, and so are the people who remembered them. This is not nihilism, it is calibration. He was the emperor. Everything on his desk was described to him as gravely important, and he needed a ruler that could tell him which ones really were. Urgency is mostly proximity — A thing looks enormous largely because it is close. Stretch the timescale to a year or five and nearly everything currently costing you sleep shrinks to its right size. The two or three that do not shrink are the ones worth the whole week. Pulling back is not opting out — The point of the wide view is to allocate attention, not to cancel action. He kept governing and went to the front in person. The exercise hands out weights, not excuses, and using it to prove that nothing matters is using it backwards. Use the same ruler on people — He turns it on whoever has just offended him: in a few decades that person is gone and so are you. It does not delete the offence. It lowers the volume of the response, and the response is usually where the actual damage comes from. Where you are: one thing has taken over and you cannot work on anything else. Ask
q: Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the ocean, a drop.
Not the thing disturbs you, but your judgement about it.

chapters.w: Go through the people you will meet today
chapters.dek: Book Two opens with a preparation, not a reflection. The claim is that offence you expected does about half the damage.
chapters.txt: The first line of Book Two is a script to be said on waking: today I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful, the envious, the unsocial. Then the reasoning. They are like this because they cannot tell good from harm; I can, so they cannot injure me and I will not be angry with them, since we were made to work together, like hands, like feet, like the two rows of teeth. It is a daily rehearsal, not a one-off complaint. Expected offence lands at half strength — Most of the force in anger comes from surprise rather than from the event. Walk through the difficult turns the day may take, and when one arrives you are in of course rather than in how dare they. That gap is where a choice about the response fits. Rehearse your own move, not their behaviour — You cannot make the other person easier. The whole preparation lands on your side of the table: how I intend to answer, when I do not answer at all, where the line is. Turned into a list of grievances about them, it does the opposite of its job. Assume they do not know, not that they are bad — His attribution is ignorance, not malice. The practical value is that ignorance and conflicting interests are both things you can work on, whereas once you decide the other person is bad the only move left is to fight him. Where you are: there is a meeting today that you already expect to
q: Today I shall meet the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful.
They are like this because they cannot tell good from harm.

chapters.w: Pricing in the consensus
chapters.dek: Two people can look at the same good company and reach opposite conclusions. Marks says the difference is which level the thinking happens on.
chapters.txt: The Most Important Thing opens on the contrast. First-level thinking says: it's a good company, let's buy the stock. Second-level thinking says: it's a good company, but everyone thinks it's a great company, so the stock is overpriced — let's sell. The first level handles facts. The second handles what everybody believes about those facts, which is also a fact, and one already sitting inside the price. His conclusion is blunt: you cannot do what everyone else is doing and expect to outperform. Different, and more right. Both, or neither. The consensus is already in the price — If everybody knows the company is good, you have paid full price for that knowledge. So the second-level question is never whether it is good. It is whether it is better or worse than the price already assumes. The object of judgement has moved. Being different is only half of it — Marks says it plainly: different and right wins, different and wrong loses worse. Contrarianism is not a strategy, it is exposure — it magnifies whichever one you are. So the weight falls on a single question: what do I know that the consensus does not? The second level is a questionnaire, not a thought — He lists what it takes: what is the range of outcomes, which do I think will happen, what odds am I giving myself, what does the consensus expect, where do I differ, and which of the two is in the price? The first level is one sentence. Where you are: you have spotted an opportunity
q: You can't do the same things others do and expect to outperform.
Second-level thinking is deep, complex and convoluted.

chapters.w: Don't forecast, locate
chapters.dek: He refuses to forecast and still bought two generational bottoms. What replaces the forecast is a reading of where we are standing now.
chapters.txt: Marks gives up on prediction: nobody knows the macro reliably, so he stops trying. Then he changes the question. We may never know where we're going, but we'd better have a good idea where we are. The cycle cannot be forecast; your position on it can be measured. He calls it taking the temperature — is credit loose or tight, are buyers begging their way in or sellers begging their way out, are the sceptics or the believers louder. Two rules sit underneath: nothing runs one way forever, and the mood swings like a pendulum that barely pauses at the midpoint. What forecasting can't answer, location can — Nobody knows what next year does. But where you sit on the arc has readings you can take today: how hard it is to raise money, how thorough diligence has become, how bad news gets absorbed. That will not date the turn. It tells you whether to lean forward or back. The extremes give the cleanest readings — Mid-arc the thermometer is vague; at the ends it is obvious. Universal fear and universal fearlessness are both easy to recognise. The hard part is acting on the reading, because the action it calls for is the exact opposite of how the moment feels. Being early is the fixed cost of this method — Acting on position means being early almost by construction: you turn cautious past the midpoint and the pendulum runs on for another year. Marks says being too far ahead of your time is indistinguishable from being wrong. That stretch is
q: Trees don't grow to the sky, and few things go to zero.
The mood swings of the securities markets resemble the movement of a pendulum.

chapters.n: Burnout has three parts. Tired is one
chapters.w: The other two warn you earlier
chapters.dek: Tired and burnt out are not the same thing. The three measures Maslach used to separate them.
chapters.txt: In 1981 Maslach built an inventory that split burnout into three components: emotional exhaustion (drained in a way sleep doesn't repair), depersonalisation (you start handling people as items, and can't summon interest in any of them), and a fall in personal accomplishment (nothing you do feels like it matters). Only the first overlaps with being tired. So somebody can look like they're working normally and still be delivering, while the other two have been running for months. Detachment warns earlier than exhaustion, and gets misread — Rest fixes tired. It does not fix detachment. Detachment looks like having nothing for colleagues, customers or family, and speech going formulaic. Others read it as someone turning cold; the person reads it as their personality changing. It's the second measure lighting up. 'I'm useless' isn't modesty, it's a reading — The third component is accomplishment collapsing: the same work finished, and where there used to be a little satisfaction there is now nothing. It gets treated as an attitude problem. On the inventory it is as measurable as the other two. They don't arrive together, so don't wait for the set — For most people detachment comes first, then exhaustion, and accomplishment collapses last. By the time all three are present, recovery takes far longer than it would have when one appeared. One of the three is enough to take seriously. Where you are: you suspect you're burnt out and keep telling yourself it's just tiredness. Ask first: which of the three do I have — drained, nothing left for people, no satisfaction
q: Sleep fixes tired. It does not fix detachment.
Still working normally and still delivering proves nothing about the other two.

chapters.n: Fix the job, not the person
chapters.w: Teaching people to relax repairs the wrong thing
chapters.dek: What to do about burnout. The mainstream answer may have the whole thing backwards, and she says why.
chapters.txt: The moment burnout was named, the market's fix became teaching people to relax: mindfulness, time management, resilience training. Maslach has argued against that direction for decades. Her claim is blunt: burnout is a problem of the work environment, not of individual resilience. Spending the effort on remaking the individual asks the person absorbing the damage to repair the thing causing it — and carries a second message along with it: if you can't take this, you aren't strong enough. Putting the responsibility in the wrong place makes it worse — Tell someone the problem is their attitude and they add a layer of self-blame, then stay in the same environment. The two together are much harder to climb out of than the exhaustion was on its own. Personal fixes aren't useless, they're second — Maslach never said sleep and exercise don't work. She said the order matters: see what in the working conditions can change, then talk about personal regulation. Reverse the order and personal regulation stops being support and starts being cover. For an individual, this means check the environment first — You may not be able to change the company, but you can do the accounting: is it too much work, or no say, or work that runs against what you care about? Each diagnosis points at a completely different move — what to negotiate, what to leave, what to refuse. Where you are: you're close to done, and everyone advises you to adjust your mindset and rest more. Ask first: if I took a month off, would
q: Asking the person absorbing the damage to repair its cause is backwards.
A mindfulness course and an unchanged rota send everyone back to the same schedule.

chapters.w: Workload is only the first
chapters.dek: Same hours, and one person breaks while another doesn't. The six places she found the mismatch.
chapters.txt: Maslach and Leiter split the sources of burnout into six areas — the places where a person and a job fail to match: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Most people watch only the first. In her data the later ones are often more lethal, particularly having no say (control) and doing work that runs against what you believe (values). At identical hours, people matched on all six rarely break; people short two or three break quickly. Little work with no control hurts more than lots with control — Control is the second area and the most underrated. Few tasks, each needing sign-off and liable to be overturned at any moment, costs far more than a heavy load you get to arrange yourself. This matches what the stress research found independently. A values mismatch is the slowest and the deepest — The sixth area is doing work that runs against what you care about. It doesn't strike the same day; it hollows out the meaning gradually — the longer you do it the emptier it gets, and the less you can say why. Fix the other five and this one still takes you down. Score them separately or you can't tell what to move — 'Work is exhausting' implies no action at all. Score the six one by one and the answer usually gets specific: what you need to fight for is decision rights, or what you need to raise is fairness, or what you need is different work. Where you are: you can't say what is draining you,
q: Little work needing sign-off costs more than lots you decide yourself.
A values mismatch doesn't strike today. It hollows the meaning out slowly.

chapters.w: Setting the mission at the price
chapters.dek: He watched a stranger drink from somebody's outdoor tap and go unscolded. The company mission he wrote out of that scene.
chapters.txt: In 1932 Matsushita named the year the first year of knowing the mission. At the founding anniversary he described the scene: a passer-by turns a roadside tap, drinks, and nobody scolds him, because tap water is so plentiful and so cheap that it is nearly free, though it plainly has value. Then the mission: the mission of a manufacturer is to make goods as inexhaustible and as cheap as tap water, and by that route to drive poverty out of the world. It is not a charitable declaration. It is a product strategy with scale, process and distribution all ordered behind one number. Write the mission as something you can measure — Most missions are adjectives, excellent or leading or people-first, and an adjective can neither be checked nor give an order. This one is a quantity: price against reach. Every quarter you can answer whether you got closer to tap water, so the mission becomes a production schedule rather than wall decoration. Cheap is a capability, not a concession — Making cheapness the mission forces the hard crafts: yield, scale, turnover, distribution efficiency. Every cent of price cut has to be paid for by a real improvement in the cost structure. Cheapness bought by giving up margin is bleeding; cheapness bought by capability is a moat. Short term the statements look alike. Below a threshold the market changes order of magnitude — Under a certain price a product changes species: from something worth considering into something used without thinking, and the market widens from those who can afford it
q: The mission of a manufacturer is to overcome poverty and bring society wealth.
Make goods as inexhaustible and as cheap as tap water.

chapters.n: When it rains, open your umbrella
chapters.w: Management by the obvious
chapters.dek: Asked for the secret of management, he answered in six words. Why the almost dismissive answer is the hardest one to follow.
chapters.txt: Somebody asked Matsushita the secret of management. His answer: when it rains, open your umbrella. There is no trick to it. Do the obvious things in the obvious way, without exception: pay your suppliers, collect what you are owed, close the books daily, fix the product until it is good. Listeners were often disappointed, and he insisted that was all of it. In the slump of 1929, warehouse full and everyone urging layoffs, his move was just as plain: not one employee dismissed, production halved, the whole workforce out selling stock. Months later the inventory was gone. Hunting for a secret is avoidance of the basics — People who ask for the secret usually want a way round the things everybody knows and nobody does daily: collection, inventory, quality, keeping your word. Six words close that road off. What looks like mastery is the obvious, executed without exceptions. The hard part is opening it while standing in the rain — The counter-examples happen daily: knowing you should chase the invoice and not chasing it because the client matters, keeping a line alive for pride, producing while the inventory towers. Between the simplicity of the principle and the difficulty of the act sit luck, face and habit. Six words treat those three. The umbrella of 1929 covered what would not move — Handling a crisis is entirely about choosing what varies and what does not. He varied output and job content, and did not vary employment itself. Putting people in the fixed column is what let a whole workforce switch to
q: When it rains, open your umbrella.
Do the obvious things in the obvious way, without exception.

chapters.w: Where the ground under power actually is
chapters.dek: Read for two thousand years as ancient humanism. It reads better as a technical claim about where a government's power comes from.
chapters.txt: The people are the most important; the altars of grain and land come next; the ruler counts least. He ranked all three, and put the ruler at the bottom. This is not a plea for kindness, it is his judgement about what keeps a regime standing. Elsewhere he is blunter. There is a way to gain the empire: gain the people. There is a way to gain the people: gain their hearts. So benevolent government, in Mencius, is not the ruler's private virtue. It is the condition of his continuing to be the ruler. Consent is a thing that gets withdrawn — The heart of the people is not affection, it is consent. People rarely revolt at the moment they turn; they stop cooperating first. The tax gets harder to collect, the levy comes up short, the order goes down and nobody carries it out with care. The power is already hollow while the name is intact. The order cannot be inverted — Put the institution, or the man at the top, in front of the people who carry the cost, and you get one specific family of bad decisions: the ones that protect a reputation or an earlier judgement by charging somebody else for it. Authority holds. The ground under it goes. Tax, service and punishment are three measurable lines — He never leaves benevolence at the level of a concept. The items are specific: do not take men away in the farming season, keep the taxes light, keep the punishments few. All three are countable, and all three
q: The people come first, the altars of the state next, the ruler last.
Gather for them what they want; do not impose what they hate.

chapters.n: Two different ways of being obeyed
chapters.w: Compliance and conviction look identical
chapters.dek: Two people are doing what you asked, and the two cases have nothing in common. This is how to tell which one you have.
chapters.txt: He sets them side by side. Those subdued by force do not submit in their hearts; they submit because their strength is not enough. Those won over by virtue are pleased in the heart and submit in earnest. Then the mechanical detail: obedience bought by force has to be paid for continuously, and the moment the balance of strength shifts it disappears. Which is why he adds that a man using force under a borrowed name becomes a hegemon, and a hegemon needs a large state, while one who acts from virtue becomes a king, and a king need not be large. The measurement is taken while you are away — In your presence the two kinds of obedience are indistinguishable, which is why watching harder tells you nothing. The difference only appears in your absence, so the test is simple: over the stretch when nobody was checking, did the standard hold or drop? Force costs the same every day, then more — Their strength is not enough names the property that matters: force has to keep being applied. Supervision, scoring and checking never get cheaper with time, and they get dearer as people learn to handle them. Conviction costs most at the start and then tends towards nothing. A king need not be large — Force needs mass behind it, so the smaller party always loses that contest. Conviction does not. This is the route Mencius leaves open to the weaker side: you cannot become stronger than them this year, but you can become more worth following than them
q: Those subdued by force submit for lack of strength, not in their hearts.
The hegemon needs a large state. The true king does not.

chapters.w: It accumulates, and it cannot be hurried
chapters.dek: Asked what the flood-like breath was, he said it is hard to put into words. Here is where it comes from, and how it leaks away.
chapters.txt: He calls it vast and unbending, and then says where it comes from: it is produced by an accumulation of right acts, and is not seized by one righteous act from outside. Then the counter-example. A man of Song, impatient at how slowly his rice was coming on, went through the field pulling every shoot up a little, and came home saying he was worn out from helping the rice to grow. His son ran out to look. The whole crop had withered. The breath cannot be hurried. Accumulated, never acquired — Steadiness comes out of the record of things you have actually got right, one at a time. That is why it cannot be rushed and cannot be borrowed. Confidence somebody else hands you does not survive contact with the first real pressure; the sort you banked yourself does. One thing done against yourself and it leaks — Do a thing your own heart cannot approve, he says, and the breath starves. The mechanism is practical rather than mystical: next time you have to hold a line, you know about the exception, and so does everyone who watched you make it. Do not pull the shoots — The opposite failure is impatience: pressure, slogans and short-term targets used to force a state of mind into existence. The shoots do look taller. His instruction is to always have the work in hand, never to forget it, and never to help it along. Where you are: under pressure you find there is nothing solid underneath you, and you want to fix
q: It is produced by accumulated rightness, not seized by one act from outside.
Do a thing your heart cannot approve, and the breath starves.

chapters.n: To philosophise is to learn to die
chapters.w: After he was thrown from the horse
chapters.dek: He tells you to think about death daily, which sounds morbid. Then he reports having very nearly done it.
chapters.txt: One essay is titled That to philosophise is to learn to die, and its method runs against instinct: do not look away, think about it daily, until it stops being strange. This is not theory. In his thirties a rider knocked him off his horse from behind; he was unconscious a long time and the people around him thought he was dead. Coming back, he wrote the whole passage down. It had been light, like falling asleep, nothing like the horror he had spent decades imagining. Mostly you fear the imagining, not the thing — He came close enough to find the moment itself quiet. Decades of dread had been aimed at a version his own head had built. The experience cannot be lent to anyone, but the sorting can: separate fear of the event from fear of your picture of it. Avoided it stays terrible, looked at it flattens — His method is to make death ordinary: mention it, think of it, keep it as an acquaintance. Only the unfamiliar is frightening; once familiar it is merely a fact. Refuse to look and the fear stays permanently new, which is exactly what keeps it strong. Learning to die is learning to weigh — He says whoever has taught people to die has taught them to live. Once the heaviest item has genuinely been handled, the arguments and the wounded pride of an ordinary week change weight. This is not detachment, it is pricing: using the heaviest thing to value the rest. Where you are: you lie awake thinking about
q: The thing I fear most is fear.
He who has learned how to die has unlearned how to serve.

chapters.w: Put your own weaknesses on the table first
chapters.dek: He wrote down his cowardice, his bad memory, his dithering. Not as confession. As a position that cannot be attacked.
chapters.txt: In 1576 he had a medal struck for himself carrying three words: What do I know? The Essays are that question worked out at length. He writes that his memory is poor, that he dislikes pain, that he hesitates and contradicts himself from one page to the next, and he softens none of it. I do not portray being, he says, I portray passing. Four hundred years on it is still read, partly because the author's faults are placed at the front, where nobody else can pick them up and use them. A card you play yourself cannot be played against you — What people afraid of exposure actually fear is somebody else naming the weakness first.
