He inverts it and names it himself, more fully than anyone else could be bothered to. Once a thing is face up on the table it has stopped being in anybody's hand. What do I know is a stance, not a modesty formula — He is not performing ignorance. He has made I might be wrong his permanent standing position. From there, being corrected requires no defence, because no claim to being right was ever made. Defending is the expensive part, and he simply removed the bill. Inconsistency is not a flaw, it is a person — He says he portrays passing, not being. Most people panic when someone says that is not what you told me last time. He does not, because he announced from the start that he changes. Admit that you move and nobody can pin you to a fixed
q: What do I know?
I do not portray being. I portray passing.

chapters.n: At thirty-eight he moved into the tower
chapters.w: He fenced off a piece for himself
chapters.dek: The famous retirement was not a retirement. What he actually did is smaller, repeatable, and the reason the book exists.
chapters.txt: In 1571, aged thirty-eight, he resigned his post as a magistrate in Bordeaux, went home to the family estate, and turned the third floor of a tower into a library, with an inscription on the wall saying he was weary of public duties and meant to give what remained to himself. The Essays were written in that room over the next twenty years. He also served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux in the middle of it. When kidney stones arrived he wrote the pain down there, page by page. Not withdrawal, a fenced-off piece — He did not become a hermit; he was mayor twice afterwards. What he did was nail down one space and one stretch of time as his and leave everything else running. Full retreat is flight, no retreat is being eaten. The position that holds is between them. Mark it, and say it out loud to yourself — He had the decision carved into the wall. That is not decoration, it is turning a vague intention into a visible fact he walked past every morning. A decision that has been written down outlives one that was only thought about. The pain got written in that room too — When the stones came he did not stop. The illness became material rather than an interruption. Having a place of your own means bad things also have somewhere to be put, which is precisely the moment most people give the place up. Where you are: the calendar is full, none of it is yours, and clearing all
q: Full retreat is flight. No retreat is being eaten.
A decision written down outlives one that was only thought.

chapters.n: Change the environment before the behaviour
chapters.w: Out of reach is what looks like defiance
chapters.dek: Children considered unmanageable changed when the room changed. What was it that actually changed?
chapters.txt: In a poor district of Rome, Montessori did something then considered absurd: child-sized furniture, tools a child could work alone, children choosing their own activity, adults stepping in only when needed. Three- to six-year-olds thought unmanageable began repeating an activity for tens of minutes and tidying up afterwards. She called the state normalisation, and drew the foundation of the whole method: a child's work isn't taught into them; it happens in a prepared environment. Check whether the environment matches — A cup out of reach, a tool only an adult can operate — these manufacture dependence and frustration. Change the environment so the child can finish alone and the behaviour problem often disappears. It holds for adults too: plenty of self-discipline problems are environment problems. Concentration grows, it isn't demanded — She saw children concentrate for a long time on self-chosen work and lose focus quickly on assigned tasks. So the route to concentration is offering attractive choices and not interrupting — and the most common interruption is an adult's well-meant attention. The adult steps back into observer — This method asks more of the adult than the child: hold back from directing, from doing it for them, from prompting early. Montessori required teachers to learn observation first — see where the child is stuck and what they need, rather than pushing a plan along. Where you are: your child repeatedly can't do something and saying it again hasn't helped. Ask first: at their height, with their grip, with these tools — is it actually possible? Which single thing in
q: A child's work isn't taught in. It happens in a prepared room.
Education is not what the teacher said. It's what the child did.

chapters.n: Help me to do it myself
chapters.w: Doing it for them saves your time
chapters.dek: Doing it for them takes two minutes. What those two minutes bought, and what they cost.
chapters.txt: Montessori compressed the whole method into a child's request: help me to do it myself. That draws the boundary of help — the goal is that they can finish alone, not that the task finishes sooner. What an adult saves by taking over is their own time; what is spent is that one chance to learn. She also described sensitive periods: stages when a child absorbs a particular capacity with almost no effort. Hit the window and it is nearly free. Miss it and the same thing costs several times as much. Lower the difficulty to just within reach — The right intervention is neither taking over nor leaving them to it. It's adjusting the difficulty: break the task to a step they can do now and leave that step to them. It's the same thing deliberate practice calls the edge of the comfort zone, happening at three. Sensitive periods: wrong timing doubles the work — At two, a child is intensely sensitive to order, and habits of putting things away form easily. Try to establish the same rule at seven and the difficulty is completely different. Reading which period they're in beats working from an age chart. Slow is a cost and an investment — Letting a child do it will be slower and messier. Accepting that cost requires a longer time horizon: the ten extra minutes today buys years of not having to be involved. When the arithmetic doesn't get done, adults take over indefinitely. Where you are: they're slow and doing it badly and you can't stop
q: Help me to do it myself.
Every unnecessary help is an obstacle to development.

chapters.w: Study the ways it dies first
chapters.dek: He was asked how to have a good life and answered the other question instead. The swap is the whole method.
chapters.txt: Invited to address a graduating class, he announced he would explain how to guarantee a miserable life, and then worked through it: be unreliable, learn only from your own experience, go down when you take your first reverse, be consumed by envy and resentment. If you knew where you were going to die, he liked to say, you would simply never go there. The talk is the method demonstrated on itself, and it is more usable than any list of virtues he could have read out instead. One list is short and the other isn't — There are countless ways a thing can go well and a small number of ways it reliably goes wrong. The inverted question is simply a smaller problem, and a smaller problem is one you can actually finish. Failure modes are checkable; success stories aren't — You can go and look at whether the runway is short, whether one customer is half the revenue, whether the one person who understands the system is leaving. 'Is this a great idea' has no such test. It does not tell you what to do — Avoiding every failure mode leaves you alive, not successful. Inversion clears the ground; something still has to be built on it. Used alone it produces people who are very good at not losing and have not won anything. Where you are: about to commit to a plan you believe in. Ask first: spend twenty minutes writing only the ways this fails, then check how many are already true today. Where it goes wrong:
q: Invert, always invert.
If you knew where you were going to die, you would never go there.

chapters.w: The danger is the skill, not the ignorance
chapters.dek: What he warned about was not ignorance. It was being very well trained in exactly one thing.
chapters.txt: At USC in 1994 he laid out the method of his life: you have to carry a number of models in your head and hang experience on that latticework. He put the count at eighty or ninety, drawn from mathematics, psychology, physics, biology and engineering. The warning attached to it is the line everyone knows: to a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail — and the man with the hammer is not the ignorant one, he is the well-trained one. The deeper the training, the better hidden the distortion — The hammer problem is not incompetence. It is that your discipline arrives with a viewfinder: the finance person sees a cost problem, the growth person a funnel problem. Each account is coherent, because any problem does have that face — and the coherence is what stops the search. Problems do not arrive by department — A pricing decision is economics and psychology and, because the competitor reacts, something close to biology. The latticework means laying several models over the same situation and seeing which one explains the most, rather than which one you already own. Load the models before you need them — A model you go and look up during the decision arrives too late to shape it. The models have to be in the head and automatic. There is no shortcut: take the two or three hardest ideas from each field and keep them. Where you are: diagnosing a problem inside your own speciality. Ask first: how would someone from a completely different
q: To a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.
The hammer man is not the ignorant one. He is the trained one.

chapters.n: Stop while it is still running
chapters.w: So tomorrow has somewhere to start
chapters.dek: Not being able to write is the normal case. What to do on the day it is flowing, and why he stops there.
chapters.txt: Writing a novel, he holds himself to one rule: ten pages a day, four hundred characters a page, no more and no less. On a bad day he fills the ten anyway. On a good day, when the sentences are coming and he wants to keep going, he still stops there. This is not a performance of discipline, he says. It is for tomorrow. Say everything today and tomorrow you face a blank page. Leave a piece unfinished and you can pick it up. Running works the same way: however good the legs feel, he finishes the day's distance and goes home. Stop where something is left to pick up — The hard part of writing is not writing, it is starting again. End the day at a point where you already know the next sentence and tomorrow's cost of entry is close to zero. Finish a section cleanly instead and tomorrow begins with hunting for the door. A ceiling matters as much as a floor — Most people set only a floor: at least this much every day. The ceiling exists to stop the good day from borrowing. What you overspend when it is flowing is usually repaid out of the next three days. The real enemy of output is not laziness but swing. A fixed amount deletes the daily question — Whether to work today and how much, decided fresh every morning, spends part of the day's energy on the deciding. Fix the amount and the question disappears, and everything left goes into the work. That is also
q: Stop while it is still flowing, so tomorrow connects.
The hard part was never starting. It is restarting tomorrow.

chapters.w: Focus and endurance can be trained
chapters.dek: Whether a person without talent should bother. He names two other requirements, and says both can be trained.
chapters.txt: Asked what a novelist most needs, he answers talent first, then points out that talent is not something you can manage. You have what you have. The energy in the passage goes to the other two. Focus, and after focus, endurance. Focus is putting your limited powers entirely on one thing for a stretch of hours. Endurance is doing that every day for half a year, a year. Unlike talent, he says, these can be acquired and sharpened through training, in the same way muscle is. Put down the part you cannot control — How much talent you were given is settled, and worrying about it produces no action. Two of the three are available to work on, so the hours belong there. This is not consolation. It is moving attention from where there is no leverage to where there is some. Focus is worth more than hours — Three hours entirely undivided beat eight broken ones. He gives the early morning to writing, no calls and no visitors, because once concentration breaks, getting back to the same depth costs time again. The quality sits in the depth, not in the total. Endurance is bought by lowering the daily difficulty — Things people sustain for years are usually not very hard on any given day. Setting the daily amount where your worst day can still finish it trades the ceiling of one day for the total of one year. Willpower alone does not survive the first bad stretch. Where you are: you want to do something for a long time
q: Unlike talent, focus and endurance can be acquired through training.
Talent is not yours to manage. The other two are.

chapters.n: Nobody asked you to do this
chapters.w: So the reason has to be your own
chapters.dek: How to hold a long effort nobody required of you. The reason he found for himself, and where he keeps it.
chapters.txt: He has run for over thirty years, finished more than thirty marathons and one hundred-kilometre ultra. Nobody asked him to run, and there is no placing worth chasing. So what keeps him going? The only opponent you have to beat is yourself, the way you used to be. A little further than yesterday, a slightly steadier stride, and that is enough. Writing runs on the same fuel. His own country's literary establishment kept him at arm's length for years, and it never became a reason to stop, because he had not been writing for them in the first place. Nobody asked, so the reason has to come from you — A job has reviews and school has exams, and in both the reason is supplied from outside. Something you chose has none of that, and the moment you make the outside response your reason, the views, the likes, other people's verdicts, that reason can be withdrawn at any time. Yesterday's version of you never runs out — Comparing yourself to others makes winning slack and losing bitter, and there is always somebody better. Yesterday's version is present every day and sets a bar you can actually reach. It does not get the blood up. It also does not stop. Silence is not a reason to stop, attention not a reason to continue — Nobody reading does not mean you should stop, and people reading does not mean you should go on. Both are signals from outside. The question worth asking is whether not doing this would hurt. That answer holds
q: The only opponent you have to beat is yourself.
If nobody asked you to do it, the reason must be yours.

chapters.w: Do not fall in love with a tool
chapters.dek: A swordsman who never lost a bout wrote down a rule against loving your sword. This is about why he bothered.
chapters.txt: In the Earth Scroll he sets down a rule of his own: you should not have a favourite weapon. Leaning too hard on one is the same error as not knowing how to use it. A long blade has long-blade weaknesses and a short one has short-blade weaknesses, and neither deserves attachment. He is his own evidence. At Ganryujima his opponent Sasaki Kojiro carried a famous long sword; Musashi came ashore with a wooden one cut from a boat oar. Late in life, in the Dokkodo, he wrote twenty-one vows for himself. One of them: in all things whatsoever, rely on nothing. Affection for a tool ends by defining you — Favour one weapon and your method quietly grows around it, until the tool is choosing which fights you can take rather than the other way round. Dropping the attachment is not a claim that the tool is bad. It is a refusal to let one object mark your edge. Long loses one way, short loses another — He never says which blade is better. He says each has a bout it must lose. Tools carry no absolute rank, only a fit with the situation, so what you train is not one weapon taken to its limit but the reading of which one this round needs. The oar won by being off the scale — Kojiro's long sword was a named blade and the centre of everything he did. The wooden one Musashi carved was longer still and belonged to no school anyone could read. Beating a man on the
q: Do not have a favourite weapon.
Over-familiarity with one weapon is as much a fault as not knowing it.

chapters.w: Two ways of looking
chapters.dek: He split looking into two words. This is about why watching the other man's blade means you have already lost.
chapters.txt: The Water Scroll gives the gaze of the strategist, and Musashi splits looking in two. Perception is strong; sight is weak. Perception takes in the whole and the intention behind it, and should be strong. Sight tracks the particular movement, and should be weak. See distant things as if close, he says, and close things as if distant. Lock onto the sword and the sword leads your eyes and then your feet. What is worth watching is the man entire, his balance and his breathing and what he means to do. The blade is the last joint of that. The gaze, he adds, must be the same off the field. Watch the last joint and it drags you — The sword is the final link in a chain of movement. By the time you see it move the thing is decided, and with your eyes fixed there your tempo belongs to him. Watch balance and intention and you are seeing what comes before the sword, which is early enough to matter. Close things far, far things close — What is right in front of you is magnified out of proportion; look at it from a distance and the proportion returns. What is far off blurs into a concept and gets discounted; look at it close and it becomes detail. Two corrections in opposite directions, and only together are they a calibrated view. Train the gaze until it is the default — He adds a line: this holds in ordinary life too. In the bout there is no time to change
q: Perception is strong; sight is weak.
See distant things as if close, and close things as if distant.

chapters.n: Boil it down to what is physically true
chapters.w: Analogy quotes the going rate; physics gives the floor
chapters.dek: The phrase is everywhere now. What is worth having is his own definition, and the arithmetic he did on a battery.
chapters.txt: In the 2013 TED interview he set it out plainly: reason from first principles rather than by analogy. Analogy is everyone does it this way, so we will too. First principles is boiling a thing down to its most fundamental truths and reasoning up. His example was batteries. Everyone said a pack costs six hundred dollars a kilowatt-hour and always will. From first principles: what is a battery made of? Cobalt, nickel, aluminium, carbon, polymers, a steel can. Buy those on the metal exchange and it comes to eighty. The other five hundred is the price of how they are currently assembled — and assembly can be reinvented. Analogy gives you the market rate, physics gives the floor — It has always cost this and the industry standard both quote the price of other people's methods, not the cost of the thing. Separate the two: where is the floor set by materials and physical law, and who collects the gap between that floor and today's price? Keep going until you hit something that cannot be reduced — Most attempts stop halfway and treat a supplier quote or an industry convention as bedrock. Those are still somebody's decisions. The test is whether you can still ask why. If you can, you are not at the bottom. The bottom feels like a physical law or a published market price. It is expensive, so spend it where the leverage is — He has said himself that analogy is usually the cheaper move, and he is right: reasoning up the whole chain costs an
q: We reason from first principles rather than by analogy.
Boil things down to the most fundamental truths and reason up from there.

chapters.w: A number that tells you where to start
chapters.dek: He gives every component a humiliating score. What it does is turn a way of thinking into something you can run on a spreadsheet.
chapters.txt: Isaacson records a hard metric inside SpaceX: the idiot index — the finished price of a part divided by the cost of its raw material. An aluminium part holding a few hundred dollars of metal, bought for tens of thousands, scores in the dozens. A score that absurd says what you are paying for is process and inertia, not physics. The rule follows: a high index is either explained or made in house. Many Falcon parts ended up built on site, at a fraction of the industry price. What makes the index good is that it turns a judgement call into a list you can sort. The index turns judgement into a scanner — First principles depends on someone deciding to think. The index makes the candidates queue up on their own: run the ratio across every purchased line, sort descending, and the rebuild priority list writes itself. The best form a method can take is decaying from an insight into a division anyone can do. A high score is a toll booth left by history — A part selling at fifty times its metal usually has no villain behind it: years of safety margin, layers of certification, small batches, a sole supplier. Every layer had a reason once; stacked up they are a row of toll booths. You do not negotiate those away, you route around them. Where the score is low, leave it alone — The tool carries its own limit. A part scoring near one is already priced against physics; making it yourself will not be cheaper,
q: The idiot index: a part's finished cost over its material cost.
A ratio that high means you are paying for process and inertia, not physics.

chapters.n: More men where it is decided
chapters.w: Being outnumbered overall is fine
chapters.dek: He usually fought with fewer men and was usually the stronger side at the moment of contact. This is how.
chapters.txt: One of his maxims holds the whole method: the art of war consists in always having more force than the enemy at the point attacked or defended, even when the army as a whole is weaker. The Italian campaign of 1796 is the textbook case. He had a little over thirty thousand men against nearly seventy thousand Austrians and Piedmontese, but they came in separate columns, and he used his interior position to move between them and meet each part with everything he had. On the ledger he was the weaker side. At every place they actually met, he was the stronger one. A shortfall in total can be traded away by movement — Resource comparisons are a summary table; outcomes happen at particular points of contact. The smaller side can still be larger at each point, and the price is moving faster than the other side and giving up the idea of holding everything at once. Their dispersal is something you can cause — The allied columns were not only careless. His line of march threatened several objectives at once and forced them to garrison each. Making the other side afraid to leave anything uncovered is the same act as making him too weak everywhere. Splitting him and massing yourself are one movement. The method runs on a time difference — Beating two forces in turn requires that finishing the first and turning on the second is faster than the two joining. Slow the movement down with longer supply or more layers of approval and the interior position inverts
q: Have more force at the point attacked, even when weaker overall.
Splitting him and massing yourself are the same movement.

chapters.w: A success with no exit condition
chapters.dek: The witticism has an origin that is not witty at all. This is about the road he was on when he said it.
chapters.txt: In December 1812 he left what remained of his army in the Russian snow and went back to Paris by sleigh. Passing through Warsaw he said it to the ambassador de Pradt, more than once: from the sublime to the ridiculous there is only one step. Six months earlier he had crossed the Niemen with over six hundred thousand men, and fewer than a tenth came back. He lost no major battle on that campaign. He entered Moscow. He lost the war for having no plan at all for winning while the other side refuses to concede. Moscow was empty, the Tsar would not negotiate, winter arrived. You can win every battle and lose the war — His script assumed that holding Moscow was victory, but the definition of victory sat with the other side. They declined, and the occupation became merely a long way in. Any victory condition that requires your opponent's cooperation is not a condition you control. Write the way home before you leave — A supply line two thousand li long for six hundred thousand men only works inside a quick-victory script. He set no automatic stop for a war still running in October. Every large bet needs an exit that does not depend on judgement, because by then judgement is the thing most heavily committed. There is no buffer between sublime and ridiculous — The exact word is step. Collapse was not gradual. Authority built on continuous victory cannot structurally survive one large defeat: the loyalty of the client states, the mood of the army
q: From the sublime to the ridiculous there is only one step.
A victory condition that needs their agreement is not yours.

chapters.n: Assets that earn while you sleep
chapters.w: Wealth is not money
chapters.dek: The first line cuts one word into three. What matters is where each of the three leads.
chapters.txt: The storm opens: seek wealth, not money or status. Each is defined. Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep — businesses, code, content, equity. Money is how we transfer wealth. Status is your place in the social hierarchy. What matters is the kind of game each is. Creating wealth is positive sum: everyone can get richer. Status is zero sum — for you to rise somebody falls, which is why people attacking wealth creators are usually playing status. And there is one road to the first: ownership. You will not get rich renting out your time, because time does not copy. Work out which game you are actually playing — A great deal of hard work leads to status rather than wealth: titles, visibility, rankings. Those prizes produce no cash flow and require you to keep showing up to hold them. One test: stop for three months. Is it still producing? If yes it is an asset. Selling time has a ceiling because time will not copy — Work priced by the hour earns rate times hours. Both factors are hard-capped, and the whole thing goes to zero while you sleep. The way out is not raising the rate, it is changing the formula — detaching output from duration. Things made once and sold many times: code, content, courses, systems, equity. Recognising a status attack saves you the reply — Anyone who does something visible attracts a portion of criticism whose purpose is not correction but position — pushing you down in a zero-sum game. Separating the two kinds
q: Seek wealth, not money or status.
Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep.

chapters.w: Specific knowledge times leverage
chapters.dek: He compresses the whole method into two words. What each of the two refers to, and why the new leverage is different in kind.
chapters.txt: The formula collapses into a phrase: productise yourself. Yourself means specific knowledge — the kind you cannot be trained for, growing out of your temperament, obsessions and history; it feels like play to you and looks like work to others. Productise means putting leverage on it. Labour and capital are the old kinds and both need somebody's permission. The new kind replicates at zero marginal cost: code and media, which need permission from nobody. What you wrote keeps working while you sleep. Specific knowledge is not on any syllabus — Any skill taught in a standard way is supplied in unlimited quantity and priced accordingly. Specific knowledge comes from the part that cannot be standardised: your combination of oddities, the crossings between fields, an obsession out of proportion to its subject. The detection method is his own line — play to you, labour to others. Permissionless means you can start today — The bottleneck in the old leverage is persuasion: nothing moves until you have hired someone or raised something. Code and media delete that step. Writing, recording, publishing — live today, at the cost of time rather than consent. The opportunity of this generation is essentially that the entry price of leverage fell to zero. Productising means taking yourself out of delivery — Where the two words end up: packaging your judgement, taste and method into something that delivers without you present. The test is replication — each additional user should cost you an amount of time approaching zero. Until then what you own is a good job. After
q: Productise yourself.
Specific knowledge feels like play to you but looks like work to others.

chapters.n: What does not kill me, conditions included
chapters.w: It is a maxim, not a law of nature
chapters.dek: Probably the most quoted sentence he wrote, and the most misused. The question is what has to be true for it to hold.
chapters.txt: Maxims and Arrows, number eight, opens with a clause the poster cuts off. Out of life's school of war: what does not kill me makes me stronger. School of war. It is not a general blessing on suffering — the man writing it spent years in violent headaches and vomiting, with his eyesight close to gone, describing how he handled his own. Four maxims later in the same book: if we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how. Read together the two complete each other. Surviving is only the input. By default suffering leaves you weaker — The maxim does not describe an automatic process. The same blow usually leaves wear and a flinch behind it. Turning it into strength takes a deliberate operation: going back over it, giving it a place, taking out the thing you can use next time. Skip the operation and the sentence is a placebo. Without a why, the pain has nowhere to go — The second maxim supplies the condition. Someone with a direction can book a blow as a cost on the way there. Someone without one can only book it as loss. The same quantity, entered in two different ledgers, is not the same thing at all. It is a first-person sentence only — Used on your own history it is a way of processing. Said to somebody who is still bleeding, it asks them to translate their disaster into your inspirational story before you will listen. He wrote a school motto, not a condolence
q: Out of life's school of war: what does not kill me makes me stronger.
Without a why, the blow goes into the ledger as pure loss.

chapters.n: Fighting monsters, and the bill for it
chapters.w: The method you borrow grows into the person who borrows it
chapters.dek: Two sentences, and between them a complete occupational hazard notice. The question is how the change actually happens.
chapters.txt: Aphorism 146 of Beyond Good and Evil. He who fights with monsters should look to it that he himself does not become a monster. And when you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you. This is not horror-story decoration. The first sentence is about the contagion of method: to beat the thing you take up its methods, and methods grow into the people who use them. The second is the price of attention. Study something long enough and it is shaping you back while you believe you are only observing it. The method grows into the user — Against an opponent who will do anything, what works is usually the same thing. The first time is an exception, the second is fluency, the third is your style. Adoption is close to irreversible: once a method has worked, it arrives first at the next difficulty. Whatever you watch for long enough calibrates you — People who study fraud all day begin to assume everybody is running one. People who analyse failures all day stop being able to place a bet. Attention is a loop: choosing what to look at for years is choosing what gets to set your defaults. The defence is a line drawn early — He gives the warning and no remedy, but the warning locates one. Before it starts, write down which things you will not do even to win. The line has to be drawn while you are not yet cornered, because the person doing the drawing at the wall is no longer
q: When you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you.
The method you borrowed to win once is now your first move.

chapters.w: The first sentence settles it
chapters.dek: Most arguments are lost in the first second of speaking. This is about the exact word that loses them.
chapters.txt: Rosenberg lays his foundation on a line from Krishnamurti: observing without evaluating is the highest form of human intelligence. He then separates two sentences that look alike. You were late three times this week is an observation, and there is nothing in it to argue with. You are always late is an evaluation, and it has to be argued with. The difference sits in words like always and never, which promote a piece of behaviour into a verdict on a person. Once the defence is up, nothing else gets in. Take the frequency words out and the sentence comes alive — Always, never, constantly and again are the markers of evaluation. Strip them and what remains is usually a checkable fact. Facts can be discussed and verdicts can only be resisted, and that is the whole divide between two outcomes of the same conversation. Adjectives that rate people are evaluations too — You are lazy and he is unprofessional look like descriptions and are labels. The checkable form describes behaviour and effect: the document he sent was missing three figures. A label turns a person into its defender; a description leaves them room to change. Observing is not softening — The common misreading is that observation means being tactful, so the point never actually gets made. Rosenberg is asking for more precision, not less edge. A fact can be very hard as long as it is a fact, and vague kindness fails exactly as a sharp verdict does. Where you are: you are about to raise a problem with someone
q: Observing without evaluating is the highest form of human intelligence.
When we combine observation with evaluation, others are apt to hear criticism.

chapters.n: Underneath the blame is a need
chapters.w: Hearing the half that was not said
chapters.dek: Somebody is shouting at you. Underneath the words they are asking for something. This is how to get that half out.
chapters.txt: His central claim is that every criticism, attack and judgement is a tragic expression of an unmet need. Speaking at the Deheisha refugee camp, he was called a murderer to his face, because American-made tear gas canisters had been used there. He did not defend himself. He asked whether the man was furious, and needed his family's safety to be understood. The man stopped, then talked for an hour, and by the end of the evening had invited Rosenberg home for a Ramadan meal. Nothing was conceded and nothing was argued. The need under the shouting was simply said out loud. The words are an accusation, underneath is a gap — All you care about is work reads as a judgement. Underneath it is a need to matter to you. Answer the words and you are in a debate about whether that is true. Answer the need and the direction changes. One sentence, two layers, two destinations. Keep feelings apart from judgements — I feel that you do not respect me is not a feeling, it is a judgement in a feeling's clothing, and the subject has slid over to the other person. I am upset is a feeling: the subject is you, and nobody can deny it. Where the subject sits decides everything. A request must be concrete enough to refuse — Could you make a bit more effort is not a request, because nobody knows what would count as doing it. Send me one line before the meeting is. A vague request fails, and after it fails both
q: All criticism is a tragic expression of an unmet need.
What others do may be the stimulus of our feelings, but not the cause.

chapters.w: Replacing the fuse, or fitting the strainer
chapters.dek: The same fault keeps coming back and the review was written. What his five whys found on one stopped machine.
chapters.txt: There is an example in the book. A machine stopped. Why did it stop? An overload blew the fuse. Why the overload? The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated. Why not? The lubrication pump was not pumping enough. Why not? The pump shaft was worn and rattling. Why was it worn? No strainer had been fitted, so metal scrap got in. Only the fifth answer reaches the thing to repair: fit a strainer. Ask once and you replace the fuse, and it blows again next week. He called this the basic discipline of the Toyota floor. The first cause is almost never the cause — A blown fuse is a fact, not a cause. It is the first link in the chain to show itself, and most reviews stop there because it is the easiest to see and the cheapest to change. Change it, and next time it is the same link again. Five is not a ritual. It is the length of the chain — Fuse to strainer is exactly five steps, and each step is the answer to the why before it. Skip a level and you stop halfway, repairing something that will fail again. The number is not mystical. It is roughly how long these chains run. The bottom layer is usually small and cheap — A strainer costs less than a pump, less than a bearing, far less than the stoppage. Chasing a fault to its root usually ends at the smallest available action, and that is the reason to keep asking: not to be thorough, but
q: Repeat why five times and the real cause shows itself.
The first cause is only the first link to appear.

chapters.w: The problem surfaces where it happens
chapters.dek: What you hand out comes back wrong every time. Why Toyota let any worker on the line halt the entire line.
chapters.txt: Toyota began as a loom maker. Sakichi Toyoda's loom had one design feature: when a thread broke the machine stopped itself, instead of weaving out a whole bolt of ruined cloth. Ohno moved the idea onto the car line. A cord hangs above every station, and anyone who sees a problem can pull it and stop the whole line. Management feared the lost output. He held. The result is that a fault surfaces in the second it occurs and is handled there, rather than accumulating into a pile of scrap found at the month-end count. The earlier a defect stops, the cheaper it is — An error caught at the first station costs a minute. The same error found at the last one costs the whole unit. Work that comes back to you wrong every time is telling you there was no point along the way where anyone could halt it. Give the power to stop to the people furthest down — Whoever sees the problem first is on the line, not in the office. If only a manager may stop, the problem has to travel upward and wait for permission, and by then it has flowed past. Give the stop to whoever can see, and it stops where it started. Fear of stopping the line manufactures defects — The instinct of management is to keep running, because output matters. But what keeps running is defective output, and more of it is worse. His ordering is the reverse of the instinct: stopping is what produces, and refusing to stop is
q: A thread breaks, the loom stops, and nothing ruined is woven.
Give the power to stop to whoever can see the problem.

chapters.n: Inventory is there to hide problems
chapters.w: Lower the water and the rocks appear
chapters.dek: Everything obvious has been cut and the cost will not move. Why he treated stock as a cover rather than a cushion.
chapters.txt: He had a picture for it. Inventory is water and problems are rocks on the riverbed. With the water high the boat runs smoothly, because every rock is submerged: an unreliable machine, a supplier who misses dates, a handover nobody has sorted out, all of it carried by the stock. Lower the water and the rocks come up one at a time; hit one, repair it, and the channel is genuinely open. Toyota cut stock not to save warehouse rent but to leave problems nowhere to hide. Wherever there is slack, something is being covered — An extra week in the schedule, extra material, an extra pair of hands: every piece of slack is underwriting some problem. A problem that is underwritten never gets repaired, so the slack turns into a permanent cost. Hunt the slack first. There is a rock beneath it. You lower the water to hit rocks, not to save water — His purpose in cutting stock was never the storage bill. It was forcing problems into the open. Lower the water and leave the exposed rocks unrepaired and the boat is holed, which is why the imitators failed: they copied the cutting and skipped the repairing. A little at a time, one rock per pass — He did not drain the river. Lower the level slightly, one rock appears, repair it, lower it again. Take it all out at once and ten rocks arrive together and none of them get fixed. Cost comes down in layers, never in a single cut. Where you are: every obvious
q: Inventory is water, problems are rocks, and high water runs smooth.
Every margin is underwriting a problem, and underwritten problems go unrepaired.

chapters.p: The Old Regime and the Revolution
chapters.w: Loosening the grip is what detonates
chapters.dek: The twenty years before the Revolution were the old order's most prosperous. The law Tocqueville drew out of that paradox.
chapters.txt: The archives told Tocqueville the opposite of what instinct says. The Revolution did not arrive in the poorest years or in the most oppressed provinces — the reign of Louis XVI was the most prosperous period of the old monarchy, and the rising came where the burden was felt least. His explanation became a law. The most dangerous moment for a bad government is when it begins to reform. The mechanism sits in one sentence: people bear an evil patiently while it seems beyond redress, and the moment someone proposes removing it, it turns unbearable. Discontent is set by expectation, not by conditions — Hold conditions still and raise expectations and discontent rises — and reform is the strongest generator of expectation there is, because it is an official admission that the old state was not right. So complaints go up first, not down. That is the mechanism working, not the reform failing. Half reformed is the most dangerous setting — The old constraints are loose and the new arrangement has not landed. In that middle state the old reason for patience, that it could not be helped, has been dismantled, and the new satisfaction is still in transit. Louis XVI was stuck there. Never park at the halfway point. Each abuse removed magnifies the ones left — Every abuse that goes makes the remaining ones easier to notice. Solve one problem and the rest become less tolerable by contrast. That is not greed; you updated the frame of reference yourself. So sequence improvements, starting with those that do not
q: The most dangerous moment for a bad government is when it begins to reform.
A grievance becomes intolerable once the possibility of removing it crosses men's minds.

chapters.p: The Old Regime and the Revolution
chapters.w: Overturn everything, inherit the core
chapters.dek: The Revolution claimed a clean break with the past. The unbroken line Tocqueville dug out of the provincial archives.
chapters.txt: In the provincial archives Tocqueville found that the central administration everyone credited to the Revolution or to Napoleon was in fact an institution of the old regime, and the only part of it left standing afterwards. For a century and more the monarchy had used its intendants to hollow out the nobility and pull every matter to Paris; by 1789 local self-government was already a shell. So the Revolution destroyed the crown, the nobles and the church as appearances, and took the centralising machine over intact, then ran it harder. What gets replaced is the appearance; what stays is the structure — Signs, slogans and the names of the people in charge are the easy part. The pipes power actually runs through are the hard part, because whoever takes over discovers on day one how useful they are. Judge a change by approvals, budget authority and information flow. Revolutionaries fall in love with the tools of the people they overthrew — A centralising machine is irresistible to anyone governing: ready-made, efficient, point and shoot. So those who overthrow it almost always inherit and reinforce it. If you want a bad structure to die, dismantle it during the handover, before the new owner grows attached. The stronger the sense of rupture, the harder to look for the continuity — Tocqueville's method is worth stealing. Everyone was saying 1789 divided two worlds; he read deeds, tax rolls and the correspondence of intendants, and found the line nobody could see. For any earth-shattering change, ask what passed through it untouched. Where you are:
q: Centralisation is an institution of the old regime, not a creation of the Revolution.
They built the new order out of the debris of the old.

chapters.w: You fight in order to settle
chapters.dek: The most famous line in the book gets read as a cynical observation. It is in fact a restraining clause.
chapters.txt: Clausewitz defines war on two levels. First its nature: an act of force to compel the enemy to do our will, and force left to its own logic escalates without limit. Then the rein: war is merely the continuation of policy by other means. The second statement exists to bind the first. War is not a thing standing on its own. It is begun by a political purpose and serves one. The political object is the goal, war is the means, and the means can never be considered apart from the goal. He spent his life warning soldiers that the longer a war runs, the easier this is to forget. A means left alone starts eating the end — War has an internal logic, win this one and then the next, and once running it powers itself until the fighting is the point. Every strong instrument behaves this way: price wars, litigation, public campaigns. They demand continuation once started, so the rein goes on at the beginning or not at all. Audit every step against the purpose — The working version of the means never being separable from the goal: each move has to answer whether it brings the political outcome nearer. Taking a city that makes the negotiation harder is a military success and a net loss. The test is the purpose, not the spoils. When the aim changes, resize the means — The political object determines the effort and the scale it warrants, so limited aims call for a limited war. Aims shifting mid-course is ordinary. The danger
q: War is merely the continuation of policy by other means.
The political object is the goal, war is the means.

chapters.w: Even the simplest thing is difficult
chapters.dek: He borrowed a word from physics for the study of war. This is where friction comes from and why it can only be budgeted for.
chapters.txt: In the seventh chapter he coins it: everything in war is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult. The difficulties accumulate and produce a friction that nobody who has not seen war can imagine. His picture of it is concrete. The machine is made of individuals, each of whom keeps his own friction: an order passes through hundreds of people who get tired, frightened, or misunderstand it, and on top of that come weather, ground and false reports. Friction makes what looks easy hard. It is, he says, the one concept that distinguishes real war from war on paper. Friction comes from a plan having to pass through people — A plan is a frictionless abstraction; execution is warm-blooded transmission, and each person it crosses adds a layer of fatigue, misreading, self-interest and delay. So the complexity of a plan is not counted in logical steps but in how many people it must pass through. Friction cannot be removed, only allowed for — He does not teach you to eliminate it, because it cannot be eliminated. He teaches conversion. The good commander prices friction into the plan and leaves slack at every link. Scheduling to the theoretical limit is not efficiency; it is never having been in the field. What resists friction is habit, not willpower — The only lubricant, he says, is the habit of war: drill and combat grinding a force until difficulty is the default. Willpower in the moment does not hold against systematic friction. Only rehearsing the common failures into muscle keeps friction from eating
q: Everything in war is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult.
Friction is what distinguishes real war from war on paper.

chapters.n: Do things that do not scale
chapters.w: The early work is meant to be handmade
chapters.dek: Founders think about scale constantly. He argues for the opposite direction — and is specific about what the handmade phase actually buys.
chapters.txt: The essay opens against the instinct: startups do not take off by themselves; the founders make them take off. The common mistake is chasing something scalable on day one, when the early period calls for recruiting users by hand. Airbnb had stalled, so the founders flew to New York week after week, knocked on hosts' doors and photographed their apartments themselves. Completely unscalable — and it found the switch that moved conversion. The output of that phase is not the handful of users; it is an unusually concentrated understanding of them, plus people so over-served they will tell others. Doing it by hand is the highest-bandwidth research there is — Surveys and dashboards show the shadow a behaviour casts; being in the room shows the behaviour. In people's living rooms it turned out photograph quality was the bottleneck — an insight the analytics could only ever have shown as low conversion. The expensive thing early on is not slow growth, it is understanding wrongly. Over-serving is how you manufacture the first advocates — If early users get service indistinguishable from a large company's, they have no reason to speak about you. The handmade phase gives what no scaled operation could — a founder replying in minutes, the product bent around one person. That unreasonable care is the raw material of word of mouth. Unscalable is a stage, not a creed — The essay gets quoted in halves. The correct loop is: do it by hand, extract the one move that was actually doing the work, then build that move into
q: Startups do not take off by themselves. The founders make them take off.
In the early days you have to recruit users manually.

chapters.w: Run this number before anything else
chapters.dek: He asks founders one question first, and most of them cannot answer it. Why it comes before every other conversation.
chapters.txt: The first thing he asks a startup is are you default alive or default dead? The definition is hard-edged: assuming expenses stay constant and growth continues as it has been, do you reach profitability on the money you have left? If yes, default alive. If no, default dead. What surprised him is how many founders do not know which they are. It comes first because it sets the character of every other conversation: a default alive company can talk about ambition; a default dead one has a single agenda item, getting out of that state — and is usually still discussing hiring, assuming the next round will arrive. You have to run it yourself, because nothing raises an alarm — A default dead company looks entirely normal from inside: the product ships, the team grows, there is money in the account. Death is scheduled months out on a calendar nobody turns to. The question brings that date forward to today — three numbers, ten minutes. Counting on the next round outsources your survival to a mood — He names the standard consolation: investor appetite swings with the market and your death date does not. The right move when default dead is not to fundraise harder but to move the two variables under your control — expenses and growth — until you are back on the living side. The usual cause is hiring too early — His first-named cause of default dead is over-hiring — using growth needs people to raise the burn ahead of growth that then does not arrive.
q: Are you default alive or default dead?
With expenses flat and growth as it is, do you reach profitability in time?

chapters.n: Security and desire want opposite things
chapters.w: Which is why the better it gets, the flatter
chapters.dek: The steadier life gets, the less you feel, and most people assume they changed. Perel says the structure did it.
chapters.txt: Perel has done couples therapy for over thirty years, and the sentence she hears most is: everything is fine, we just don't feel anything. Her explanation blames nobody. Intimacy wants closeness, familiarity and predictability; desire wants distance, the unknown, the thing not yet fully held. Both are real needs and they point in opposite directions. So the more settled a relationship, the more easily the second gets squeezed out — not love going wrong, but one thing perfected until it crowds out the other. It isn't love fading. Two needs are crowding each other — Read as love fading, the only available moves are blaming yourself or blaming them. Read as two needs crowding, the move is clear: not repairing the love, but making room again for the one that got squeezed out. Familiar to the point of no unknown leaves nothing to miss — Desire needs a little opacity. When their schedule, thoughts and reactions are all inside your predictions, missing them has nowhere to land. So the problem often isn't too little communication — it's everything being accounted for. Room comes from separateness, not more closeness — The instinct is more time together, more talking. Perel's prescription often runs the other way: each go and do something the other isn't part of, become two people again, then come back. Distance isn't the enemy of love. It's the fuel of desire. Where you are: no fights, no crisis, and no feeling, and you can't say what's wrong. Ask first: when did we last each do something separately and come
q: Intimacy wants closeness. Desire wants distance. Both are real.
'Everything's fine, we feel nothing' says nothing about love failing.

chapters.n: Feeling nothing isn't the same as something being wrong
chapters.w: First tell a wound from an emptiness
chapters.dek: 'We can't go on like this' can sit on top of two completely different things. Tell them apart before you act.
chapters.txt: Perel warns about a common misdiagnosis: treating flatness as if it were rupture. Rupture has a wound — contempt, betrayal, sustained attack — and that needs mending. Flatness has no wound; it is simply empty, and emptiness needs filling, not mending. The two moves point in opposite directions: mending a wound means stopping first, apologising first, making it safe first; filling an emptiness means going outward and adding something new. Get it wrong and it worsens — apologising when you should be adding, booking trips when you should be apologising. Check for a wound before choosing a move — The test is concrete: in the last three months, has there been contempt, dragging up old grievances, belittling in front of others? If yes, that's the wound and it comes first. If none of it, this is emptiness, and the treatment is entirely different. For emptiness, more communication makes it worse — Repeatedly sitting down to discuss the relationship when it's empty talks away the last of the ease. What it needs is experiencing something new together, not analysing why there's no feeling — the analysis itself turns the relationship into a task. Only after telling them apart is 'should we leave' answerable — People decide about leaving while the two states are mixed together, so the answer keeps swinging. See first whether it's a wound or an emptiness, then ask — the answers under those two premises were never meant to match. Where you are: you don't fight and you aren't close, and you're weighing mending against leaving. Ask first:
q: A wound is mended, an emptiness is filled. Opposite directions.
Talking it through while empty talks away the last of the ease.

chapters.n: It isn't how often. It's not being there
chapters.w: Present in the room, absent in attention
chapters.dek: You live in the same place. So why does it feel like long distance? What she says to count instead.
chapters.txt: Most people count time: how many evenings a week, how many meals together. Perel says that's the wrong ledger — what decides the quality isn't how long you're together but how many moments both people were actually there. Two people on the same sofa on separate phones have spent a whole evening together and zero minutes present. She asks clients something very concrete: when did you last look at each other and talk with no screen interrupting? Count 'together' and 'present' separately — They're different ledgers: together is duration, present is attention. The first stacks up easily; the second can be zero for a whole week. What makes someone feel loved is the second, and it has almost nothing to do with the first. Presence can be practised, and it's cheap — It doesn't need large blocks of time: fifteen minutes a day, person facing person, phones face down, is enough to change how it feels. The difficulty isn't the duration, it's not glancing away — one break and that stretch is over. Long enough absent and it reads as not caring — They don't know what your head is busy with. All they can read is where your attention goes, and from that, where they rank. So sustained distraction doesn't communicate 'I'm busy'. It communicates 'you're not important'. Where you are: you're together every day and drifting further apart. Ask first: when did I last look at them and talk without touching my phone? If you can't name the day, start there before discussing the relationship. Where it goes
q: Together counts duration. Present counts attention.
Same sofa, separate phones: zero minutes present.

chapters.w: A theory that explains everything explains nothing
chapters.dek: Astrology explains events and so does physics. This page is about the line Popper drew between them.
chapters.txt: As a teenager in Vienna he was reading Einstein alongside the theories then in fashion, whose followers could account for any case at all and treated that as proof of strength. General relativity did the opposite. It predicted that starlight passing the sun would bend by a specific amount, and a different measurement would have finished it. The 1919 eclipse matched. A theory which is not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific, he concluded, and irrefutability is a vice rather than a virtue. The difference was never explanatory power. Ask what would refute it, not what supports it — Facing any claim, the useful question is not what evidence there is but what observation would make you drop it. If nothing would, the claim carries no testable content, and being internally consistent does not make up for that. The refuting condition has to be written down first — People are extremely good at reading any result as support. The only reliable antidote is to nail the criterion in place before the result arrives. Setting the standard afterwards leaves you a position that cannot lose, which is the same as one that cannot inform. Being refuted is not the same as being discarded — The common misreading is that a falsified theory goes in the bin. His demand is that a theory be exposed to serious attempts to break it, and good ones usually come out stronger. What matters is whether you genuinely tried. Where you are: somebody has handed you a claim that sounds thoroughly reasonable. Ask first: under
q: A theory which is not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific.
Irrefutability is not a virtue of a theory but a vice.

chapters.w: One black swan beats a hundred white ones
chapters.dek: No number of white swans settles the question. This page is about what you should be collecting instead.
chapters.txt: The swan is his illustration of the problem of induction. However many white swans you observe, none of it establishes that all swans are white, and a single black one settles it. Evidence is wildly asymmetric. A confirming instance carries almost no information; a refuting one is decisive. People run the other way by default, gathering supportive cases and feeling steadier at the hundredth than at the first. So his method: propose boldly, then attack your own proposal as hard as you can. Go and ask the people who left — Where you take the sample decides the answer. Ask current users whether they like it and the reply is close to guaranteed. The information lives with the ones who stopped. This is the most practical thing that falls out of Popper. Bold conjectures, severe attempts to refute — He is not asking for cautious hypotheses. He wants large ones, paired with serious efforts to destroy them. The two halves go together: conjecture without refutation is daydreaming, refutation without conjecture is timidity. Confirmation bias is the factory setting — Hunting for support is pleasant and fast, because the motive sits on that side. Good intentions do not correct it. Only procedure does: make finding the counter-example a step on the checklist rather than something you remember to do. Where you are: the more you check, the more certain you get. Ask first: in the last hour, were you collecting support or hunting a counter-example? What is the strongest evidence against, and did you look for it? Where it goes wrong:
q: No number of white swans establishes that all swans are white.
One black swan is enough to settle it.

chapters.n: Forty years of sitting the exam
chapters.w: Never passing, and never a turning point
chapters.dek: There's a kind of failure with no decisive battle in it. How you get through that kind of life.
chapters.txt: At nineteen Pu Songling sat the entry examinations and came first at county, prefecture and circuit level. He was locally famous. Then he sat the provincial examination for the rest of his life, from his twenties into his sixties, and never once passed, supporting his family as a live-in tutor. At seventy-one he was granted a minor honorary status by seniority. No single year in all of it was decisive — not one big defeat and a restart, but once every three years, each time just short, until he was old. Failure with no turning point is the hardest kind — Lose a battle and you can review it and change direction. Forty years of being just short offers no single event worth reviewing and no signal about whether to stop. Most advice about handling failure assumes there is a turning point to point at. Here there isn't one. He didn't stop, and he didn't make it everything — Worth noticing: he neither gave up the exam nor staked the whole of his life on it. The tutoring continued, the family was kept, the stories were collected. Running them in parallel means that when the thing that never worked fails again, something else in your hands is working. You may keep more than one ruler — The examination was a ruler handed to him from outside, clear and unambiguous — which is exactly what makes it easy to let it become the only one. He had a second: how many stories this year. The second doesn't make the first easier.
q: No year was decisive. Just short every time, until he was old.
A lost battle can be reviewed. Being just short cannot.

chapters.n: The main thing failed. The side thing didn't
chapters.w: And he never knew
chapters.dek: What he spent his life trying to do never happened. What he did on the side did. Can that be arranged?
chapters.txt: Pu Songling's real work, as he saw it, was the examination. Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio was a diversion — forty years of writing, circulated in manuscript among friends, and he did not live to see it printed. Of the people who remember him today, essentially none do so for his examination essays. The thing ranked first didn't happen and the thing ranked last did — and he died not knowing it. You don't get to set the ranking — Where a thing sits in your own ordering and what it eventually grows into are unrelated. The first is decided by today's standards; the second takes decades to show. So 'which is the main thing' is a question that, asked at the time, usually gets the wrong answer. But don't therefore do both casually — Strange Tales wasn't written carelessly — forty years, nearly five hundred pieces, revised repeatedly. It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment. A side thing can only grow into something if it gets real investment; it just doesn't get the status. Don't wait until you approve of it to take it seriously — He never considered it his achievement. If you have to wait until you can admit 'this is my real work' before putting the hours in, a great many things simply never grow. The steadier practice is to work seriously and leave the ranking undecided. Where you are: your day job is flat and the thing you do in the evenings keeps growing, and you don't know whether to
q: The thing ranked first failed. The thing ranked last didn't.
It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment.

chapters.w: Using the hours nobody wants
chapters.dek: Forty years of a tutor's scattered hours. What he did with them, and how the material accumulated.
chapters.txt: There is a persistent account that Pu Songling set out tea by the roadside and asked passers-by for strange stories, waiving the price of a bowl for each one, then wrote them up at home. It comes from later writers, not from him, and may not be literal. But it matches a checkable fact: he spent forty years as a live-in tutor in gentry households, with a great deal of scattered time around the teaching, and the nearly five hundred pieces accumulated across exactly those years. He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job. Accumulation needs somewhere fixed for things to land — Scattered hours turn into something not because there are many of them but because there is one fixed place that catches them. A thing overheard, a sentence that occurs to you — all into the same notebook. Without that catch, the same forty years simply disperse. The material is local. You don't go far for it — His sources were the ordinary talk of villagers in the county he tutored in, not the fruit of travels through famous mountains. What's genuinely scarce isn't remarkable experience. It's the eye that treats what's around you as material — most people have as much of it and aren't collecting. Not quitting is what let it run so long — The tutoring fed him and gave him forty uninterrupted years. Had he staked everything on writing, he probably couldn't have lasted. What kills a side project isn't too little investment. It's gambling your living alongside it and
q: He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.
Scattered hours add up because something catches them, not because there are many.

chapters.n: Swap the cage for a park
chapters.w: Same rat, different situation
chapters.dek: The most famous addiction experiment gave a conclusion against intuition. What happens when you change the cage.
chapters.txt: The standard 1970s addiction experiment went like this: put one rat alone in an empty cage with two bottles, one water and one laced with morphine. The rat drinks the morphine until it dies. The conclusion looks solid — touch it once and you're finished. Bruce Alexander in Canada asked a different question: what if the cage weren't empty? He built a much larger enclosure with companions, wheels, tunnels and places to hide. Same two bottles, and the rats in the park were far less interested in the morphine. The variable isn't only the bottle. It's the cage — The original design treated the cage as background and the drug as the only variable. Once Alexander made the cage a variable too, the conclusion moved: same rat, same bottle, different situation, very different behaviour. The drug's effect isn't denied. It just isn't the only term. The empty cage is manufacturing the demand — The park rats weren't restrained; they didn't much want it. Alexander later used the word dislocation: pull an individual out of the relationships and position they belong in and they will look for anything that fills the gap. The gap is what's being filled. This has a boundary, and it has to be stated — Rat Park's replications were not uniformly successful and its interpretation is still argued over. The safe reading is that situation is the chronically underrated term, not the only one. Explaining everything with it delays people who need medical care. Where you are: you want to stop something — the phone, drinking, whatever
q: Same rat, same bottle. Different cage, different behaviour.
They weren't holding out. They didn't much want it.

chapters.n: Back home, most of them simply stopped
chapters.w: The hardest natural experiment there is
chapters.dek: Is there harder evidence than rats? What the numbers on returning soldiers actually showed.
chapters.txt: In 1971 the US government discovered an awkward problem: a substantial proportion of American servicemen in Vietnam were addicted to heroin. Everyone braced for a disaster — these men would carry it home into the cities. Robins's team followed them and found the opposite. The overwhelming majority simply stopped once home, with only a small fraction relapsing within a year. Same people, same drug, different place. It is one of the very few natural experiments in addiction research with a sample this size. Its strength is that nobody designed it — Laboratory findings always carry the worry that they were engineered. This one wasn't — nobody sent hundreds of thousands of people to a war and brought them back in order to prove a point. Not being designed is exactly what makes it more persuasive than any experiment. What changed wasn't the place. It was the whole situation — Coming home swapped out an entire set of conditions: no longer possibly dying at any moment, family instead of fellow soldiers, a job and a schedule, and the substance much harder to get. So changing environment isn't moving house. It's withdrawing the conditions holding it up. The fraction who relapsed says something else — Some did continue after returning. That fraction is the reminder: situation explains the bulk, not all of it. Who lands in it has more to do with what home was like and what else was going on than with the drug. Where you are: you're trying to help yourself or a family member stop something, and you've
q: Same people, same substance. Home again, and they stopped.
The weight of this data is that nobody designed it.

chapters.n: Take the cage apart before the willpower
chapters.w: And where this stops being true
chapters.dek: Once you know the situation matters, what exactly do you move? How to take the cage apart one bar at a time.
chapters.txt: Put the last two pieces together and you get a method that runs against common sense: to stop something, don't fight the thing itself first. Look at what keeps it alive. A habit that lasts usually has a whole set of props — a fixed hour, a fixed place, nothing else to hand, people doing it with you. Withdraw those one at a time and the thing gets harder by itself, whereas fighting it head-on withdraws only your willpower, which is the first thing to run out. Keep the log before you move anything — Log ten in a row: the hour, the place, whether anything else was in your hands, who was there. Most people finish the log and find the trigger isn't craving, it's one recurring empty slot. Finding the slot is worth more than studying how to resist. Whatever replaces it has to actually work — Removing something leaves a gap, and a gap gets filled back the same way. What worked in Rat Park wasn't the absence of morphine, it was companions, wheels, somewhere to go. So the second step is putting something you genuinely like into that slot, not leaving it bare. When the cage can't be moved, this doesn't apply — The method assumes the cage is movable. Some situations aren't — you can't leave the job, move the family, replace the person. Forcing 'change your environment' there only adds a layer of failure. That's when to find professional help rather than keep pushing on the situation. Where you are: you want to stop
q: Take apart the props holding it up, not the thing itself.
The trigger is often not craving. It's one recurring empty slot.

chapters.w: The credit and the damage in one paragraph
chapters.dek: Six characters from a later historian, and still the standard for the form. What makes doing it so hard.
chapters.txt: Ban Gu's verdict on the Records: the writing is straight, the facts checked, no empty praise and no concealment of evil, and so it may be called a true record. The weight of that shows only in the entries. He wrote Li Guang as the general beneath whom a path wore itself smooth, and also as the man who put eight hundred men who had surrendered to death, and who cut his own throat after losing the way and missing the rendezvous. He wrote Huo Qubing's indifference to his soldiers. He wrote his own emperor hunting immortality. Concealing nothing is hardest about your own side — Recording the faults of people you dislike is easy. Recording the faults of people you admire is very hard, because it amounts to admitting your own judgement was not pure. He plainly sympathised with Li Guang and set the problems down anyway. No empty praise is a protection for the reader — Write someone as flawless and the reader takes nothing usable away, because flawless people do not exist and there is no way to tell which part to copy. Set out where a person was strong and how exactly they wrecked things, and the record becomes usable. The standard has to bind the most powerful subject too — He wrote Emperor Wu while serving under Emperor Wu, including the cost of the sacrifices, the magicians and the campaigns. The credibility of any recording system is decided by whether it still applies to the one person you cannot afford to offend. Where you are:
q: No empty praise, no concealment of evil: therefore, a true record.
Peach and plum trees do not speak, yet a path forms beneath them.

chapters.n: I find myself in much perplexity
chapters.w: Write down what you could not work out
chapters.dek: He admits in the first of the biographies that he cannot work it out. Why those words outrank any conclusion.
chapters.txt: In the Biography of Bo Yi he lays out a problem he cannot solve. The saying goes that Heaven's way has no favourites and always sides with the good man. Yet Bo Yi and Shu Qi, who kept themselves clean, starved to death; Yan Hui, who loved learning, died young; Robber Zhi killed innocent men daily, gathered thousands and ranged over the empire, and died of old age. So he writes: I find myself in much perplexity. Is this so-called Way of Heaven right, or is it wrong? He supplies no answer. Admitting there is no answer beats supplying a false one — Forcing an unexplained thing into an existing explanation is the cheapest move available and the most damaging, because everyone after you will assume the matter is settled and stop asking. Writing down that you do not understand hands the question on intact. A perplexity has to be specific enough to be checked — His is not abstract doubt. It is three concrete cases held against each other: Bo Yi, Yan Hui, Robber Zhi. Being specific is what lets later people carry the question forward. A vague sense that life is unfair is not a question, only a sigh. He put it first — Seventy biographies, and the one with no answer opens the sequence. The placement is itself a statement: what follows deals with a world where even basic cause and effect is uncertain. Declare what you do not know first and the rest can be trusted. Where you are: a review or an analysis contains a
q: I find myself in much perplexity.
Is this so-called Way of Heaven right, or is it wrong?

chapters.w: Talking bankruptcy in a record year
chapters.dek: In the company's best year he circulated an essay about failing. The parts that turn a mood into a mechanism.
chapters.txt: In 2001, revenue just past twenty billion yuan and profits high, Ren published Huawei's Winter. It opens with a question: what do we do on the day sales fall, or the company goes under? Then the admission: for ten years I have thought about failure every day, blind to success, with no sense of honour or pride, only a sense of crisis. Then the verdict, that the day of failure will certainly come and everyone should be ready to meet it. He insisted this was an assignment rather than a mood. Winter passes and spring arrives, but the coat is sewn beforehand. Make the sense of crisis in a good year; a bad one makes only panic — Raise the alarm while results are falling and people scatter. Raise it in the best year and there is slack to convert worry into coats: contingency plans, cash, spare capability. The timing of the essay is the method. The drill happens while nothing is burning. Thinking about failure daily is a way of aiming attention — Blind to success is not modesty theatre, it is allocation. Good news arrives by itself and bad signals have to be hunted. Wherever a leader's scarce attention rests, the organisation grows an information system to match: watch success and you grow pipes that carry congratulations. Hand how do we survive to every single person — The essay keeps saying every one of us. A sense of crisis owned only by the founder is just the founder's insomnia. Translate it into a question anyone can answer: if
q: For ten years I have thought about failure every day, not success.
The day of failure will certainly come. Be ready to meet it.

chapters.n: Let those who hear the gunfire call for artillery
chapters.w: Turning authority toward the front
chapters.dek: Headquarters that will not release authority leaves the front line unable to fight. The organisational inversion behind the slogan.
chapters.txt: In 2009 Ren named the big-company disease inside Huawei: right now the front line fights and the rear directs. Authority sat with the headquarters furthest from the customer, and by the time resources were approved the opening had closed. His direction was to move the command post to where the guns can be heard: let the people who hear the gunfire call in the artillery, the front line drawing resources itself, headquarters converting from a control centre into a service and support centre. He added the counterweight in the same breath. Calling for artillery costs money, and the caller carries it. Command belongs where the information is — The front line learns first that a customer has cooled or a rival has moved, but the resources are decided by a headquarters that knows the battlefield through reports. Five retellings sit between the decision and the fact, each adding distortion and delay. Move authority to the information, rather than making information climb to authority. The call for artillery has to carry a price — Devolve authority without accounting and the front treats firepower as free, which is exactly why headquarters will not devolve it. His design pairs them: resources drawn are booked against the unit's own results, wins share more, waste is carried locally. Authority, responsibility and reward descend together. Headquarters is now measured on response time — The other half of the inversion happens at the rear. If headquarters becomes a service rather than an approver, the scorecard has to move too, from how many non-compliant requests we stopped to
q: Let the people who hear the gunfire call in the artillery.
Right now the front line fights and the rear directs.
