chapters.w: A company is a story too
chapters.dek: Chimpanzees top out at a few dozen collaborators. Sapiens run to millions. Harari says the difference is something nobody can touch.
chapters.txt: Harari's claim is flat and strange: any large-scale human cooperation is rooted in myths that exist only in our collective imagination. States, money, laws, human rights, limited companies — none can be touched, and each works the moment enough people believe at once. His example is Peugeot. The plant could burn, every employee could leave, every shareholder could sell, and Peugeot would still exist, because it was never the building or the people. Money he calls the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised: two men who hate each other will still take each other's cash. The organisation is the story people still believe — Assets can be sold, staff replaced, offices moved. While the story of who we are and what we are for still holds, the organisation exists. When the story goes, the assets and the people are all still there and the thing has already dissolved. Rewriting the story beats rewriting the process — Harari's point about Sapiens is that we can revise a fiction fast and change behaviour with it — France went from divine right to popular sovereignty inside a year. Change the process without changing the story and people will read the new process through the old one. Trusting the note is cheaper than trusting the person — What makes money the strongest of the fictions is that it converts trust in a person into trust in a system. Cooperation stops requiring that either side like or understand the other. It requires only that both accept the same token. Where
q: Any large-scale human cooperation is rooted in common myths.
Money is the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised.

chapters.w: The luxury trap
chapters.dek: The agricultural revolution multiplied people and made the average life worse. This is how a species can win while every member of it loses.
chapters.txt: Harari turns the standard account inside out: we did not domesticate wheat, it domesticated us. Sapiens bent over weeding, hauling water, spreading manure; the diet narrowed, the hours lengthened, disease arrived. Counted in copies of DNA, wheat became the most successful plant on earth. Counted in how a life went, the farmer did worse than the forager. He calls the agricultural revolution history's biggest fraud. The mechanism is the luxury trap: luxuries tend to become necessities and to spawn new obligations. Each step made the day easier and the sum was one-way, because by then the population was too large for the old life to feed. A total can rise while every unit inside it falls — The species wins and the individual loses is a structure that shows up everywhere: headcount, revenue, users, gross domestic product. Aggregate measures and individual conditions are not two views of one thing. They can move apart, and they can move in opposite directions. The luxury trap is a one-way door — Every new convenience arrives as an option. Once it is in use, life reorganises around it, and then it is a requirement carrying maintenance of its own. The test is simple: if this broke for a week, could I go back to how things were? The exit closed when the scale changed — Why not go back to foraging? Because farming had already raised the population past what foraging could feed. Every step of expansion raises the minimum output needed just to stand still, and that floor is the real lock —
q: We did not domesticate wheat. It domesticated us.
Luxuries tend to become necessities and to spawn new obligations.

chapters.n: Built for escape, left switched on
chapters.w: The problem is that it won't turn off
chapters.dek: People and zebras run the same stress system. Why only one of them gets sick from it.
chapters.txt: The title is the whole argument. Zebras don't get ulcers because their stress response runs for a few minutes. A lion charges: heart rate up, glucose released, immune function paused — and the moment they've escaped, it shuts off. Ours is identical, and we run it against mortgages, managers and an unanswered email. So Sapolsky's verdict is that what makes people ill isn't the stress, it's the response staying on. Its price is suspended repair, digestion and long-term building. Fine briefly. Left on, it diverts the maintenance budget indefinitely. It isn't intensity, it's duration — A week-long sprint doesn't damage anyone. Two years of being permanently on call does. To assess your own state, the question isn't how tired you've been lately. It's when the system was last genuinely switched off. The cost is charged somewhere you can't see — What gets paused under stress is immunity, digestion and tissue repair, and those debts don't show up the same day. So people misjudge how well they're coping. By the time symptoms appear the account has usually been running a long while. The specifically human problem is imagination — A zebra starts the response on seeing an actual lion. A person can start the entire thing by thinking about something that might happen. That's the core mechanism of chronic human stress, and why working on the thoughts themselves is a real intervention. Where you are: tense for a long time, unable to point at what's wrong. Ask first: when did this system last actually switch off? Has there been any stretch
q: Zebras don't get ulcers because the response runs for minutes.
What makes people ill is the response that won't switch off.

chapters.w: Predictability and control
chapters.dek: Same pressure, and one person breaks while another doesn't. What the actual variable turns out to be.
chapters.txt: Sapolsky spent thirty years watching wild baboons in East Africa. Low-ranking animals ran chronically high stress hormones and worse health across the board. But rank wasn't the key thing: at the same low rank, individuals who could anticipate when they'd be harassed, and who had social allies, had markedly better markers. The lab agrees. At the same pressure, predictability and a sense of control cut the damage sharply. That moves the intervention from reducing stress to adding certainty and autonomy — usually far cheaper. Definite bad news beats being left hanging — People and animals adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to uncertainty. Which is why delaying an announcement often does more harm than the announcement — for the whole delay, everyone is on call. Control is a cheap buffer — At identical workload, people who decide their own order and pace show a markedly lower stress response. Adding autonomy doesn't require removing any tasks and cuts the wear substantially. Social support is a physiological variable — Baboons with allies, and people with stable relationships, show better markers under equal pressure. This isn't reassurance, it's a measurable difference. Isolation is itself a health risk. Where you are: under heavy pressure that isn't going to decrease. Ask first: is there any way to make what's coming more predictable — a fixed date, a definite answer? Can I take back some say over the order and pace? Where it goes wrong: turning 'control helps' into needing to control everything, which is a new load of its own.
q: Same pressure. With predictability and control, far less damage.
Low-ranking baboons ran high hormones. The ones with allies didn't.

chapters.n: The iceberg: layers under the act
chapters.w: The fight is happening on the surface
chapters.dek: The same argument for ten years and no movement. The reason is that it is being had on the wrong layer.
chapters.txt: Satir splits a person into the behaviour above the waterline and, below it, feelings, perceptions, expectations, yearnings and the self. Conflict happens almost entirely on the surface and is settled underneath: his anger is behaviour, under it sits disappointment, and under that sits I want to be treated as though I matter. Argue about who is right at the surface and it never ends, because the sentence at the surface was never the point. The problem is not the problem; coping is the problem is her own summary of the whole method. Look for the expectation under the words — A partner complains that you come home late. On the face of it this is scheduling; underneath it is usually where do I rank in this house. Answer the face of it and you are in an argument about calendars. Answer the expectation and the conversation turns. Under the feeling there is a reading — Many people think naming the feeling is the end of the work, but feelings are produced by readings. The same late arrival, read as he does not care about me and read as he is flat out today, makes two different feelings. What often needs changing is the reading. The yearning layer is common ground — The further down you go the more alike people are: to be loved, accepted, of some worth. Two people locked in opposition at the surface usually want the same thing three layers down. Seeing that layer takes the hostility out of a room faster than any argument. Where you
q: The problem is not the problem; coping is the problem.
The conflict is on the surface. The solution is underneath.

chapters.w: Placate, blame, compute, distract
chapters.dek: In a fight people turn into somebody else. This is the list of who they turn into.
chapters.txt: Under pressure, Satir found, people fall back into placating, blaming, being super-reasonable or distracting. Placating gives up the self, blaming gives up the other, super-reasonable gives up both and keeps the logic, distracting gives up the subject. All four are automatic and all four avoid what is actually happening. She proposed a fifth, congruence, holding self, other and situation at once, and insisted it is trained rather than inherited. She would also stand a family up as a sculpture: who is near whom, who has their back turned. Set it up, she said, and everyone sees it at once. The stances set each other off — Blaming usually pulls placating or super-reasonable out of the other person; distracting pulls harder blame. So escalation is not a question of who went too far, it is two stances locking together. Reading the pair is more use than establishing who started. Placating has the best-hidden bill — Placating costs least in the moment, which is why it so often passes for maturity. What it does is take your own needs out of the account, and the account gets settled somewhere else: in a sudden detonation, or in years of quiet distance. Congruence is not saying whatever you feel — Congruence holds three things together: what I feel, where the other person is, and what this occasion is. Drop any one and it is not congruence. Only yourself is venting, only the other is placating, only the occasion is being super-reasonable. Where you are: the conflict starts and both of you turn into somebody
q: Under pressure people placate, blame, go super-reasonable, or distract.
Congruence holds three things: myself, the other person, the situation.

chapters.w: Every shortage takes the same mind
chapters.dek: People short of money get called short-sighted. This piece asks whether that is a character trait or a description of the situation.
chapters.txt: They tested Indian sugarcane farmers twice: the same men before the harvest, when money was tight, and after it, when the money had arrived. The same person scored differently on the same cognitive tests. They call it the bandwidth tax — scarcity captures the mind, and what it captures is not available for anything else. So being short-sighted may be a consequence of having no money rather than the cause of it. The size of that effect has been contested since. This piece takes the direction and leaves the number alone. One bandwidth, and both shortages draw on it — This is the model's most useful move: it folds two apparently unrelated troubles into one. Doing the month's arithmetic and racing a deadline draw on the same attention, which is why the two arriving together are so much worse than either alone. Not weak will. Bandwidth pulled from both ends. The test is whether he does it when things are loose — Swapping a character explanation for a situational one needs something you can check. The sugarcane study is strong precisely because it compares one group of men at two moments, instead of comparing poor people with rich ones. The conclusion is for institutions, not for self-blame — The real use of this model is in design: take away things a stretched person has to remember, forms to fill in, decisions to make. That beats telling him to think more clearly. Turned on yourself it is a reminder, not an amnesty. Where you are: money or time is tight, and
q: Scarcity captures the mind.
Being short of money and short of time draw on one bandwidth.

chapters.w: The urgent crowds out the important
chapters.dek: The busier you get, the less the important things get done. This piece argues that is a mechanism rather than bad planning.
chapters.txt: Scarcity narrows attention, and the narrowing has a name: tunneling. The most urgent thing is lit brilliantly, and everything outside the tunnel — the check-up, the insurance, the repayment plan, the call you owe somebody — goes dark. It is not purely a loss; focus inside the tunnel genuinely rescues the emergency. The cost simply lands outside it, and lands late. Their companion idea is slack: with slack, one small accident stays one small accident. Without it, the same accident capsizes you. The efficiency inside the tunnel is real, and so is the bill — People genuinely work faster and sharper near a deadline. That speed is borrowed: it is drawn from attention that belonged outside the tunnel, and the loan comes due in weeks or in years. Run it as a normal operating mode and every quarter goes on clearing the last one. Slack is not waste, it is room to be wrong — Filling the calendar and the account to the last unit looks like maximum efficiency. It is actually setting your tolerance for error to zero. With room, one surprise stays one surprise. Without it the same surprise chains: borrowing, penalties, the real work missed. You fix a tunnel with structure, not with reminders — Reminders fail inside the tunnel, because you did not forget — at that moment you could not see it. What works is moving the important thing somewhere that needs no attention: the automatic payment, the appointment already booked, the schedule somebody else watches for you. Where you are: everything lately is firefighting,
q: The urgent is lit up; everything outside the tunnel goes dark.
Slack is not waste. It is room to be wrong.

chapters.w: Trade options away for credibility
chapters.dek: Game theory says more options are better. This is about the case where Schelling proved the opposite.
chapters.txt: The Strategy of Conflict sets up a proposition against instinct: the power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself. In bargaining, tying yourself to a position and burning the way back can win. The mechanism is credibility. You say you will never concede, and what the other side reads is not your tone but whether you still can. Anyone holding a concession in reserve has his threats discounted. His extreme case is the game of chicken: the driver who pulls the steering wheel off and throws it out of the window, in full view, wins. Credibility comes from cannot, not from will not — I do not want to concede is a preference and can change at any moment. I cannot concede is a fact the other side has to plan around. A strong commitment therefore converts preference into structure: a public statement, a clause, an agent with no authority to vary. Each welds will not into cannot. Whoever binds first sets the problem — While both sides can still move, bargaining is a two-way pull. The moment one side locks itself irreversibly, the whole remaining room to adjust belongs to the other, who either crashes or goes around. The order of commitment is therefore a weapon in its own right. Bind the wrong hand and it stays bound — The cost is written into the principle: credibility comes from irreversibility, so a mistake cannot be walked back. Two checks before using it. Is this position worth all of your flexibility, and might they prefer
q: The power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself.
In bargaining, weakness is often strength.

chapters.w: Meeting without being able to talk
chapters.dek: Two people are lost in New York and cannot call each other. This is about why most of them pick the same spot.
chapters.txt: Schelling ran a famous informal experiment. You have to meet someone in New York. Neither of you was told where or when, and you cannot communicate. Where do you go, and at what hour? The answers clustered hard: the information booth at Grand Central, at noon. Nothing makes that place better on any logical test. It wins on prominence, because everybody guesses that everybody else will guess it. Schelling called such places focal points: when people cannot communicate, they converge on the place each expects the other to expect. The force is not in being reasonable. It is in everyone knowing that everyone knows. Coordination runs on shared prominence, not optimality — When several parties must line up without enough communication, the winner is not the best option but the most visible and the most easily guessed at by everyone else: round numbers, precedent, last time's place, first on the list. Designing a default means looking for the point everyone would blindly point to. Focal points are the hidden floor of a negotiation — Where does haggling actually land? Often on a focal point: split it down the middle, a round price, last year's terms. Once you move off the focal point every particular number needs a reason, and reasons are a new battlefield. Controlling a negotiation is sometimes just placing that point in advance. A convention is valuable because it is focal — Plenty of conventions are not defensible on their merits, and they are still the point everyone knows everyone knows. Abolish one without supplying a new focal
q: When people cannot communicate, they converge on what each expects the other to expect.
A focal point wins on prominence, not on merit.

chapters.n: Time is the one cost you cannot earn back
chapters.w: Price things in hours before you price them in money
chapters.dek: The same man haggles over a small bill and gives away a whole evening without a thought. Where the arithmetic goes wrong.
chapters.txt: The essay has one argument. It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it. He is savage about the busy — men occupied with everybody's affairs but their own, who find at the end that they spent the whole of life getting ready to live. And he points at an asymmetry: people guard money down to the last coin and hand out their time to anyone who asks. Money lost can be earned again. His conclusion is not gloomy: life is long enough, if you know how to use it. Convert the cost from money into hours — The question to ask of a commitment is not what it costs but how many of your hours it takes, and where those hours would otherwise have gone. Run the conversion and a mass of apparently free consumption shows up: the free meeting, the small favour, the thing you had to attend. The most expensive waste is living on someone else's agenda — His busy men are not idle. They are the most industrious people in the book, and their time is full of other people's business, every item of it with a good reason. That is exactly the danger: no single item looks refusable, and the sum of them is a life. You do not have to be ready in order to begin — His sharpest observation is that people postpone living: after the promotion, once the children are grown, in retirement. The future is the least reliable asset there is.
q: Life, if you know how to use it, is long.
You live as if you were destined to live for ever.

chapters.n: Anger has a gate, and it is the second step
chapters.w: You cannot stop the impression. You can withhold the assent
chapters.dek: Anger looks like a single explosion. It is three movements, and exactly one of them is available to you.
chapters.txt: He takes anger apart into three movements. An impression arrives on its own: that was an insult. Then you assent to it: yes, an insult it was. Only then comes the decision to hit back. The first is reflex and cannot be stopped; by the third you are already moving. The middle one is the only place reason can get in. So the training is not to bottle the heat, it is to withhold the stamp: refuse to sign and the chain comes apart. Certain of the wise men, he notes, have claimed that anger is temporary madness. His own prescription is duller. The greatest remedy for anger is delay. Only the assent is catchable — The racing heart and the blood in the face are physiology. They cannot be suppressed and do not need to be. The choice arrives a second later: do I certify this as malice aimed at me? A great many insults are clumsiness, exhaustion, or somebody with no attention to spare. Delay is the plainest technique and the best one — His advice is to push the response out — to tomorrow, or to the far side of a walk. Not because time solves anything, but because the assent passes most easily at the peak. Once the tide goes out, the same event weighs less on its own. Not being angry is not the same as not acting — The method gets read as swallowing it. What he wants is the handling separated from the heat: hold people to account, draw the line, end the
q: The greatest remedy for anger is delay.
Certain of the wise men have claimed that anger is temporary madness.

chapters.w: Prove you mean it before you ask
chapters.dek: The new code was already drafted and he went and moved a piece of timber first. This is about what the timber solved.
chapters.txt: The laws were written and not yet published, and he was afraid the people would not believe them. He had a pole thirty feet long set up at the south gate of the capital and offered ten pieces of gold to anyone who would carry it to the north gate. Nobody moved; they thought it strange. He raised it to fifty. One man carried it across and was handed fifty on the spot — to make clear that there was no deception. Then the laws were published. The act had nothing to do with their content. A rule takes effect only once it is believed — A rule nobody expects to be enforced does not exist. So the first spending on a new system should not go on explaining the content; it should go on one small, certain thing you can deliver immediately. Prove delivery first, argue content second. The reward has to be unreasonable — At ten nobody moved; at fifty someone tried. He was not economising, he was manufacturing a signal impossible to ignore. The stranger the price, the further it travels and the longer it is remembered. On this particular job, proportionate is ineffective. Credit has to be paid in advance — He delivered before he had a single achievement to point at. The order cannot be reversed: you cannot say that once the reforms work people will naturally trust them. A system's credit must exist before it starts asking anyone to pay, or the first demand is met at a discount. Where you are: you are
q: They thought it strange and nobody dared move it.
He paid the fifty on the spot, to show there was no deception.

chapters.n: The law does not bend for rank
chapters.w: The first exception is the end of it
chapters.dek: A year into the new code the crown prince broke it. This is about how that one hour set the strength of the system for a decade.
chapters.txt: A year in, thousands of Qin subjects came to the capital to say the new laws were unworkable. Just then the crown prince broke one. When the law is not carried out, it is because those above break it, Shang Yang said. The heir could not be punished, so his tutor Prince Qian was, and his other tutor Gongsun Jia was branded. The next day the people of Qin obeyed. Ten years on, nothing dropped on the road was picked up and there were no bandits in the hills. The first exception is the end of it — A system's strength is not set by its text but by what happens to the first person important enough to test it. Let one through and everyone immediately learns that the real rule is who you are. After that, restating it changes nothing. If you cannot touch him, touch the man beside him — He did not go at the heir directly; he took the tutors. That is a workable compromise: the fact that the law acts is preserved, and a head-on collision nobody could survive is avoided. If you cannot enforce it fully, enforce it where everyone can see. A real system eventually catches its author — Shang Yang was finally trapped and killed by the code he wrote. That is not irony, it is the proof. A set of rules that binds everyone except the designer is still personal rule wearing a different word. A real one will one day stop you. Where you are: the first person to break
q: When the law is not carried out, those above have broken it.
One punishment means no grades of punishment, from ministers to commoners.

chapters.n: Once Born, No Longer Open to Debate
chapters.w: The Temple of Earth and I
chapters.dek: Whether to keep asking why this happened to you. Which questions Shi Tiesheng closed during fifteen years in a park.
chapters.txt: His legs stopped working at twenty-one. For fifteen years after that he wheeled himself almost daily into the old Temple of Earth park near his home and sat there. He says he was working on three things: whether to die, why to live, and why write. The first one he settled took years: once a person has been born, that is no longer a question open to debate. Nobody chooses to arrive, so it is not yours to rule on. With that off the list, the other two finally had somewhere to sit. Some questions are closed, not answered — Why me has no answer and needs none, because it is only a fact. It took him years to concede that: this one is not solved, it is crossed off the list. Once it is crossed off, the strength goes to questions that have answers. Sit down first, rally later — He did not go looking for a way forward. He sat in one place for years. The sitting is not passivity; it is time given to letting the worst layer of feeling finish. People who rally early have not finished, and they collapse a second time later on. The park was not scenery, it was somewhere he went back to — What he stresses is the daily part: the same place, fifteen years of it. A person who has come apart needs one coordinate that does not move. It solves nothing at all. It is there every day, and that turns out to be enough. Where you are: something
q: Why me is not solved. It is crossed off the list.
Rally too early and the feeling comes back for a second collapse.

chapters.n: Being Ill Is the Job; Writing Is the Sideline
chapters.w: Put the illness in first position
chapters.dek: How to lay out a day around a long illness. What Shi Tiesheng meant by calling illness his profession, and how to use it.
chapters.txt: From 1998 he had kidney failure: dialysis three times a week, four hours at a time, and a day afterwards with nothing left in him. The book he wrote in those years was written in the gaps between sessions, and the title says so. In it he puts the arrangement plainly: being ill is my profession; writing is what I do on the side. Not a joke about himself. A working order. Once the order is admitted, there is no need to be angry every evening about how little got written, and the few usable hours all get used. Illness goes first so the rest of the time can work — Anyone who refuses to admit the illness is the main job spends each day competing with it for time, loses, and then spends what is left in resentment. He reversed it. Give the illness every hour it demands first; what remains is genuinely yours, with no minute lost to anger. A book can be written in the gaps — Two or three hours between sessions will not hold a novel, so he wrote fragments instead, one piece at a time. The form followed the time available rather than waiting for a clear stretch. Clear stretches were not coming back, and waiting for them is giving up. On the side does not mean carelessly — He calls the writing a sideline, and that book took four years. On the side describes the ranking, not the standard: behind the illness, and every paragraph written properly. Admitting that your strength is limited
q: Give the illness its hours first; what is left is yours.
The clear stretches are not coming back. Waiting is giving up.

chapters.n: Death Is a Festival That Will Certainly Arrive
chapters.w: Nothing to hurry toward
chapters.dek: For people who lie awake until dawn thinking about dying. Why Shi Tiesheng called death a festival, and what that did for him.
chapters.txt: After several years in the park working on whether to die, the conclusion he arrived at is very calm: death is not a thing to hurry toward; death is a festival that is certain to arrive. Since it is coming anyway, there is no need to go and meet it. Once he had seen that through, he said, what is left is the question of how to live. The problem of dying had not been solved. It had been put back where it belongs: certain, therefore not to be thought about, and every day of being alive turns out to be his. Certain is what makes it possible to put down — Most people who fear death are afraid of the uncertainty: when, and how. He fixed it as something settled that requires no management. It is coming; do not rush it. Once settled, the item comes off the daily list. Thinking it through once is not thinking about it always — He did not avoid the subject. He went at it seriously and followed it to the end. Having gone to the end, there is no need to return. The version that surfaces at three in the morning is the one that was never followed through. Put death back and living has room — His conclusion is that what remains is the question of how to live. Two questions were competing for the same attention, and the one about dying produced no result while occupying the space. Put it back and the other one has a surface to lie
q: It is certainly coming, so there is no need to hurry.
The thought that returns at night was never followed through by day.

chapters.n: Why he did not kill himself
chapters.w: The letter to Ren An
chapters.dek: The convention was clear and he broke it. Years later he wrote one man a letter explaining exactly why.
chapters.txt: In 99 BC a general named Li Ling surrendered to the Xiongnu. Sima Qian, the court historian, spoke a few words in his defence, and the emperor had him imprisoned and then castrated. For a man of his rank the honourable course was to kill himself, and he did not take it. Years later, writing to Ren An, he gave the reason plainly: what he could not bear was to die with the work unexpressed and leave nothing behind. He had moved the question of staying alive off his honour and onto an unfinished thing. Swap the question about face for a question about work — The first question has no answer and sinks the longer it is held. The second has one, and the answer points at something to do. That substitution is the whole move in the letter: not that the shame was resolved, but that it was taken off the switch controlling whether he lived. The hardest sentence went to one person — The letter is addressed to Ren An, not to the world. For roughly twenty years nobody knew what he thought, and he explained himself to no one else. A thing you cannot say does not have to be said to everyone. Said properly once, it stops being held in. He did not wait to stop hurting — The letter is explicit that the shame never left: every time he thinks of it, he writes, the sweat soaks through his robe. He finished the history carrying that, not after curing it. Waiting until it no
q: Every time I think of this shame, the sweat soaks my robe.
A death may be heavier than Mount Tai or lighter than a feather.

chapters.n: Those books were all written at the worst time
chapters.w: King Wen was in captivity when he expanded the Changes
chapters.dek: One paragraph of the letter is almost entirely a list of names. What the names have in common is not talent.
chapters.txt: The passage runs almost as a roll call: King Wen was in captivity when he expanded the Book of Changes; Confucius was in distress when he made the Spring and Autumn Annals; Qu Yuan was banished and wrote the Li Sao; Zuo Qiuming lost his sight and there is the Guoyu; Sun Bin lost his feet and set out his military methods. Seven or eight of them in one breath. He calls this writing pressed out by frustration, not spare capacity in good times. Then he puts his own name at the end of the list. Find yourself a row of precedents first — While someone believes nobody has ever had it this bad, no argument gets through. His first move is not reasoning but assembling a line of people whose situation resembled his and who went on to make something. The list itself is the remedy. What was taken away is often why they could sit down — King Wen had time because he was locked up. Sun Bin could concentrate because he could no longer campaign. Nothing good is being claimed about suffering. The things stripped away, the dinners, the promotions, the standing, were what had been occupying the hours. Frustration is fuel, not mood — What he means is not venting. It is taking the sense of injustice and burning it inside one long piece of work. The same charge aimed at people becomes resentment; aimed at a task it becomes output. Same fuel, different direction, entirely different result. Where you are: you are being squeezed out,
q: King Wen was in captivity when he expanded the Book of Changes.
Not spare capacity in good times. Pressed out in bad ones.

chapters.n: Staying alive takes one unfinished thing
chapters.w: To complete the words of one school
chapters.dek: The task he set himself was absurdly large. That size is doing work, and so is the fact that he did not choose it.
chapters.txt: His father, dying, handed him the history, and he knelt and wept and agreed. In the letter he states the scale without flinching: to examine the boundary between heaven and man, to penetrate the changes of past and present, to complete the words of one school. Not to record a few events. To set in order everything from the Yellow Emperor to his own day. After the mutilation this is what held him up, and he says so directly: with the book finished, ten thousand deaths would bring no regret. Big enough to be worth it, small enough to touch today — The words of one school is the far end. The daily end is copying a passage, checking a date, drafting one life. Worth dying for at one end, advanceable by a line at the other. With only the far end people spin; with only the near end they run out. Handed to you beats thought up by you — This was not a meaning he constructed for himself. It was a charge from a dying father. An obligation received from another person still stands on the days you do not want to be alive, because it does not depend on your current state. Self-made meaning moves with the mood. Only I can finish it is the load-bearing condition — The archives were in his keeping, his father's notes were in his keeping, the chronological frame was in his head. Nobody else could have produced that book. The irreplaceability is not vanity, it is fact, and it is what
q: To complete the words of one school.
Worth dying for at one end, a line at the other.

chapters.n: A thousand li in eight days
chapters.w: Their schedule is built on your procedure
chapters.dek: Your opponent has your arrival time worked out precisely. What he got wrong is not the distance but whether you keep to the rules.
chapters.txt: In 227 Meng Da was plotting at Xincheng to leave Wei and go back to Shu. He had done the arithmetic in a letter to Zhuge Liang. Wancheng is eight hundred li from Luoyang and twelve hundred from me; when Sima Yi hears, he must first memorialise the throne and wait for a reply, and that is a month, and by then my walls will be finished. Sima Yi did not memorialise. He marched at once and was under the walls in eight days. Meng Da's next letter is stunned: I raised my standard eight days ago and the army is already here. Sixteen days later the city fell. Their timetable is a list of your openings — Every item in Meng Da's arithmetic was right. The single error was assuming the other man would complete the procedure. Any plan resting on he must finish this before he can do that is writing your opponent's choreography for him, and he is free to decline to dance. Acting before reporting has a price — Marching without a memorial exceeded his authority and he would answer for it afterwards. His justification was arithmetic: spending a month of supply against a year of preparation only makes sense if it is fast. The value of speed has to cover the cost of breaking the rule, or it is recklessness. Timing matters more than strength — His reading before marching was that Meng Da had no credit with anyone, that this was the moment of mutual suspicion, and that he should be forced to a
q: He did not report. He was under the walls in eight days.
A month of supply against a year of it. Only speed justifies it.

chapters.n: Waiting for the moment that will not repeat
chapters.w: Wait until they stop watching
chapters.dek: How far do you have to take feigned weakness before it works? This is about the moment the porridge went down his chest.
chapters.txt: With Cao Shuang in power, Sima Yi pleaded illness and stayed out of affairs for ten years. Cao Shuang was still uneasy and sent Li Sheng to look in on him. Sima Yi had two maids hold him up, pointed at his mouth to say he was thirsty, and could not hold the cup when the porridge came: it ran out and soaked his chest. Li Sheng said he was leaving for Jingzhou; Sima Yi kept hearing Bingzhou and repeating the mistake. Li Sheng reported back that the man was a breathing corpse. At the new year the Cao brothers left Luoyang, and he shut the gates that day. Feign weakness until the watching stops — Half-hearted quietness achieves nothing, because they keep an eye on you anyway. To get the surveillance genuinely withdrawn, the display has to reach the point where watching any further looks like a waste. Porridge down the front of a robe exists to cross exactly that line. What you wait for is a structural gap — He was not waiting on a mood but on one specific condition: the Cao brothers out of Luoyang on the same day, the centre of power and the centre of force both gone at once. Windows like that are recognised, not made. The point of the patience is to still be there when one appears. When it comes, finish it in one move — Ten years of nothing, and when he moved there was no probe and no phasing: the gates that day, the armoury, the guard. A window
q: It ran out of the cup and soaked his chest.
A breathing corpse, they reported. Past worrying about.

chapters.w: Discipline handed to the system
chapters.dek: The best-returning fund on record forbids its brilliant people from improvising. This piece asks who that rule is actually protecting against.
chapters.txt: Medallion has compounded at better than thirty-nine per cent a year after fees for decades, and Simons described the method in one rule. If you're going to trade using models, you just slavishly use the models; you do whatever the hell it says, no matter how smart or dumb you think it is. The reason is mechanical. Allow one override and you can never again say whether a loss belonged to the model or to the person, so the system stops improving. And the urge to override peaks exactly when the model most needs leaving alone. One override and attribution is dead — Improvement depends on clean attribution: was this loss the model or the execution? The moment a person intervenes the two are inseparable, every loss can be blamed on the other party, and nothing gets changed. The rule's real job is protecting traceability. Write the rule when calm, run it when frightened — The urge to intervene scales with how extreme things get, and extreme is precisely when the system most needs to be trusted. So the authority has to be fixed in advance: what lets a person touch it — a code error, corrupted data — and what never does. People move out of execution and into improvement — This division of labour is not an insult to judgement, it is a promotion for it. Instead of a thousand decisions taken while emotional, you make one change to the model that alters a thousand decisions. The leverage sits in the system, not in the seat. Where you
q: Slavishly use the model, however smart or dumb it looks today.
Override it once and you never learn what actually failed.

chapters.w: He published his own principles
chapters.dek: A man who made his fortune out of algorithms summed up a career in five principles. Not one of them is about mathematics.
chapters.txt: In 2010 Simons went back to MIT and compressed a career into a short list. Work with the smartest people you can find, ideally smarter than you are. Be guided by beauty — he said it applies not only to theorems but to a company that runs well or a problem solved elegantly, and that following it rarely goes wrong. Don't give up easily: the paper he wrote with Chern took years. And the last one he refused to dress up. Hope for good luck. The room laughed. He said he meant it. Hiring above yourself is a rule, not a pose — The first teams he built after leaving academia were mathematicians, astronomers and speech-recognition scientists, none of whom knew finance. He was betting on raw problem-solving power, not domain experience. The rule has a hard test: if you are always the sharpest person present, you are not following it. Beauty is compressed experience — Be guided by beauty sounds mystical and works as a fast classifier. After years in a field, a solution that is spare and well-jointed registers as beautiful, and one patched on top of patches registers as wrong, before the argument is finished. The signal is not proof. It says where to dig. Putting luck on the list is honest and also strategic — Admitting how much was luck stops you filing a random success under personal genius. The outward consequence is that if luck matters you should enlarge the surface you expose to it: more attempts, more years still in the game, more time
q: Be guided by beauty.
Work with the smartest people you can find, ideally smarter than you.

chapters.w: The whole margin is that thin
chapters.dek: The poster says he knew that he knew nothing. This page is about the narrower and far more useful thing he said.
chapters.txt: A friend asked the oracle at Delphi whether anybody was wiser than Socrates, and was told nobody was. Socrates did not believe it, so he went out to test it: politicians, poets, craftsmen, one after another, questioning each. The result came back the same every time. They supposed they knew things they did not. I do not think I know what I do not know, he says, and that thin margin is the whole of his advantage. He kept questioning until Athens executed him for it. His response to good news was to go and test it — He was handed a judgement flattering to himself and his first move was to look for a counter-example rather than to accept it. The habit is independent of content: the more agreeable a conclusion, the earlier you should go looking for what would break it. Competence in one place leaks into confidence everywhere — He found the craftsmen genuinely expert, and precisely because of it convinced they were wise about the greatest matters too. Somebody whose judgement has been repeatedly validated in one domain is the least able to say I do not know in another. Examination is a procedure, not a posture — His examining had a fixed shape: make the other person define the term they are using, then test that definition against concrete cases. Modesty can be performed. A procedure produces something every time, either a definition that holds or a gap that opens. Where you are: about to give a confident verdict outside the field you are good
q: I do not think I know what I do not know.
The unexamined life is not worth living.

chapters.w: No answers, only delivery
chapters.dek: His mother delivered babies and he said he had inherited the trade. This page is about why he withheld answers.
chapters.txt: In the Theaetetus he explains his own method outright. My art of midwifery is in general like theirs, except that my patients are men, and my concern is with the soul in travail rather than the body. The god compels him to act as midwife and never allows him to bring forth. The young men who come to him seem to know nothing at first and later produce a great deal, all of it found in themselves. He keeps the other half of the craft too: telling a real child from a wind-egg, and disposing of the false one. A given answer has no roots — Tell somebody the conclusion and they hold a sentence they can repeat. Bring them to it by questions and they hold a route they walked. The first gets dropped at the first counter-example. The second gets defended, because it is theirs. Delivery is slower and harder than handing it over — The answer takes ten seconds; questioning somebody into producing it can take an hour. The slowness buys a filter. Only what is already forming in them can be delivered, and if nothing comes, telling them would not have helped either. The false one has to be removed on the spot — The second half of the craft is judgement. What gets produced is not automatically true, so he tests his interlocutor's own conclusions against counter-examples and throws out what fails. Delivery without inspection manufactures confident error. Where you are: you can see the answer and are about to say it. Ask first: has
q: My art of midwifery is in general like theirs.
They have never learned anything from me.

chapters.w: Perception rewrites the thing
chapters.dek: Textbooks say prices reflect fundamentals. This piece asks why Soros says the arrow runs both ways, and how that loop manufactures a bubble.
chapters.txt: The Alchemy of Finance turns on a two-way arrow. Market prices always distort the underlying fundamentals — and the distorted price then changes the fundamentals it was supposed to be reflecting. The mechanism is concrete. The share price rises, so the company raises money at a better valuation, acquires more cheaply, hires more easily, and the results genuinely improve, which confirms the rise. The participants' bias has entered reality through the price. Markets are not forecasting the future so much as helping to make the one they forecast. First check whether the loop is connected — Reflexivity is not everywhere. Whether price can rewrite the fundamentals depends on the pipe: funding, hiring, customer confidence. Where the pipe is wide — finance, property, platforms — trends make themselves true. Where it is narrow, a price move does not improve the product. A self-feeding error can outlast you — If perception can manufacture reality for a while, then the market is wrong is not by itself a reason to trade against it. Mispricing feeds itself through the loop and can stay funded longer than your margin lasts. Soros often rode the thing and watched for the leak. The turn comes when the loop bites back — Self-reinforcement always has a limit: high prices start crushing buyers, high valuations start forcing fraud, expansion starts burning through the cash. The point where positive feedback becomes negative is the trend's expiry date. Watch the sign of the effect, not the level of the price. Where you are: you have decided something is overvalued and you
q: Market prices always distort the underlying fundamentals.
Markets can influence the events that they anticipate.

chapters.w: Not right or wrong, but how much
chapters.dek: A man famous for enormous bets credits his survival to admitting mistakes. This piece asks why those two things are not in conflict.
chapters.txt: His summary of himself is unexpectedly humble. I'm only rich because I know when I'm wrong. I basically have survived by recognizing my mistakes. Beside it sits the line traders keep on their desks: what matters is not whether you are right or wrong, but how much you make when you are right and how much you lose when you are wrong. Together they are a system. The judgement may be wrong often, and his frequently was, as long as wrong is recognised fast and cut small, and right is backed heavily. Hit rate and payoff are two different accounts — Most people optimise the hit rate, wanting every call to come good, which leaves them too timid to size up and too invested to admit an error. This system optimises payoff. The precondition is moving your self-worth off being right and onto the shape of the wins and losses. Admitting error needs a mechanism, not a mood — He said a backache told him a position was wrong. Underneath the mysticism is a real point: recognition cannot depend on your reasoning at the time, because a trapped judgement is the least trustworthy thing you own. Write the signs down in advance and act on them without debate. Small when wrong is what makes big when right possible — The nerve behind an enormous position does not come from courage. It comes from being certain you can get out fast. Loose stops force small bets, so the rare good opportunity arrives and you cannot fill it. Small losses are the
q: I'm only rich because I know when I'm wrong.
There is no shame in being wrong, only in failing to correct our mistakes.

chapters.w: Institutions follow costs
chapters.dek: This book explains a thousand years of institutions without ideas and without great men. One variable does the whole job.
chapters.txt: Davidson and Rees-Mogg build a frame as cold as physics: what shapes history most is the cost of using force and the cost of defending against it. Armour and stone made defence expensive and effective, so power broke into pieces and Europe went feudal. Gunpowder made castles pointless, returns to scale went up, and power gathered into nation-states the size that could pay for artillery. Run the same logic forward and you get their prediction: information technology is changing the payoff to violence. When the most valuable thing a person owns moves at the speed of light, there is less and less for force to seize. Read the cost structure before you read the creed — The reigning ideas of an age are often the manual written afterwards for that age's arrangement of force. Feudal loyalty and national patriotism each supplied a story for whatever protection was cheapest at the time. Treat ideas as the driver and you are permanently one step behind. How seizable an asset is decides who it obeys — Land can be taken and a factory cannot be moved, so wealth in the agrarian and industrial ages had to pay tax to whoever held the guns. Knowledge, code and relationships can be neither seized nor held, which hands their owner a bargaining position for the first time. When returns to scale flip, the right size flips too — In the gunpowder era force paid better the more of it you had, so states grew. In the information era the cost of defence collapses — encryption, distribution
q: What shapes history most is the cost of using and resisting violence.
Gunpowder ended the armoured knight. Information technology ends something else.

chapters.w: Jurisdictions start competing
chapters.dek: Written in 1997, the book predicts governments will have to compete. This is the chain that gets them there, and who pays.
chapters.txt: Written in 1997, the chapter reads like a memoir. Digital cash will appear, outside the reach of any government's printing press. Work will come loose from place, so the most productive people can create wealth anywhere. Then the chain closes: once both the money and the people can move, leaving stops being a threat and becomes a Tuesday. Governments then have to bid for residents the way a company bids for customers, with tax rates, courts and services as the quotation. The citizen is turning into a customer. The cold part of the argument is who is left: those who cannot move and depend on what redistribution pays. The right to leave is the hardest card at the table — The mechanism under the whole book is exit beating voice. When the cost of walking away is low enough, you no longer have to persuade anyone to improve; the possibility of leaving does the arguing. So the first move in a personal strategy is making income and assets portable. Run due diligence on a jurisdiction like a supplier — If the citizen is a customer, then where you live, where you incorporate and where you pay tax are three separable contracts, each with a price and a service level. Most people take the place they were born as the default on all three and have never once compared. The predictions came true unevenly — Digital cash and remote work arrived. What the authors underrated was the staying power of the nation-state: identity, welfare and safety are needs nobody can pack
q: Digital cash will appear, beyond the reach of any government's printing press.
The information age divides people into those who can move and those who cannot.

chapters.w: Buying what the ledger cannot hold
chapters.dek: The man sent to collect the debts burned the contracts instead. This is about how that apparently pure loss was finally settled.
chapters.txt: Lord Mengchang sent Feng Xuan to Xue to collect debts, and asked before he left what he should buy with the proceeds. Whatever the house is short of, he was told. At Xue, Feng Xuan called the people together, checked the bonds against them, then announced a pardon in his lord's name and burned every contract. The people cheered. Asked what he had bought, he said righteousness, since the house lacked nothing else. Lord Mengchang was displeased. A year later, out of office and back at Xue, he was met a hundred li out by the whole population. Today, he said, I see what you bought for me. Some assets are not on the books — A debt is a measurable asset and goodwill is not. What Feng Xuan performed was a conversion: a receivable most of which was never coming back, exchanged for something carried at zero and useful in exactly one kind of moment. Whether the trade was right depends on whether you counted that moment. You do not choose when it pays out — He was displeased on the spot and understood a year later. Spending of this kind shares a shape: the cost is now and certain, the return is later and uncertain, and the trigger is usually bad news about you. Which is exactly why it is the first line cut. Feng Xuan did not ask permission — He acted and reported afterwards, which from another angle is exceeding his authority. He could do it because the brief he was given was extremely wide: buy
q: I bought you righteousness. Your house lacked nothing else.
Today I see what you bought for me.

chapters.w: Three people praise you, three motives
chapters.dek: Wife, concubine and guest all said he was the handsomer man. This is about the three different things he heard in one answer.
chapters.txt: Zou Ji asked his wife whether he or Xu Gong of the northern city was the better looking. Far handsomer, she said. His concubine said Xu Gong was not his equal. The next day a guest said the same. Then Xu Gong came in person, and Zou Ji judged himself the lesser man. Lying awake he worked it out: my wife praises me because she favours me, my concubine because she fears me, my guest because he wants something. He told the king of Qi, then applied it to a kingdom of people who favour, fear or want. Seen this way, your majesty is very thoroughly screened. One compliment, three different sources — Partiality, fear, want: three motives producing wording that is word for word identical, so the sentence itself cannot tell them apart. The only way to sort them is the structure of the relationship. What someone stands to gain from you decides what he says to you. The higher you sit, the fuller the set — Zou Ji's inference is the hard part. He had three people and the king had a kingdom. Every step up adds another cohort with a reason to praise you and removes people willing to say the hard thing. The screening grows with the position, with nobody deceiving anybody. He calibrated against Xu Gong — He worked it out because Xu Gong actually turned up and gave him a reference point uncontaminated by any relationship. Without that external ruler, three people agreeing is the whole body of evidence. Breaking the screen is not
q: My wife favours me, my concubine fears me, my guest wants something.
Seen this way, the king is very thoroughly screened.

chapters.n: No wind, no rain, no sun
chapters.w: Switching off the scoring
chapters.dek: Everyone else on the road was miserable. He was not. What exactly did he switch off in that moment?
chapters.txt: In 1082 Su Shi — a Song poet two years into exile, recently released from a prison that nearly killed him — was caught in rain on a country road. The servant with the rain gear had gone ahead. Everyone was wretched; he wasn't. When it stopped he wrote a short poem. It ends by looking back at the road he had just walked: there had been no wind, no rain, and no sun either. Wretched is a verdict, not a fact — Same rain, same road. The difference isn't who got wet. It's who filed the afternoon under 'this is going badly.' Misery needs a scoring system to exist. Switch that off and what's left is water hitting you. Why not walk slowly — The rain gear is gone. Walking faster gets you marginally less wet and costs you the walk. His line isn't bravado; it's arithmetic: don't spend more of yourself accelerating through the part you can't change. The last line is the hard one — 'No wind, no rain, no sun' doesn't claim it never rained. It says that from far enough along the road, neither the storm nor the sun is an event. That view is only true afterwards — which is why it's worth borrowing early. Where you are: something bad is settled and you keep replaying it. Ask first: is the pain the thing itself, or the frame I keep putting around it? Where it goes wrong: reading this as permission not to deal with the problem, or using 'this too shall pass' to
q: Don't listen to the rain in the leaves. Walk on, and hum.
Looking back at that bleak road — no wind, no rain, no sun.

chapters.w: Doing real work where you were sent to rot
chapters.dek: Asked at the end of his life to name what he'd accomplished, he named three places he'd been banished to. Why those?
chapters.txt: A year before he died, Su Shi saw a portrait of himself in a temple and wrote a few lines under it. He had been a Hanlin academician and a minister of rites. He listed none of that. Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou — his three places of exile, each further from the capital than the last, the third on a tropical island then considered the edge of the world. Treat the exile as a term in office — Sent somewhere with no resources and no future, most people wait it out. He treated each posting as a term: what does this place most lack, and what can I leave behind. Rank sets your authority, not whether you work. Leave things somebody can point at — A lake dredged and a causeway built. A society to stop infant drowning. A public clinic. A school on an island that had never produced a scholar. Abstract achievements evaporate when the scoring changes; objects stay. He set the measure himself — By the official ledger his career was the titles. By listing three places of banishment he announced that the ruler measuring his life was in his own hand. That isn't consolation. It's taking the scorekeeping back. Where you are: you've been put somewhere with no resources and no prospects. Ask first: what does this place most lack right now, and what could I leave behind that someone could point at? Where it goes wrong: treating endurance as a strategy; scoring yourself in titles instead of finished things.
q: Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou.
While I am here, the water will not take this city.

chapters.w: Treating a person as a person
chapters.dek: A man whose enemies nearly had him executed said he could see no bad people anywhere. This is not naivety.
chapters.txt: Su Shi was jailed over lines from his own poems and came close to execution. For twenty years afterwards, as two factions traded power, he was demoted again and again — the last time to a tropical island. He opposed the reformers' new laws, then opposed the conservatives when they scrapped every one of them. Neither side could keep him. Late in life he told his brother: I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar. I see no bad people. Refusing to sort people into sides — Faction logic labels the person first and lets the label decide every interaction after. He judged each measure on its merits and was exiled by both sides for it. Not neutrality — a refusal to use the frame. 'Bad person' is an expensive verdict — Once you decide someone is bad, your available moves collapse to guarding and fighting, and both burn enormous amounts of you. Seeing a person with their own situation and interests is what lets you work the actual disagreement. This is not the same as having no judgement — He knew exactly who was working against him, and knew his own mouth was the danger. 'No bad people' describes how he treated people, not how he assessed them. Confuse the two and you become either a pushover or a cynic. Where you are: there's history with someone, and now every contact is defensive. Ask first: if I treat him as a person with his own situation, can this specific disagreement be discussed? Where it goes wrong:
q: I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar.
I see no bad people.

chapters.w: The first thing he did when the salary stopped
chapters.dek: Exiled to Huangzhou, his salary essentially gone. The first thing he did was not write poetry.
chapters.txt: In 1080 Su Shi arrived in Huangzhou holding an empty title, barred from official business, with almost no income and twenty-odd people to feed. What he did first was unglamorous: he petitioned for an abandoned military plot east of town — fifty acres of scrub hillside, which he and his family broke themselves — and planted wheat and rice, dug a well, built a house. 'East Slope' is not a poetic sobriquet. It's the name of the field. The poems came after the ground did. Solve eating before you solve meaning — When income stops, the easiest thing to do is work out what this means about you. His order was the reverse: get this month and next year fed, and put the rest later. Not a refusal to think — thinking done hungry doesn't count anyway. He also kept a ledger — Arriving in Huangzhou he split what money was left into thirty portions and hung them from a beam, taking one a day and saving the remainder in a tube for guests. The point isn't the amount. It's that 'how long can I last' became a number he could see. What you make gives you a place to stand — The field produced more than grain: it produced a name. He stopped being a demoted official and became the layman of East Slope. When the old position is taken, finishing one concrete thing grows a new one faster than waiting to be recognised again. Where you are: the income has stopped, or is about to, and you're circling
q: Meaning arrived at while hungry mostly doesn't count.
When the old place is taken, finish one small thing.

chapters.n: The mud had to go somewhere
chapters.w: Turning the by-product into the thing
chapters.dek: Dredging a lake leaves you holding the mud. What he did with it is still there a thousand years later.
chapters.txt: By 1090 West Lake at Hangzhou was half weed and silt, and Su Shi, posted there as prefect, put twenty thousand men on clearing it. That solved one problem and created another: the spoil had to go somewhere, and carting it out of the city would have cost more than the dredging. He laid it across the water instead, as a causeway with six bridges. A walk that had taken most of a day around the shore became a short crossing. It still carries his name. The waste is only waste until you name a use — Nobody asked him to build a causeway; the job was to clear the lake. The mud became a road because he was willing to ask what else it could be, at the moment everyone else was asking where to dump it. Solve it where the work already is — He did not start a second project. The men, the boats and the spoil were already on the water — the causeway cost the difference between carting mud away and setting it down in a line. The real job came first — The causeway is what people remember, but the case he argued was for the lake: without it the farms lost their water, the canal silted, the brewing tax fell. The road was what the work left over, not the reason for it. Next time a job leaves you with something to get rid of — a half-finished draft, a dataset built for one question, a team freed up by a cancellation —
q: The spoil from the dredging is the causeway.
Everyone was asking where to dump it. He asked what it could be.

chapters.w: Stopping the defence is a decision
chapters.dek: After his own words were used to build a case against him, did he keep writing? The question is which kind he stopped.
chapters.txt: In the Crow Terrace case, Su Shi's poems were read line by line as evidence of slander against the throne. He spent over a hundred days in prison and nearly lost his life. Afterwards, in letter after letter to friends, the same sentence: I dare not write. It wasn't fear — he wrote his most famous work in those same years. What he stopped was a different thing: defending himself, arguing who was right. He kept the two clearly apart. You pay for the defence yourself — Arguing over who was right spends your hours and the other person's patience, and winning returns neither. Worse, it has no end: every reply earns another, unless somebody stops. Stopping isn't conceding. It's capping the cost. It's an action you can tell you took — 'Let it go' can't be executed — there's no way to know you've done it. 'I don't write that kind of thing anymore' can: next time your fingers move, you know what you're doing. A mood can't be kept. An action can. Know which kind stops and which continues — He stopped the defending, not the writing. The distinction matters: putting down the pen entirely is self-punishment and takes the real work with it. Only one kind should stop — the kind whose purpose is to make someone admit you were right. Where you are: you're being misread or blamed, you keep explaining, and it keeps getting worse. Ask first: is the next thing I write meant to make the facts clear, or to get someone to say
q: He stopped defending himself. He did not stop writing.
Every reply earns another, unless somebody stops.

chapters.w: How to overturn an order from above
chapters.dek: The strategy settled above him sent his force south across the river. This is how a subordinate turned a standing order around.
chapters.txt: Early in 1948 the plan from above was for Su Yu to take a hundred thousand men across the Yangtze and operate in the south. Working it through, he reached the opposite conclusion: keeping the main force in the central plains for large battles of annihilation would change more than dividing it for the crossing. On 22 January he sent a long telegram, daring to state it plainly, with his whole reasoning. The reply restated the crossing. He kept the crossing preparations running at full speed and kept recalculating, and on 18 April sent a second telegram. He was called in, and the recommendation was taken. Dissent lands when the execution is already ready — Through both rounds of argument the training, the boats and the officer assignments for the crossing never stopped. That posture separates dissent from unwillingness: I can go on your plan at any hour, and I am asking you to look at my figures once more. Refused once, come back with a finer account — The April telegram did not repeat January's position; it changed the arithmetic. How many enemy divisions a crossing would pull away, how many could be destroyed by staying, and the gap between the two. Against a settled judgement, position and feeling are worth nothing. The lever is the sum they have not done. Sign the risk over to yourself — Adoption came with a requirement: a stated result inside a set number of months, and he took it. Changing an order means the person above carried a risk for you, and
q: I venture to state my view plainly. Correct me if it is wrong.
Concentrate in the central plains and fight large battles there.

chapters.n: Turning a small plan into a large one
chapters.w: Enlarging when the opening appears
chapters.dek: The name of the campaign came from his telegram. This is about how an operation got enlarged into a decisive battle while it was running.
chapters.txt: On 24 September 1948, with the Jinan operation not yet finished, he sent a telegram recommending that the Huaihai campaign be undertaken. That is where the name comes from, and the first version was limited: destroy the enemy on the Huaiyin and Haizhou line. Once it opened the field changed. The forces at Xuzhou showed signs of a general withdrawal south. On 8 November he telegraphed again, proposing that they not be allowed back across the Yangtze but held around Xuzhou and destroyed there in stages. The small plan had become a decisive battle, and the proposal was approved. Leave an upgrade socket in the plan — The limited version was open by design: take the first step, watch the response, then decide the second. A plan's value is not in predicting the whole route but in standing at each step where a win can be widened and a stall folded up. A plan with a fixed endpoint watches openings go past. Enlarge on their movement, not on your excitement — The trigger was the sign of a withdrawal. The moment they contract, the window for destroying the main force opens and will not open twice. The legitimate reason for enlarging always comes from a new fact in the situation. The test is whether you can name the new variable. An enlargement re-prices the supply immediately — Going from the small plan to the large one shifted the balance to six hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand, and it held because the logistics behind it were scaled at the same
q: Recommending that the Huaihai campaign be undertaken.
Hold the main force around Xuzhou and destroy it in stages.

chapters.w: The work happens before the clash
chapters.dek: Everyone quotes it as bravado. Read slowly it says the opposite: by the time you are fighting, it is mostly decided.
chapters.txt: The line is four characters longer in Chinese than in any translation, and it is built as a pair: the victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards, the defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards. It is not advice about how to fight. It is a claim about when the outcome is set. The book spends its early chapters on measurement — ground, numbers, supply, weather, the character of the commander — because that is where the decision actually happens. Preparation is not the same as planning — A plan is a description of what you intend to do. Preparation is changing the conditions until the intended thing becomes easy. The first can be done at a desk in an afternoon; the second takes months and shows up as very little visible activity. If it needs courage, something upstream went wrong — Reaching for nerve is usually the sign that the conditions were not set. Sometimes there is no choice. But treating courage as the plan converts an upstream failure into a personal one, and hides the part that could have been fixed. Not starting is a move — If the conditions are not there, the strongest available action is to not begin yet. This is the hardest part to practise, because waiting looks identical to doing nothing, and only one of them has a reason. Where you are: something is coming that you are bracing for. Ask first: what would have to already be true for this to go well? Write the list, and see
q: The victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards.
The defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards.

chapters.n: Know both, and know which is harder
chapters.w: Your own numbers are the flattered ones
chapters.dek: Quoted for two thousand years, usually as a case for research. The half everybody skips is the one about yourself.
chapters.txt: The Estimates chapter is not a maxim, it is a form to fill in: five dimensions and seven comparisons — whose ruler has the way, whose commanders are abler, who has the ground and the season, whose discipline is enforced, whose troops are stronger, whose are better drilled, whose rewards and punishments are clear. Then a coldly practical conclusion: if the count comes out favourable, fight; if it does not, don't. He called it reckoning in the temple — settle it before you decide whether to go at all. Knowing is a filled-in table, not an impression — 'I have a rough sense of the competition' is not knowing. The value of a list of comparisons is that it forces out the row you cannot answer, and the row you cannot answer is usually the one that decides it. Your own side is the harder half — Their information is outside you and can be gone and found. Yours has been through several people who each had a reason to round it kindly. The order in the sentence puts them first; the difficulty runs the other way. The count has to be allowed to say no — More reckoning wins, less reckoning loses. The point of the exercise is not to find a way to win; it is that it can output 'this one should not be fought'. A process that ends in action whatever it computes is not a decision, it is a ceremony. Where you are: about to commit to something competitive on the strength of a general
q: More reckoning wins. Less reckoning loses.
Theirs is outside and findable. Yours has been through people.

chapters.n: The best fight is the one nobody has
chapters.w: Winning a hundred times is not the top of the list
chapters.dek: A hundred victories sounds like the ceiling. He says it isn't, and the reason is arithmetic rather than modesty.
chapters.txt: The chapter gives a ranked list that runs against instinct: attack the enemy's plan first, his alliances second, his army third, and his walled cities last. Each step down costs more and returns less. On sieges he is unusually specific — three months to prepare the engines, three more for the ramps, and a commander who loses patience and sends men up the walls like ants, a third of them dead and the city still standing. He calls that the disaster of assault. Winning is also spending — A hundred victories is not the height of skill; subduing the enemy without fighting is. Every win costs people, money, time and trust. The side that won five times can easily be stronger than the side that won a hundred. Plan, then alliances, then force — Attacking the plan means making their approach stop making sense on its own terms. Attacking alliances means removing the support it rests on. Neither requires contact. By the time only fighting is left, the first two were skipped or botched. The most expensive move is the one you take personally — Assault happens when there is nothing else left, or when someone cannot stand to walk away. He singles out the commander who attacks in anger. Losing a third of your strength to a wall you did not need is a decision made by a mood. Where you are: locked into a fight you expect to win. Ask first: what does winning this cost, and what would have to be true for it not to be
q: Winning a hundred battles is not the height of skill.
Every win you take spends people, money, time and trust.

chapters.n: The flank only works if the front holds
chapters.w: A clever move on its own is a donation
chapters.dek: Everyone wants the unexpected move. The chapter is mostly about the unglamorous thing it has to stand on.
chapters.txt: The Energy chapter asks why the same troops behave like a rolling log one day and a scattered crowd the next. His answer is the pairing: engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary. The orthodox is the part that meets them head on and holds; the extraordinary is what comes from the side. He insists the two convert into each other endlessly — which means today's surprise, once used, becomes tomorrow's front. Without the front, the flank hits air — The surprise works because the other side is already gripped and cannot turn. Let the front go slack and the clever move lands on nothing, with your best people stranded out in the open. A surprise used once becomes the expected thing — Any unexpected move, once used and written up, enters the other side's expectations and becomes part of the front. Planning to live for years off one trick is spending a one-time resource as if it were income. Position, not heroics — The chapter ends not on cleverness but on structure: put the rock at the top of a thousand-foot mountain and the force of it coming down is not the rock's. Seek it in the position, and do not demand it of the people. Where you are: pinning your hopes on one inventive move. Ask first: what is holding the front while that move happens, and is it actually holding? Where it goes wrong: concluding that only the basics matter — the front alone defends and never wins.
q: Engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary.
Used once, the surprise becomes the thing they expect.

chapters.n: Take the shape of what you meet
chapters.w: Avoiding the strong part is the hard half
chapters.dek: 'Be like water' became a poster. The chapter is stricter than the poster, and most of it is about what not to do.
chapters.txt: The chapter is about who is setting the terms: bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him. Strike what he must defend and he has to come. Decline the engagement and he cannot force it. Then the image everybody knows: water has no constant shape, it avoids the heights and runs to the low ground, and an army has no constant form either — it avoids what is solid and strikes what is hollow. Having no fixed shape is the point — What water resembles is not softness, it is the absence of a preset form. Its shape is decided entirely by what it meets. Which makes 'what is our style of competing' a question with a flaw built into it. Avoiding the solid part is discipline, not opportunism — The hard half is the avoiding. The places that look most worth taking, most prestigious, most expected of you are usually exactly where they are thickest. Declining them means absorbing internal pressure, which is harder than spotting the gap. Who wrote this week's calendar — Initiative is not moving first. It is that the other side has to answer at your tempo. There is a simple test: look at the week you just had and ask whether you scheduled it, or whether their moves did. Where you are: reacting to a competitor, or defending the position you are proudest of. Ask first: where are they actually thin, and what would it cost you internally to walk away from the thick part? Where it goes wrong: using it
q: Bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him.
Water has no constant shape. That is what it is being praised for.

chapters.w: The evidence peaks just before the break
chapters.dek: What conclusion does a turkey reach if it thinks statistically? This piece asks why the day with the most evidence is the day before the accident.
chapters.txt: Taleb borrows Russell's turkey to show where induction dies. Consider a turkey that is fed every day.
